Investigating the Origins of Piracy in the Aegean
Trade and Maritime Raids during the Early Bronze Age



Nadia Giagkoudaki
National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
kgiagoudaki@hotmail.com




ABSTRACT

During the Early Bronze Age II, the presence of imported raw materials, artifacts and technologies reveals an active
­exchange system and widespread maritime networks in the Aegean. Overseas contacts and the accumulation of wealth
 as the result of those practices changed the dynamics of society. Opportunities for economic benefits and social promotion
 became available, intensifying competition between those involved in maritime networks. The accumulation of wealth
 in the Aegean is usually interpreted as the result of intensive trade and gift exchange. At the same time, however, some
 scholars have argued that the distribution of exotic or valuable objects and raw materials may also have been the result of
 raiding, thus dating the origins of piracy to the Early Bronze Age II period. Other scholars dispute this view, arguing that
 there are fundamental differences that distinguish trade from raiding and warfare, and there can be no question of piracy
 in such an early period, while others accept the existence of piracy but claim that, in the absence of written sources, such
 activities cannot be documented, as their archaeological signature is weak.
This paper examines the possibility of the existence of piracy in the Early Bronze Age Aegean. For this purpose, the
­differences between piracy and war are discussed, and evidence of material culture possibly related to the phenomenon of
 piracy (e.g., ship technology and iconography, material culture and its use, settlement patterns and settlement features)
 are examined. It is argued that in such early societies there were no absolute distinctions between activities like trade,
 piracy, raids and war, and that these activities cannot be approached in a modern way of thinking. The evidence in the
 material culture may be indirect, but seems to suggest that piracy could have been practiced in the Early Bronze Age
 Aegean by the same people who participated in maritime trade and other “legal” activities.




INTRODUCTION

The Early Bronze Age (EBA) II is characterized by a burgeoning interaction in the wider Aegean region, often
called “international spirit”. This phenomenon is evidenced in the intensification of maritime activity, the
­increase in trade and exchanges, the widespread distribution of common traits of material culture across the
 Aegean and the movement of raw materials, objects and technical knowledge, mostly of Cycladic origin or
 influence, while towards the end of the period large-scale contacts were established between the Cyclades and
 Mainland Greece with the eastern Aegean and Asia Minor (e.g., Renfrew 1972, 451; Broodbank 2000, 279–83).
 Most scholars agree that the pursuit and exploitation of new metals sources led to an expansion of pre-existing
 networks of interaction, the archaeological evidence of which, apart from the presence of tin bronze in the
· 68 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



Aegean, can be seen in a new group of drinking and serving vessels with oriental characteristics (e.g., Şahoğlu
2005, 339; Day et al. 2009, 335–37; Kouka 2014, 43–4).
    These maritime activities provided opportunities for wealth accumulation, which could be acquired either
by trading or raiding. The quite large number of fortified settlements and the destruction layers found in some
of them, the presence of weapons in settlement or burial contexts and the iconography of the period that in-
cludes ships and daggers, have led many scholars to accept the important role of raids in the EBA Aegean (e.g.,
Agouridis 1997, 20; Broodbank 2000, 253; Sherratt 2000, 135; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 139–42).
    On the basis of the high maritime activity of the period and the positive correlation between trade and
piracy (see Samaras, this volume), this paper discusses the possible nature of the raids in the EBA Aegean and
attempts to investigate elements that may relate to the phenomenon of piracy during that period. Initially,
different views on piracy in the Aegean during the EBA are presented and discussed. Then, the motives of
pirate activity are explored, as derived from the possible perceptions, the iconography and the archaeological
evidence. Several aspects of the material culture of the EBA Aegean, e.g., the use of some objects and their sym-
bolisms, the changes in settlement patterns and the existence of settlements with strong defensive systems, offer
indications of potential pirate activities conducted by certain island communities.




VIEWS ON PIRACY IN THE EBA AEGEAN

Wealth accumulation in the Aegean was traditionally considered to be the result of intensive trade and/or gift
­exchange (e.g., Cherry 1981, 41–68; Cosmopoulos 1991, 155–67; Halstead and O’Shea 1992), so any influences
 or innovations observed in material culture were explained as a result of peaceful exchanges, while interpre-
 tations concerning the transfer of materials, people and technical knowledge by raiding or looting were only
 ­tentative or simply absent. At the same time, relevant studies have tended to emphasize the risks of sea travel,
  which were mainly attributed to weather conditions and the small capacity of ships of this period (e.g., ­Agouridis
  1997, 2–6; Broodbank 2000, 92–6), while the dangers from human hostile activity were ­underestimated, if not
  omitted, resulting in a somewhat one-sided approach to a complex phenomenon.
    Nevertheless, a small number of scholars has occasionally supported the possibility of pirate activity in the
EBA Aegean. Renfrew (1972, 440, 763) was probably the first to date the origins of piracy in the Aegean to the
EBA II, based on Thucydides’ claims (1.4.1) about unsafe navigation before the time of Minos due to pirates and
taking into account archaeological data, such as fortified settlements and the circulation of precious metals in
the Aegean. Renfrew’s opinion was accepted by Doumas (1988, 27–9) to explain the destruction at the end of
the Early Cycladic (EC) IIA in the northeastern Aegean and Asia Minor, and the east Aegean influences on the
material culture of the EBA IIB Aegean. He argued that “refugees-pirates”, following the familiar trade routes,
settled in major trading sites of the previous period, but also established new ones at key-points. This way, he
links trade with the conflicts and destruction that took place during this period and relates them to possible
pirate incidents. More recently new arguments have been added to the debate about the changes in the Aegean
during this period, adopting somewhat different interpretation and arguing that, beyond the movements of
people actively involved in sea trade, the spread of ideas, technical knowledge and objects may also be due to
conflicts and possible pirate activities (Yeagley 2022). Also, as discussed in more detail below, longboats of the
period have been suggested to be linked to piracy (Tzovaras 2020, 17).
    On the other hand, several scholars have presented counter-arguments to the above views that either have
to do with the existence of piracy in such an early period or with the (in)ability of the research to detect this
phenomenon. For example, Agouridis (1997, 20) argues that the archaeological footprint of piracy is similar
to that of trade, so no distinction can be made between these two activities. According to de Souza (1999, 2,
15), in periods without written sources piracy cannot be documented, as it leaves no archaeological footprint.
Moreover, it should be mentioned that Broodbank (2000, 410) denies the existence of piracy in the EBA Aegean,
N . G IAG KO U DA K I • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                          · 69 ·




not because he is opposed to the idea of raiding during this period, but on the basis of the view that piracy is an
illegal activity, so in order to exist in any place and time, there must be recognized laws and rules for sea travel.
Given the fact that it is very much unlikely that such recognized laws and rules for sea travel existed in the EBA
Aegean, essentially all that applied was the sea-law of the most powerful islanders.




RAIDS IN THE AEGEAN: PIRACY OR WAR?

Despite the varying views in the debate on piracy, it seems generally accepted that maritime raids were ­conducted
in the EBA Aegean, so what should be investigated is the exact nature and purpose of these raids. Broodbank’s
objection to the recognition of these raids as pirate activities is mainly based on researchers attempting to
characterize the distant past using modern terms, perceptions and considerations. Indeed, in the EBA Aegean
there were no recognized rules equivalent to today’s maritime laws and therefore the legality or the illegality
of an action was not perceived in the same way. However, the A.P.Pir.A. project’s research about the history
of piracy reveals that pirates rarely described their activities as piracy and usually used arguments to “justify”
and “legalize” them. Also, it was very common for an action to be characterized as piracy in order to justify the
pursuit and punishment of certain people, regardless of whether they were really pirates or not and regardless
of the existence (or lack of) laws (see more in Samaras, this volume). Therefore, for a more secure approach and
understanding of the phenomenon of piracy, it seems that the characterization of an act as piracy should be
based on the examination of its objective parameters (such as, for example, means and motives) rather than on
how it was perceived and characterized by the people involved (perpetrators or victims) or whether there were
any recognized laws about maritime activity.
    Therefore, it seems necessary to investigate the nature of the maritime raids in the Aegean Sea and whether
these raids can be classified as piracy or be included in the scope of war, as it is undeniable that every war has an
economic-pillaging dimension, both in terms of motives (i.e., to boost the economy of a community or a group)
and in terms of results, as it is customary for the victors to pillage the losers. The boundaries between war and
piracy are often blurred, but an analysis of this issue is beyond the scope of this study (see Samaras, this volume).
    However, as far as the ΕΒΑ Cyclades are concerned, on which this paper focuses, based on the general
characteristics of the period and the size and organization of its communities, it seems that the conflicts were
not large-scale organized acts with campaigns and sieges. Warfare using ships requires manpower and com-
plex social organization, and it is very costly, as many ships, weapons and people –all limited in number in the
­Cyclades during the 3rd millennium BCE (Broodbank 1989, 321, 333; 2000, 86–7)– would have had to be used.
    Moreover, since, with the exception of a few large settlements, the small communities of the EBA Cyclades
do not seem to have had a complex social and political organization, it is difficult to argue that the raids carried
out were organized and systematic and aimed at permanent results, such as the annexation of a territory or the
destruction of an economic rival. On the contrary, it is more likely that they were of small scale, carried out on
an occasional and perhaps opportunistic basis and were primarily motivated by the economic benefit of those
taking part in them. Therefore, and despite the aforementioned difficulties in distinguishing between piracy and
warfare, maritime raids in the EBA Cyclades seem to have been much closer to the characteristics of the former
than the latter.
     It should be also noted that the motive for a pirate raid may not have been only economic but also socio-po-
litical. The leaders of a community, by conducting a raid and risking themselves because of their participation
in such a dangerous action, which brought benefits to all community members, gained prestige and confirmed
and legitimized their social status within their own community. Considering the means of the period, the EBA
sea voyages were in themselves “heroic” acts, as one had to face the dangers caused by both sea and weather
conditions during travel and the resistance of the people under attack; an act could be even more “heroic”, when
the participants fought and the raiders returned with booty for the community.
· 70 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



    Therefore, it should be considered what these benefits were, both individually and collectively, i.e., how was
the community benefitting by risking the survival of its population by choosing to expose people to the dangers
of the high seas and raids? Before these motives can be explored, however, the means of navigation of the period
and whether they were suitable for raiding should be examined.




SHIP TECHNOLOGY

The information available on the EBA ships is limited and indirect, as it comes almost exclusively from the
iconography and not from the ships themselves (for the Early Helladic II shipwreck on the islet of Dokos in the
Argosaronic Gulf, see Papathanasopoulos 2003; Vichos 2003). Ship depictions appeared as early as the Final
Neolithic (FN) period, as can be seen from the rock-engravings at Strophilas on Andros (Televantou 2009, 128,
137, 139, pls. 86, 88, 96a; 2018a, 390–5, fig. 40.10) and then in the beginning of EBA at Vathy on ­Astypalaia (Vla-
chopoulos 2021, 106–9). Many ship representations have been found at these two sites, with some of them deco-
rating the main entrances of the above fortified settlements, revealing the importance of ships for these commu-
nities. During the EBA II period, ship depictions are known mainly from frying pans, most of which have been
found at the Chalandriani cemetery on Syros (Tsountas 1899, 90–2, figs. 16–22; M      ­ arthari 2010, 116), and from
rock-engravings found at Plaka on Andros (Televantou 2006, 12–14; 2018b, 58, fig. 14b), ­Chalandriani and
Kastri on Syros (Marthari 2015, 303, 307, fig. 2, pl. 3; 2019, 239, fig. 6), and Korphi t’Aroniou on Naxos (Doumas
1965, 49, 53, pls. 4, 7; see also Legaki 2016 for a discussion on the interpretations of the EC rock-­engravings).
     Thanks to the above depictions, two ship types are identified, all paddled crafts, without masts or sails. The
first ship type is the one depicted in most rock-engravings and has an almost semi-circular hull and unevenly
raised foresides, which makes it suitable for the transport of goods (cargo boat) (Tzovaras 2020, 9–11). The
second type is depicted in the frying pans and has an elongated, narrow, hydrodynamic shape and an an-
gular hull (longboat) (Basch 1991, 46–7; Tzalas 1995). The ships depicted in the rock-engravings from Korphi
­t’Aroniou fall into the same category because of the shape of the hull (Tzovaras 2020, 6–7), but are likely to be of
 smaller size, since only two oars are depicted (Broodbank 1989, 332).
    Longboats had slender hulls and shallow draught, which made them unstable. In addition, their ­technological
characteristics and the fact that they carried at least twenty-five people meant that there was limited free space.
It seems, therefore, that these ships were unsuitable for the transport of large volumes of goods (Broodbank
1989, 332–33, 336; Tzovaras 2020, 12–4). Thus, in cases of large cargoes, it was more appropriate to transport
them mainly by cargo boats, which were built for that purpose.
    Based on the above features and ethnographic parallels concerning the use of canoes with many oars,
­ roodbank (1989, 336) concluded that the initiatory use of longboats was not intended for trade but for raids
B
(see also Tzovaras 2020, 17). Moreover, due to the large number of rowers and the risks of a sea voyage, he
argued that such raids could only be conducted by large, prosperous and self-sufficient communities, which
in the Cyclades were extremely few, no more than seven or eight, according to his estimates (Broodbank 2000,
211–23). On the contrary, the numerous small Cycladic communities either could not carry out such raids, or
they banded together under the leadership and guidance of the larger ones. On their own, all they could do was
undertake small-scale sea voyages of short distances, using small ships with a crew of no more than two or three
people, as can be seen in the rock-engravings from Korphi t’Aroniou.
    Raids were carried out either from ship to ship or from ship to settlement. Ship-to-ship raids were ­probably
easier, as a single ship with two or three rowers, loaded with goods was an easy target for a longboat with
twenty-five people. Consequently, ship-to-ship raids were probably more frequent, but there were also
­
ship-to-settlement attacks despite the objective difficulties. The fatigue of a voyage followed by an attack, as
well as the supervision of sea passages from coastal settlements would have made it difficult for the attackers to
land the ship, disembark and attack a settlement, whose inhabitants were of a greater number. However, these
N . G IAG KO U DA K I • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                          · 71 ·




actions were based on ambush, so fewer people would be required to raid a settlement, damage it and leave
with spoils. Moreover, the existence of coastal fortified settlements, the layers of destruction and the weapons
found in them, including sea pebbles used as slingshot projectiles (Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 139–41), lead us
to conclude that ship-to-settlement attacks probably took place.
    In conclusion, during the FN and EBA I, when sea voyages are increasing (Papadatos and Tomkins 2013,
355, 374), cargo boats appear to serve the trading needs and are likely to continue to be used in the following
period for the same purpose. As mentioned above, during the EBA II, maritime contacts intensified, causing
an increase in wealth in the Aegean, which acted as an attraction and could be acquired either by trading or
raiding. Since trade acts as a motive force for raiding, the emergence of the longboat in the period of trade
intensification is unlikely to be coincidental. During this period, the need for the construction of a new light,
maneuverable and fast ship suitable for raids seems to have arisen. In diachronic perspective, speed and maneu-
verability are the essential features of all pirate ships (e.g., see Nakas, this volume about the pirate ships in the
Classical and Hellenistic periods).




MOTIVES FOR PIRACY

Since conditions and ships appropriate for pirate raids existed during the EBA, the question of the motives
for these raids inevitably arises. According to anthropological studies (e.g., Torres-Rouff and Costa Junqueira
2006, 60; Erdal and Erdal 2012, 78), social stress, resource constraints, and ecological problems (for example,
droughts and population decline), may lead to violent behavior such as raiding and looting. In the case of piracy
in the EBA Aegean, on which this paper is focused, the most obvious motive was the acquisition of valuable
objects and raw materials and as has already been mentioned, the enhanced social status of those who brought
them through such a “heroic” act. However, equally (or even more) valuable spoils may have been animals and
people, as they were necessary for the survival of a community, the former as a means of food and production,
the latter as a means of strengthening the human resource and reproduction through exogamy (Broodbank
2000, 86; Sherratt 2000, 135).
    In one of the rock-engravings from the Korphi t’Aroniou, for which it has been suggested that they date back
to the end of EC II or the beginning of EC III, an armed man leading an animal in a boat is depicted (Doumas
1965, 48–50; Fig. 1). Animals in ships are also represented in rock-engravings at Strophilas on Andros, which
date to the FN period (Televantou 2008, 47; 2009, 128; Fig. 2). These depictions are usually interpreted as the
movement of animals to smaller islands for grazing and/or breeding (Broodbank 1989, 332–33; 2000, 127–28;
see also Cherry 1985, 20), a practice still in use today in the Aegean (e.g., Chaniotis 1999, 191; Marketou 2023,
45).
     However, it should not be omitted that animals have always been included in pirate spoils and generally
bandit raids. At least in the case of the rock-engraving of Korphi t’Aroniou, the animal snatching seems to be
the most convincing interpretation (Sherratt 2000, 135), firstly because the man who leads the animal to the
ship is armed, which could be interpreted as either defensive or offensive, and secondly because the above
practice confirms martial skills and brings social prestige, especially in societies that are accustomed to robbery
and piracy. Such scenes could therefore be depicted as a reminder of heroic achievements, like later hunting
scenes. The movement of flocks for grazing and/or breeding is an undeniable practice, but it is part of everyday
­activities, which are essential and necessary for survival, but do not carry the same social prestige and therefore
 are less frequently depicted.
    Similarly, it should be considered that over time the most valuable pirate booty might have been people. The
history of piracy reveals that the most common motives for the capture of persons were in obtaining ransom for
their release and enslavement for exploitation or sale. These two motives are extremely difficult to decipher in
the ΕΒΑ Cyclades, but the possibility of the abduction of women for reproduction cannot be excluded (Sherratt
· 72 ·                                     T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




              Fig. 1. Rock-engraving from Korphi t’Aroniou with an armed man leading an animal to a boat (Doumas 1965, fig. 4).




                           Fig. 2. Rock-engraving from Strophilas with animals on a ship (Televantou 2009, pl. 88b).



2000, 135–36).
    The population decline was one of the most serious problems faced by EC communities, which, among
other causes, could have been attributed to infertility and the unequal ratio between men and women. To
address this, the movement of people (especially women) between communities or even between islands was
crucial, as healthy descendants were ensured by exogamy. It is reasonable to assume that exogamy was generally
consensual, by mutual agreement between families or communities. However, the forcible abduction of women
also seems possible, especially given the “heroic” context in which such actions are carried out by societies that
often accept and undertake robbery and piracy. Thus, the abduction of women may have increased significantly
in times of crisis, when the population was dramatically reduced (e.g., due to a shipwreck or disease), so that
the forcible transportation of women from another region or island for procreation was one of the few available
options for community survival.
    The potentially important role of the abduction of women and animals in the ΕΒΑ Cyclades is further
strengthened by ethnographic parallels from societies with weak or absent major state organizations and high
mortality due to wars or ways of life, in which such practices were commonplace. For example, at least in the
13th century CE, in the Chaco Canyon region of the United States, raiding for women for reproductive or labor
reasons was a well-established practice, and successful warriors were associated with polygyny (Kohler and
N . G IAG KO U DA K I • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                            · 73 ·




Fig. 3. Frying pan from Chalandriani with longboat and pubic triangle. Athens, National Archaeological Museum, inv. no. Π4974 (photo by G.E. Koronaios).



Turner 2006). In South Sudan, the traditional practices of woman abduction and cattle raiding among ethnic
groups are still in use, as women and cattle are the main source of household wealth even today (e.g., Lacey
2013; Wild et al. 2018, Mayik 2020). According to the customary laws of these societies, cattle –in addition to
the milk and meat they provide to a household– are linked to the bride-price and the practices of arranged and
forced marriage (Lacey 2013, 94–6). Consequently, cattle owning allows a man to marry, not only economically
but also symbolically. On the other hand, a woman’s social value is closely related to her procreative potential to
continue the lineage (by giving birth to boys) and to increase the family’s wealth (by giving birth to girls, who
will be exchanged for cattle and other valuable objects and goods when they reach marriageable age). Women
who are raiding trophies are even more valuable, since they are added to the workforce of the family and provide
descendants without a price being paid.
    Considering the ways and means of living, the high mortality rate and the isolation that sometimes existed
on the islands (for isolation in the EBA Cyclades, see Broodbank 2000, 191–94), there can be no doubt that for
the small and fragile EC communities the role of women was vital. The constant iconographic combination of
longboats with pubic triangles on the frying pans from Chalandriani (Fig. 3) seems to suggest the relationship
between sea voyages and women on a symbolic or even a real level (Broodbank 2000, 251–53; Mina 2010,
236), reinforcing the possibility of a link between raiding and the demographic strengthening of a community
through procreation with women imported from outside the normal community.
    Regarding the importance and the role of women in the EBA Cyclades, Sherratt (2000, 135), observing the
· 74 ·                                           T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4

passive stance of the numerous marble female figurines and the emphatic depiction of the pubic triangle and
the breasts (i.e., the predominant symbols of female fertility), argues that in the EC communities women were
treated as booty or trophies that were even moved by force in order to provide healthy descendants. This view
seems to be strengthened by the fact that some of these figurines are depicted in a state of pregnancy (see also
Broodbank 2000, 61, fig. 9a; Marangou 1990, 152, cat. no. 158; Fig. 4).
    In sharp contrast to the passive stance of the female figurines, the active stance of the few (but existing) male
figurines of the “hunter-warrior type”, with a dagger emphatically depicted (Fig. 5), may express the perceptions
and social roles of the period (Nakou 1995, 9–13; Broodbank 2000, 253). In the rare class of male figurines,
bravery and achievements are indicated, through the use of violence (dagger), in contrast to female figurines,
which are passive and emphasize the symbols of fertility. This intense contrast between the male and female
figurines probably reflects the role of the genders in EBA society. In the EC communities, high-status activities
such as sea voyages with longboats and raids were largely associated with men (Broodbank 1993, 327; 2000,
215; Sherratt 2000, 135–36), while women appear passive and mostly associated with sexuality and procre-
ation. Nevertheless, the large number of female figurines may reveal that, despite their passivity, women were
extremely valuable to the EC communities.
N . G IAG KO U DA K I • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                               · 75 ·




 Fig. 5. Drawing of a male marble figurine of the “hunter-warrior type”. London, British Museum, inv. no. 1955,0820.9 (© Trustees of the British Museum).



      Relationships between sea voyages, trade, and women, as well as manifestations of violence, may be
­suggested by the deliberate breakage of folded-arms female figurines in the Kavos “special deposit” on Keros
 ­(Androutsopoulou 2013, 47). Because of the large number of figurines found in the deposit and the deliberate
  breakage, most scholars attribute this breakage to ritual practices that took place in a funerary or religious
  context (e.g., Doumas 1972, 163; Davis 1984, 16; Renfrew 1984, 27–8; Barber 1987, 132; Sotirakopoulou 2005,
  329–30). If this is the case, the quantity of the figurines, the way they were handled, and the fact that only frag-
  ments of the abdomen, vulva and legs have been found in the depository may shed light on the way women were
  treated in religion and, by extension, in EBA society.
    The role of men and women in the ΕΒΑ society and economy, as reflected in the aforementioned aspects of
material culture, namely in the anthropomorphic figurines, the frying pans, the general presence of weapons,
and the way of using the above objects, as well as the importance and the “heroic” character of sea voyages for
island communities, suggest that exogamy and the acquisition of objects, raw materials, and animals were of
vital importance and that in order for community survival and growth everything was legitimate. In the context
of raids, therefore, woman and animal abductions were probably a common practice, and constituted a major
source of social power and prestige for the warriors-pirates who provided them to the community.
· 76 ·                                 T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



SETTLEMENT PATTERN

Major changes in the settlement patterns and the ways of living are usually considered to be a result of the
­emergence of new needs and demands. In this regard, the abandonment of coastal sites and the move to fortified
 sites away from the sea are often attributed to threats and invasions from the sea. Therefore, a brief synopsis of
 the settlement patterns of the EΒΑ Cyclades and the identification of such changes may be able to contribute
 to the debate on the phenomenon of piracy during this period (see Angelopoulou, this volume for a more
 ­comprehensive discussion on the EC settlement patterns).
     The EC I settlements appear to be scattered and short-lived (Broodbank 2000, 150–51, 154–56; ­Angelopoulou
2016–2017, 134). They were small settlements, based mainly on the agricultural economy, while their external
contacts were limited. The settlements of the EC IIA period were also small in size and duration, with a few
­exceptions of larger and more organized settlements, such as Ayia Irini on Kea (Caskey 1971, 368–72; B­ roodbank
 2000, 216–18; see also Wilson 1999, 2013), Dhaskalio on Keros (Boyd 2013, Renfrew 2013), and Skarkos on Ios
 (Marthari 1997, 2008a, 2018). The settlements of this period were mainly coastal or near the sea and at nodal
 points of sea routes, indicating the interest of their inhabitants in sea voyages. There seems to have been some
 concern for protection from sea raids, by choosing either defensible sites, as in the case of Dhaskalio, or sites
 at a short distance from the sea, as at Skarkos (Broodbank 2000, 212–21; Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 134–35).
      An even stronger concern for protection from the sea emerged in the following EC IIB period. Several
­settlements were now situated on defensible hilltops, and many of them were reinforced by strong fortification
 walls. For example, settlements like Kastri on Syros (Marthari 1998, 2017), Panormos on Naxos (Angelopoulou
 2014, 67–88), Kynthos on Delos (MacGillivray 1980) and Markiani on Amorgos (Marangou 2006, 81–93)
 ­indicate feelings of danger and insecurity. Kastri and Panormos were indeed destroyed and then abandoned,
  probably after a maritime raid. This change in the settlement pattern from sites near the sea to defensible sites on
  high and steep hills and with strong fortification walls, combined with the evidence of attack, destruction and
  abandonment observed in at least two settlements, are indications of the fear during this period and the violent
  raids that seem to have come from the sea.




SETTLEMENTS WITH POSSIBLE PIRATE ACTIVITY

In order to be able to recognize that a small or large part of the community of a settlement was involved (­ either
occasionally or systematically) in pirate activity, this settlement should present some or all the features identified
by the A.P.Pir.A. project: coastal and defensible sites, not easily visible but close to at least one safe harbor, nodal
point for the nearby sea routes, fortification walls, etc. (see in more detail Samaras, this volume). ­Moreover, in
settlements of this type, valuable and exotic objects are often found, the presence of which is sometimes not
adequately explained by other “legal” activities (see also Samaras 2015, 191–92).
    Settlements in naturally defensible sites, close to the sea, and with strong fortification walls have already
been witnessed in the FN period and the EBA I, as can be seen at Strophilas on Andros (Televantou 2006, 2008,
2018a) and Vathy on Astypalaia (Vlachopoulos and Angelopoulou 2019; Vlachopoulos 2021). As mentioned
above, ship rock-engravings have been found at both these sites, some of which even decorate the main gates
of the fortified settlements. It is noteworthy that in Strophilas there are over a hundred rock-engravings with
this theme, making the ship a symbol of the community and revealing its naval orientation. Several metal
objects have also been found in the same settlement, including a metal spearhead, while in Vathy there are
rock-­engravings of a unique theme with daggers, symbols of bravery and heroism indicating violent actions.
Considering that material culture is a powerful means of social display, it may be possible to accept the view that
ships transmitted messages of collective power and weapons that of individual power.
N . G IAG KO U DA K I • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                         · 77 ·




    Both the position of these two settlements, at defensible locations close to the coast and with supervision of
the sea passages, and the presence of fortifications, metal objects, as well as the themes of the rock-engravings,
indicate prosperity, seafaring, and involvement in warlike activities. So, even before EBA II, participation in sea
voyages brought wealth to the communities, but at the same time there was fear from the sea. After all, island
communities were systematically engaged in trade and sea voyages as early as the FN–EBA I period (Papadatos
and Tomkins 2013, 355, 374); therefore, it is not unlikely that banditry was practiced in the context of these
voyages, even if during this period these phenomena seem to have been sporadic and opportunistic.
    As mentioned above, the intensification of maritime contacts during EBA II may have motivated the ­increase
in pirate raids, a fact that seems to be documented by the presence of more fortified settlements. The possible
outbreak of piracy may even suggest the existence of pirate settlements, without this necessarily implying that
there were communities exclusively engaged in pirate activities.
    Kastri on Syros (Marthari 2006, 2007, 2008b) displays several characteristics usually found in pirate bases
(see also Yeagley 2022, esp. 95–7). It is a short-lived settlement, since it was inhabited only during the EC IIB
period, and is located on a high and steep hill above the sea, in a position that is extremely difficult to access.
The natural defense of the site was further reinforced by the construction of a complex fortification system, in
which the main wall had horseshoe-shaped bastions. At the same time, the site provided visual control of the sea
routes to Tenos, Andros and southern Euboea towards the north, and to Rheneia, Delos, Mykonos and Naxos
towards the south (Broodbank 2000, 243–44). In addition, bronze objects made of tin bronze have been found
at the site, which are prestige objects because of the raw material used in their manufacture, especially tin, which
is imported from the east. A metalworking workshop has also been found within the fortified settlement.
    Taking into account the fact that during the previous period Chalandriani seems to have been a community
with a sufficient number of inhabitants to man a ship, with rich graves that have yielded many metal objects,
Cycladic figurines and frying pans with ship depictions, it turns out that the community actively participated
in sea voyages and perhaps flourished because of them (Broodbank 1989, 324–25; Hekman 2003, 17; Marthari
2010, 116). During the following period, the settlement of Chalandriani was abandoned, and a new one was
founded on the adjacent defensible hill of Kastri with the above-mentioned characteristics.
    Therefore, on the one hand, the inhabitants of Chalandriani and Kastri were involved in maritime activities,
with piracy probably being one of them, which enabled them to transport goods, people, and valuable objects
to their community. On the other hand, it seems that they were also afraid of raids from the sea, especially in
the EC IIB phase, since they took strong defensive measures, even though in the end the settlement was most
probably destroyed by such an attack.
   Panormos on Naxos (Angelopoulou 2014, 67–88), Kynthos on Delos (MacGillivray 1980), and Markiani on
Amorgos (Marangou 2006, 81–93) display similar characteristics, as they were fortified settlements in naturally
defensible sites, where the inhabitants have in their possession valuable oriental objects.
     According to the above, defense and protection measures are a timeless feature in the Cyclades already
from the FN and at least up to the end of EBA II. They appeared with the establishment of maritime contacts
and increased when these contacts intensified and valuable goods were concentrated in the Aegean. Moreover,
the same people who took defensive measures, possessed valuable objects that could be obtained either by
participating in maritime trade or by raiding. Taking into account that during the period under consideration,
activities such as robbery and piracy probably did not have the negative connotation that is given to them today,
and that in the face of survival such activities were not only legitimate but could even constitute “heroic” acts,
it seems very likely that the same people who participated in trade would have carried out pirate raids in times
of crisis or when the opportunity arose. Besides, according to Agouridis (1997, 20), “trading and raiding are
often the two sides of the same coin”, which means that no distinction can be drawn between them, and con-
sequently between their archaeological footprints. It is true that the boundaries between trade and piracy are
blurred, especially in such early periods, but at the same time this assumption concludes that the same people
were engaged in both activities.
· 78 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



   Also, in periods of intensive large-scale contacts and without the existence of a strong central power, as is the
case of the EBA Aegean (see also Driessen, this volume), it is almost unlikely that raids for quick and immediate
profit would not take place. More generally, most island communities were able to practice piracy, some more
and some less, and probably did so alongside other activities.




CONCLUSIONS

In summary, it seems quite likely that in the context of the EBA sea voyages, not only trade was practiced, but
also piracy. The frequency of this phenomenon cannot be determined, but there are other aspects that can be
understood with greater certainty. During the period under discussion, and especially in EBA II, there were
both the appropriate means (i.e., ships suitable for raiding) and strong motives, sometimes even linked to sur-
vival. At the same time, the absence of a central power created ideal conditions for piracy to flourish. Indeed,
it seems that in prehistory such acts did not carry the negative connotations that are attached to it today, as the
legality or the illegality of an action was not perceived in the same way. On the contrary, a daring and dangerous
action may have been considered an act of bravery and glory.
    Therefore, the motivation for piracy was not only driven by material factors, which would ensure survival
and/or the acquisition of wealth. Participation in risky activities, such as sea voyages and piracy, increased
the reputation and power of those who took part in them. It proved their martial and naval prowess and thus
gained the respect of the whole community. Through the possession of valuable objects and people it ensured
the ­perpetuation of future generations and the community, the warrior-pirates also demonstrated their power
and thus strengthened their social status and legitimized their authority.
     The evidence in the material culture may be indirect but, complementary to the possible perceptions of
the period, seems to suggest that piracy may have been practiced in the EBA Aegean by the same people who
­participated in maritime trade. It is very likely that the traders of the EBA were at the same time warriors, pirates
 and hunters, charged with the duty of providing their community with essential goods, animals and women,
 either through exchanges or through raids. In general, the trap of interpreting all relevant finds as the result
 of trading activities should be avoided, especially in periods with no written sources, such as the EBA. On the
 contrary, the strong possibility that a greater or lesser part of the maritime traffic of people and goods is due to
 piracy should always remain open.

The Art of War in Prehistoric Aegean
Early Cycladic Fortified Citadels and Weapons



Anastasia Angelopoulou
Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades
natashaangelopoulou@yahoo.gr




ABSTRACT

The development of habitation in the Cyclades during the Early Bronze Age (3rd millennium BCΕ) is little known,
as a result of the limited number of investigated Early Cycladic settlements. The proliferation of fortified sites and the
development of weaponry imply an increased interest in defense during the Early Cycladic II period (middle of the 3rd
millennium BCΕ). The establishment and the violent abandonment, following war-like conflict, of the fortified citadels at
Kastri on Syros and Korphari ton Amygdalion on Naxos (2500–2300/2200 BCΕ), are considered signs of the arrival of
new populations that marked an era of crisis and intense competition in the islands.
The aim of this paper is to evaluate the significance of both fortifications and weaponry for the evolution of the Cycladic
civilization. The war conflicts associated with the phenomenon of piracy are not a symptom of an era of cultural decline
and regression. Hostility intensified in a period of prosperity as this is reflected in settlement patterns, demography,
economy, society, and last but not least in the expanded cultural contacts in the Aegean during the Early Bronze Age. The
Early Cycladic fortified citadels are outstanding examples of collective work – a milestone in the evolution from small
farming communities to large “urban” ones.




INTRODUCTION

The enduring phenomenon of war is a complex process in which the role of defense systems has undoubtedly
been crucial. As far as the Cyclades are concerned, the development of fortifications during the Early Bronze
Age (ΕΒΑ) (3rd millennium BCE) was an integral part of the evolution of Early Cycladic (EC) settlements with
important social, economic and cultural implications. The aim of this paper is to give a brief overview of the
EC fortified settlements and to assess their significance for the knowledge of cultural continuity and change.
EC weaponry is also presented, hoping to show its importance for a number of aspects related to war tactics,
technological innovations, social status and cultural interactions.




NEOLITHIC ANTECEDENTS

The defensive wall of Strophilas on the western coast of Andros is considered to be the precursor of the EC
­fortifications (Televantou 2006, 4–5; 2008, 43–5, 53; 2009, 122–24; 2017, 264; Figs. 1a–b, 2a–b). Τhe wall of
 Strophilas, dated to the final phase of the Late Neolithic (LN), i.e., the Final Neolithic (FN) or Chalcolithic
 period (late 4th millennium BCE), is the earliest known example of fortification construction in the Cyclades.

                                                                       2009, pl. 81b).




Fig. 2: (a) Strophilas, the fortification wall (Televantou 2009, pl. 82b); (b) Strophilas, the central bastion of the fortification wall. Rock-art representations of
                                                                   ships (Televantou 2017, fig. 6).



      The discovery of Strophilas revealed significant new evidence regarding the development of Cycladic
c­ ivilization. Common characteristics recognized in the topography of settlement sites, the arrangement of the
 fortification and the material culture, represent the uninterrupted cultural continuity between the Neolithic and
 the EBA.
    The settlement occupies the top of a naturally fortified promontory, in close proximity to the sea and in a
privileged position to control sea and land routes of communication (Fig. 1b). The location of the stone-built
wall with solid, curvilinear bastions and a possible outer wall to the north, which was easily accessible from the
land, and for this reason more vulnerable side of the settlement, testifies to an organized defense plan (Figs. 1b,
2a).
   Also unique in the history of Aegean art are the complex rock-art compositions of Strophilas, among which
those with depictions of ships, symbols of power and wealth, found on the defensive wall stand out (Televantou
2006, 6–7; 2008, 47–8; 2009, 127–8; 2017, 267, fig. 6; Fig. 2b).
A . A N G E L O P O U L O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                    · 85 ·




     The rock-art depictions of ships testify to the involvement of the inhabitants in maritime activities such
as trading (Televantou 2008, 47, 51). They offer important new evidence for the emergence of the longboat
and of a wide network of maritime contacts and cultural interactions between the Cyclades and other Aegean
­communities, for example Kephala Petras on east Crete, as early as the FN period (Televantou 2008, 47, 51;
 Papadatos and Thomkins 2013, 355, 369–76). Last but not least, the participation of Strophilas’ community in
 collective endeavors, such as navigation, and the construction of communal works, such as fortification walls,
 is considered to reveal a significantly high level of social organization (Televantou 2006, 11; 2008, 53; 2009,
 138–40; 2017, 270).




GROTTA-PELOS AND KEROS-SYROS EVIDENCE

The study of settlement patterns in the Cyclades, as well as the evolution of defensive systems during the
­succeeding EC period (3rd millennium BCE), is a broad but difficult field of research due to the extremely
 ­limited number of excavated EC settlements. The end of the Neolithic period and especially the first phase of
  the EC period (EC I) correspond to the floruit of the so-called Grotta-Pelos culture (3200–2700 BCE) and mark
  the beginning of important cultural changes in the Cyclades.
    Our knowledge of the EC I settlements is restricted (Doumas 1972, 151–52; Broodbank 2000, 151; ­Stampolidis
and Sotirakopoulou 2011a, 32; Angelopoulou 2016, 55; 2016–2017, 134), and, compared to the Neolithic era,
EC I installations are scattered, more numerous, limited in size and short-lived. Confirmed e­ xamples of EC I
fortified settlements are not known, with the only possible exception being Markiani on Amorgos. The high
hill of Markiani is a naturally defensive site overlooking the steep slopes of the southern coast of Amorgos
(Marangou 2006a, 5–7; Fig. 3a). Markiani was first occupied at the beginning of the EC period (Renfrew 2006,
248). The small agricultural installation of EC I was replaced by a significantly larger fortified settlement during
the following EC II phase (around the middle of the 3rd millennium BCE) (Whitelaw 2006, 19–20). Although
the defensive wall of Markiani dates to EC II (mid-3rd millennium BCE; Fig. 3b), it is likely that it was founded
much earlier, during EC I (Marangou 2006b, 86; Renfrew 2006, 248), proving the existence of a well-organized
early community (Renfrew 2006, 253).
    The succeeding EC II phase of the so-called Keros-Syros culture (2700–2200 BCE) is the preeminent period
of expansion of the Cycladic culture, as shown by the profound cultural developments and population growth
with the dispersion of habitation sites throughout the geographical range of the Cyclades (Doumas 1972, 158–
68; Broodbank 2000, 179; Angelopoulou 2016, 56; 2016–2017, 134). Among the settlements of this time are
elements of differentiation in terms of size and wealth, with typical examples being those of Chalandriani on
Syros, Skarkos on Ios, Ayia Irini on Kea, and Dhaskalio on Keros (Broodbank 2000, 212–21).
     On the plateau of Chalandriani on the northeast coast of Syros, an important EC II settlement as well as a
cemetery are located (Marthari 1998; 2017a, 142–44; Broodbank 2000, 212–6; Hekman 2003; Fig. 4a). Remains
of the prehistoric settlement are preserved under the modern village of Chalandriani. Although the settlement
is little known, it is considered to be one of the most significant habitation sites on the island of Syros (Marthari
1998, 22; 2017a, 144; Broodbank 2000, 214; Hekman 2003, 85–6). This is indicated by the nearby burial ground
of Chalandriani, the largest, so far, known cemetery in the Cyclades (Tsountas 1899, 77–115; Doumas 1977,
128–30; Hekman 2003; Marthari 2017a, 144–52).
    The discovery of the cemetery of Chalandriani brought new perspectives to our knowledge of the Aegean
prehistory. Variations observed in the number and quality of the burial gifts, but also in the way the tombs were
constructed, testify to the existence of distinguished social groups in the community (Hekman 2003, 191–97).
The close connection of the inhabitants with maritime activities is revealed by the depictions of ships, the largest
in number images of Cycladic longboats dated to the 3rd millennium BCE, on vessels such as the “frying-pans”
found in the cemetery of Chalandriani (Coleman 1985; Broodbank 2000, 215; Jarriel 2018, 64, 69).
 · 86 ·                                          T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




Fig. 3: (a) Map of Amorgos (Archive of the Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades); (b) Markiani, the fortification wall showing the north bastion (Marangou
                                 2006b, fig. 6.1); (c) Markiani, lead seal and clay sealings (Angelopoulou 2006, fig. 8.25).



   The area remained the focus of significant cultural activity during the EC II Late (2500–2300/2200 BCE),
when the local residential center is thought to have moved to the naturally fortified hill at Kastri, on top of
which a smaller and fortified settlement was founded (see below) (Davis 1987, 33; Broodbank 2000, 214).
   The EC settlement of Ayia Irini was built on a low promontory on the northwest coast of Kea and in the
same location as the city of the Late Bronze Age (2nd millennium BCE). The discovery of the early settlement
of Ayia Irini is of special importance for the residential development in Kea. Ayia Irini is characterized by
successive phases of occupation dated to the LN/FN and the EC II (Ayia Irini I–III) (Wilson 1999; 2013). It is
an extensive and well-organized settlement with multiple building phases, communal works (sewage system,
cobbled roads) and spacious well-built houses in some cases, possibly two-storied (House ED) (Caskey 1971,
362, 368–72; 1972, 370–75; Wilson and Eliot 1984, 83–6; Schofield 1998, 119–20; Broodbank 2000, 218; Wilson
2013, 394–95).
A . A N G E L O P O U L O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                               · 87 ·




Fig. 4: (a) Map of Syros (Archive of the Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades); (b) Kastri, aerial view (Marthari 2017a, fig. 1); (c) Kastri, plan of the fortified
                                                           acropolis (after Marthari 2006, fig. 2).




    Ayia Irini is considered to have been more of a commercial than an agricultural settlement, due to its loca-
tion in the sheltered bay of Ayios Nikolaos. Imported pottery and metals from the Cyclades, Attica and Euboea
bear witness to the prominent role of the settlement in the Aegean interaction networks (Cherry et al. 1991, 226;
Schofield 1998, 119; Wilson 1999, 20, 228, 231–39; 2013, 403, 408).
    The excellent state of preservation of the site of Skarkos on the western coast of Ios provides us with the
­opportunity to study a significant EC II village-level community (Marthari 1997, 1999, 2001–2004, 2008a,
 2017b, 2018). The low hill of Skarkos is located in the most fertile valley of the island and overlooks the natural
 harbor of Ios. The extensive Keros-Syros settlement has a well-organized plan with building insulae, big two-
storey edifices and public works such as streets, squares and a drainage system.
    There are indications of craft specialization and differences in the social status of the inhabitants, suggesting
the existence of a socially and economically sophisticated community with active participation in the network
of external contacts of the time (Marthari 1997, 377; 1999, 23–8; 2008a, 79–84; 2017b, 133–34; 2018, 175–93).
   Dhaskalio (Renfrew et al. 2013) proves the existence of different development models between the ­islands.
On the islet of Dhaskalio, close to the western end of Keros, the largest known EC settlement with three ­successive
phases of occupation (Phases A–C) is considered to be located, dating to EC II and EC III (2750–2300 BCE)1
(Renfrew et al. 2013, 74; Bronk Ramsey et al. 2013, 702–3, table 33.6; Sotirakopoulou 2016, 351–77, 391).


1 Radiocarbon dates from Dhaskalio place the end of Phase C to the EC III (2300 BCE), a century or two earlier than suggested for
the end of the EC period (Renfrew 1972, 221). As noted by the authors, this is a matter to be assessed further based on comparable
evidence from other sites (Bronk Ramsey et al. 2013, 702–3).
· 88 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



     The habitation site is located in a particularly privileged position for maritime activities, considering the
fact that during the EBA the islet was connected to Keros through an isthmus with two protected natural
­harbors-anchorages (Dixon and Kinnaird 2013, 45–55; Renfrew 2013, 705; Jarriel 2018, 66, 69). The importance
 of Dhaskalio as a major trade center in the Aegean is emphasized by the exceptionally large number of imports
 (artifacts and raw materials) attested (Renfrew 2013, 718–19; Sotirakopoulou 2016, 388).
    The settlement of Dhaskalio was densely built, with structures of public, possibly religious character, and
certified craft activities (Renfrew 2013, 705–21; Boyd 2013, 341–85; Gavalas 2013, 514; Georgakopoulou 2013,
667, 670–72, 683–85, 689–92). The habitation site is part of a wider archaeological unit and is connected to the
activities that took place on the opposite coast of Keros, known as Kavos (Renfrew 2013, 711).
    In Kavos, residential remains were discovered as well as the so-called “Special Deposits”, which represent a
unique in number, typological variety and high-quality group of objects (marble figurines and vases, pottery,
metal objects etc.) (Doumas 1964, 410; Renfrew et al. 2015; Broodbank 2000, 223–36). The finds of Kavos
have been interpreted as the remains of an exceptionally large cemetery associated with a local and prosperous
trading community (Doumas 1972, 163; Broodbank 2000, 225–30). On the other hand, Kavos is considered to
have been a pan-Cycladic sanctuary for the ritual deposition of prestigious objects around the middle of the 3rd
millennium BCE (Renfrew 2015, 555–60).
   This brief overview of the large, prosperous and unfortified settlements of EC II is necessary to assess the
importance of the fortified habitation sites that appear during the mature phase of EC II (second half of the 3rd
millennium BCE).




KASTRI GROUP AND FORTIFIED CENTERS

This period, also known as the Kastri group phase (2500–2300/2200 BCE), named after the homonymous
fortified acropolis in Syros (Fig. 4a), is characterized by the intensification of relations with the East and the
islands of the northeastern Aegean, a phenomenon probably related to the development of metallurgy and
the search for new raw materials (tin) for the manufacture of copper alloys (Angelopoulou 2003, 184; 2008,
162–63; 2014, 502–3). Through the metal trade routes, new types of pottery and especially of drinking and
pouring vessels were introduced in the Aegean, which are also considered to express the adoption of Anatolian
drinking customs and social practices (Renfrew 1972, 150, 172–73, 194, 203–4, 207, 533–34, fig. II.2, table 9.II;
Sotirakopoulou 1993; 2016, 354–77; Wilson 1999, 238; Broodbank 2000, 285, 309–19, 332–33; Αngelopoulou
2003; 2008; 2014, 117–18, 483–503). The selective emulation of eastern cultural elements and practices by the
islanders is also evident in defensive architecture, as it will be shown below.
   This era is marked by the existence of an increased threat of conflict in the Cyclades. The destruction and
abandonment of fortified settlements has been interpreted as symptomatic of a period of turmoil associated
with the intrusion of foreign hostile populations originating from Asia Minor or the northeastern Aegean
(Rutter 1979, 8–9; 1983, 71; Gale and Stos-Gale 1984, 268–71; Doumas 1988, 26–9; Manning 1995, 61).
    Fortified settlements dated to the EC II Late are known from sites such as Kastri on Syros, Korphari
ton ­Amygdalion (Panormos) on Naxos, Markiani on Amorgos and Kynthos on Delos (MacGillivray 1980,
7). Common characteristics concerning the topographic setting of the sites, i.e., the choice of naturally de-
fensive hill­tops near the sea and in privileged positions for the supervision of maritime and land routes of
­communication, as well as the organization of the fortification and the material culture, testify that the Kastri
 group fortified settlements were created by the islanders themselves and not by foreign invaders (Angelopoulou
 2014, 512; 2016–2017, 144). Among the EC fortified citadels, the best preserved are those at Kastri, Markiani
 and Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos).
A . A N G E L O P O U L O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                      · 89 ·




       Kastri, on the northeastern mountainous coast of Syros, is a point of reference for the study of forti-
  fied ­settlements and war tactics (Fig. 4b–c). The acropolis of Kastri is located in close proximity to the rich
  ­settlement and the cemetery of Chalandriani (Tsountas 1899, 115–21; Bossert 1967; Doumas 1972, 158–62;
   Broodbank 2000, 215, 244; Marthari 2006; 2007; 2008b; 2009; 2010; 2011; 2012; 2013; 2017a, 144–47). It is
   considered to have been founded during the EC II Late by the local population (Broodbank 2000, 214). Τhe
   acropolis was built on top of a steep hill, which provided the tactical advantage of being difficult to reach by
   land, while at the same time it gave the possibility to command the important sea route leading from Attica
   and Euboea to the central C ­ yclades. The defensive advantage of the site, especially in cases of surprise attacks,
   such as raids, is c­ om­plemented by three lines of defense in the form of superimposed arched enclosures on
   the northern, ­accessible from the seaside, area of the hill: an outwork, a main wall with horseshoe-shaped
   bastions and a third enceinte around the top that protected a roofed area used for storage and small ­gatherings
­(Marthari 2006, 116–18; 2007, 50–2; 2008b, 87–91; Fig. 4b–c). The type of fortification in the form of a wall with
 ­horseshoe-shaped bastions is ­considered to have originated in the East (Höckmann 1977, 161; Cosmopoulos
  1991, 156; ­Sotirakopoulou 2008, 545). Bastions are active elements of defense, related to the launching of
  flanking fire, a highly desirable warfare tactic when engaging an enemy line formation.
   The bulwark also reveals strategic planning as far as the organization of defense is concerned. As aptly noted
by Christos Tsountas (1899, 120), the rampart was lower in height than the main wall to protect the defenders
from enemy strikes in case this first defensive enclosure was taken by the attackers.
    The abandonment of the citadel is attributed to a war conflict. Between the rampart and the main wall with
the towers numerous sea pebbles were discovered, supposedly used as sling shots (Tsountas 1899, 120).
      The acropolis was densely built with small, tightly packed, irregular stone-built houses, accessible through
narrow passages. Despite its small size (approximately 0.5 ha), Kastri is clearly characterized by common
­elements in terms of social organization, economy and external contacts with the larger settlements of the
 EC II (Skarkos, Ayia Irini, Dhaskalio) mentioned above. In particular, the citadel at Kastri yielded evidence
 for ­specialized craft activities, such as metalworking and woodworking (Tsountas 1899, 124–26; Bossert 1967,
 60–4; Broodbank 2000, 215). The existence of an organized society at Kastri is implied by the discovery of the
 unique silver diadem with a scene possibly of a ritual character, which denotes the prominent social status of its
 owner (Tsountas 1899, 123–24, pl. 10; Marthari 1998, 28; Broodbank 2000, 215).
    Last but not least, pottery and metal objects, imports or local imitations of artifacts originating in the East or
the northeastern Aegean, confirm the maintenance by the local community of an active network of long-range
external contacts (Tsountas 1899, 122, 124; Bossert 1967, 61–75; Renfrew 1972, 314, 533–34; Gale and Stos-
Gale 1984, 268–71; 2008, 405; Stos-Gale et al. 1984, 23).
    A fortification wall with a possible outwork protected the aforementioned settlement of Markiani during
EC II Late (Fig. 3b). A stone-built wall with horseshoe-shaped towers, similar to that of Kastri, was discovered
in the north (landward) and easily accessible side of the settlement (Marangou 2006b, 86–7). The defensive
­advantage of the site was also enhanced by the strong north winds that sweep the area of the fortification
 ­(Marangou 2006b, 87), forcing the enemy to fight on a considerable difficult terrain.
   Markiani had a predominantly agricultural character with very little evidence of trade interactions (Renfrew
2006, 251–53). Nevertheless, the existence of Anatolianizing pottery types (depas, tankards) of the Kastri group
period (Eskitzioglou 2006, 139, 143–46, fig. 7.19:1–8, pl. 35a–d) clearly suggests that the local community was
well-connected and followed the cultural trends of an era of great mobility and change.
    The existence of defensive works, the evidence of a range of craft activities and the discovery of a lead seal
and sealings (Angelopoulou 2006, 219–22; Fig. 3c), insignia of persons of high rank, testify that the people
leaving at Markiani were not simply members of a small and isolated agricultural community (Renfrew 2006,
253–55).
    The acropolis of Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos) on the southeastern coast of Naxos has revealed
­important new evidence for the defensive architecture and the character of the fortified settlement sites of the
· 90 ·                                            T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




Fig. 5: (a) Map of Naxos (Archive of the Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades); (b) Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos), aerial view (Archive of the Ephorate
              of Antiquities of Cyclades); (c) Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos), plan of the fortified acropolis (Angelopoulou 2014, fig. 1.15).




Kastri group period (Angelopoulou 2003; 2008; 2014; 2016; 2016–2017; Fig. 5a–c). The low rocky hill named
Korphari ton Amygdalion is located in close proximity to the bay of Panormos, one of the safest natural harbors
of the island, offering protection from the strong northern winds.
     It is a naturally fortified site surrounded by higher hills. It commands the adjacent natural harbor of
Panormos, without being easily visible from the sea. Moreover, the site provides an excellent view over an
­extended area stretching from Amorgos, Keros and Kouphonisia to Schinousa and Herakleia, controlling the
 sea routes leading to these islands (Angelopoulou 2003, 170; 2008, 150; 2014, 20; 2016, 59; 2016–2017, 141).
    On the summit of the hill, the remains of a fortified acropolis of the Kastri Group period were discovered,
extending over an area of 285 m (Angelopoulou 2003, 170–71; 2008, 150–51; 2014, 20–8; 2016, 59–60; 2016–
                                             2




2017, 141; 2021, 185; Fig. 5b–c). Twenty small stone-built rooms were revealed within a massive fortification
enclosure reinforced by five horseshoe-shaped bastions. The defense was strengthened by means of a possible
outwork running along the western side of the fortification.
   The end of the Naxian acropolis was violent. An impressive bronze spearhead (Fig. 6a) and a number of
pebbles (slingshot projectiles), which were found in the wider area of the gate, amidst extensive traces of fire, are
indications of the violent destruction of the fort after an enemy attack (Angelopoulou 2003, 171; 2014, 28–33;
2008, 150–51; 2016, 59; 2016–2017, 141; 2021, 186).
   Panormos and Kastri share common features, especially regarding the organization of their defense system
(Angelopoulou 2014, 65–7). Both sites are protected by a thick stone-built wall reinforced by horseshoe-shaped
bastions and an outwork. Another common characteristic is the form of the entranceways, which are designed
A . A N G E L O P O U L O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                       · 91 ·




Fig. 6: (a) Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos), bronze spearhead (Angelopoulou 2014, fig. 5.2); (b) Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos), triangular copper
                  daggers (Angelopoulou 2021, fig. 6); (c) Korphari ton Amygdalion (Panormos), copper sword (Angelopoulou 2021, fig. 7).




as narrow passages guarded by flanking towers. Special care is also taken to protect the entrances from being
visible from afar. At Panormos, the entrance to the acropolis is hidden by two massive tower-like structures
(Towers Γ and Δ; Fig. 5c). In the case of Kastri, Tsountas notes that the entrance in the outwork was not easily
visible from far away, as it was obliquely opened to the thickness of the wall (Tsountas 1899, 116–7).
   Despite the common features discerned in the fortified settlement sites of the Kastri group period, Panormos
represents a unique, so far, architectural form. At Kastri and Markiani, the fortification is built to protect an area
occupied by a settlement. On the contrary, at Panormos the defensive wall is founded to protect not a settlement
but a single building unit (Angelopoulou 2003, 171; 2008, 151; 2014, 511; 2016, 60; 2016–2017, 141; 2021, 186).
The fortress on the summit of the hill might have served as a place of refuge in times of danger. Moreover, it was
created to protect large quantities of agricultural commodities that were essential for the survival of the local
community (Angelopoulou 2003, 171; 2008, 151; 2014, 511; 2016, 60; 2016–2017, 141; 2021, 186). It represents
an outstanding example of collective work – a milestone in the evolution from small farming communities to
more complex societies (Angelopoulou 2021, 186).
     The citadel is an integral part of an extensive and as yet unexplored settlement extending on the slopes of
the hill around the fort at the top (Angelopoulou 2008, 151; 2014, 67–8; 2016, 60; 2016–2017, 141; 2021, 186).
The settlement was naturally protected by formations of bedrock that rises steeply high above the ground sur­
face. These formations of bare rock protected the habitation area from being exposed to strong winds. At the
same time, they provided additional protection against possible enemy attacks, as they obscured the view to the
­settlement and made access to the site difficult. Traces of walls made of large stones visible on the ground surface
 need to be further explored in order to address questions, such as whether there was an additional defensive
 wall that surrounded the settlement, as one might reasonably expect there to be.
· 92 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



    While slings, the use of which is attested both at Panormos and Kastri, represent long-range weapons, others,
such as daggers and spears, were designed for hand-to-hand combat. As aforementioned, in the a­ cropolis of
Korphari ton Amygdalion a bronze spearhead was found (Angelopoulou 2014, 454–57; Mastrotheodoros and
Basiakos 2014, 460, 469–73; Fig. 6a). The spearhead is a sophisticated example of metalworking technique that
reveals familiarity with advanced technology, especially the forging of weapons. Cast in a two-piece mould and
subsequently hammered, the weapon has a solid, long and pointed blade. Sharp ribs extend along the entire
length of the narrow blade, from tip to tang. The solid, hooked tang was inserted into a shaft, possibly, made of
wood. The “Hook-tang” spearhead from Panormos has no counterparts in the Aegean. Similar examples of high
quality, durable and effective weapons are known only from the East during the mid-third millennium BCE.
Close parallels are found in spearheads from Troy (phase II), Ras-Shamra in Syria and Cyprus. The composition
of the spearhead from Panormos, which is made of a copper-tin alloy (bronze) (Mastrotheodoros and Basiakos
2014, 460, 469) and its typological parallels indicate that the weapon was imported to Panormos from the East
(Angelopoulou 2014, 454–56).
     Panormos is also considered to be the provenance of an important group of thirteen bronze weapons
­(daggers and a sword) stored in the Archaeological Collection of Apeiranthos (Angelopoulou 2021; Fig. 6b–c).
 The artifacts are dated to EC II and represent a different metallurgical tradition compared to that of the spear­
 head. The objects must come from looted graves in the area of Panormos, as indicated by their excellent state
 of preservation. Noteworthy is that some of them have been deliberately “killed” by the blade being bent, a rare
 burial practice in the Aegean (Angelopoulou 2021, 183). A possible provenance for the aforementioned objects
 is the EC II looted cemetery at Korphari ton Amygdalion, located at the west slope of the hill and close to the
 acropolis (Angelopoulou 2014, 68–9; 2021, 186). Furthermore, the existence of the daggers is consistent with
 that of the fortress, as both indicate a period marked by heightened aggression and insecurity.
    Weapons and especially daggers are considered valuable prestige items reflecting the high social status of
their owner (Broodbank 2000, 253, fig. 83; Angelopoulou 2021, 182–83). They are multipurpose objects, useful
in hunting and war, although they may also have been used domestically. The daggers from Panormos are,
among their other possible functions, powerful short-range weapons (Angelopoulou 2021, 182–83, figs 5–10).
With an average blade length of over 20 cm, they are effective weapons designed for melee combat. An example,
whose length exceeds 35 cm, can be considered an early example of a real sword. As a rule, the examples are
triangular in shape with a central rib, straight edges and a flattened heel. Rivets were used for the fastening of
the handle made of perishable material (Fig. 6b). Noteworthy is that in the case of the sword (Fig. 6c) the im-
pression of the wooden handle is preserved (Angelopoulou 2021, 181, fig. 9). Made in two-piece moulds, the
daggers were further forged by hammering in order to obtain sharp and durable cutting edges.
     Triangular daggers of similar type are particularly widespread in the Cyclades and are among the
­characteristic creations of the Cycladic workshop of metalwork during EC II (Branigan 1974, 124; Stampolidis
 and Sotirakopoulou 2011b, 55). The closest typological parallels for the examples of Panormos are known from
 islands such as Amorgos (cemeteries of Stavros, Dokathismata), Melos and Naxos. The similarities attested
 reinforce the possibility that the daggers from Panormos are creations of the Cycladic workshop during EC II
 (Angelopoulou 2021, 182).
    An exception seems to be the dagger or knife (Angelopoulou 2021, 182, fig. 6, no. 903; Fig. 6b, no. 903),
which –as in the case of the spearhead– echoes the metallurgical tradition of the East, where similar artifacts
become particularly popular in Asia Minor during the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE. Apart from the
metal objects imported, the close cultural affiliations of Korphari ton Amygdalion with the East are also evident
in pottery with the discovery of Anatolianizing pottery types (tankards) (Angelopoulou 2014, 171–76, fig. 3.33),
as in the case of Kastri, Markiani and Kynthos (MacGillivray 1980, 25, 45).
   The acropolis of Panormos has considerably enhanced our knowledge of the strong cultural links with the
East attested in material culture as well as in architecture. The citadel surrounded by a settlement recalls large
EBA II settlements in Asia Minor, which are organized around fortified citadels that include public buildings
A . A N G E L O P O U L O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                    · 93 ·




(Troy, Karatas-Semayük, Liman Tepe) (Mellink and Angel 1966, 245; 1970, 247; 1973, 294; Warner 1979, 137;
Erkanal 1996, 78–80; 1999, 240–41; 2008, 182–83; Düring 2011, 284, 287).
    The identity of the intruders who destroyed the citadels at Panormos and Kastri is and will remain unknown.
However, it appears that the nature of the attacks was that of predatory raids, as both sites are abandoned after
their destruction. The latter implies that the main aim of the attackers was to acquire the wealth that was kept
inside the fortified areas. Thus, the destruction of the acropoleis could be interpreted as the result of a pirate
attack (Angelopoulou 2008, 159; 2014, 512–13). Thucydides (1.4.1–8.3) states that piracy was a serious problem
in the Cyclades until Minos, the mythical king of Crete, restored safe navigation by expelling the pirates and
colonizing the islands. He also relates the rise of piracy to advances in maritime expertise and notes that early
settlements on the coast were most vulnerable to pirate attacks and plundering. For that reason, people living
on the islands and on the mainland preferred to settle at a distance from the sea.
    Thucydides’ comments are of vital importance for understanding the differences in settlement and growth
patterns during the Middle and Late Bronze Age in the Aegean. Nevertheless, it cannot be excluded that piracy,
closely connected with the intensification of maritime activities and the use of the longboats, had already be­
come an acute problem for the islanders as early as the EBA. For example, it is probably no coincidence that the
inhabitants of the fortified sites of the Kastri group period were prepared for an attack from the sea, as is implied
by the location of the settlement sites close to but at a safe distance from the shores and on hills that command
the sea routes leading to the islands. The fortified acropoleis of the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE are
closely related to an era of increased threats and conflict, as implied by the developed war tactics, fortification
systems and weaponry used. The root cause for the occurrence of predatory raids is a question to be answered.
Nevertheless, an interesting scientific inquiry is whether the ascertained aggressiveness was related to climate
factors such as aridity that might have affected agriculture and other aspects of social life in the Aegean during
the last centuries of the 3rd millennium BCE (Jarriel 2020, 3–5, 10–1).
     Creations of prosperous communities with an advanced social organization and an extensive network
of ­external contacts, the Kastri group acropoleis are the continuation of the cultural tradition of the large
­unfortified settlements of early EC II, such as Skarkos, Dhaskalio, Ayia Irini and Chalandriani. At the same time,
 they ­probably foreshadow the developments at the end of the 3rd and the beginning of the 2nd millennium
 BCE, when the residential model in the Cyclades changes with the concentration of the population in fewer in
 number but larger in size settlements, which can be characterized as small towns, as, for example, Phylakopi
 on Melos, Akrotiri on Thera, Paroikia on Paros (Renfrew 1982, 38; Barber 1983, 77; Broodbank 2000, 326–
 31). Perhaps this change was necessary to deal more effectively with the dangers and instability in the Aegean
 ­(Angelopoulou 2016, 66–7; 2016–2017, 145), gradually entering a new era of cultural growth.
