Searching for Piracy in the Middle and early Late Bronze Age
Aegean


Dimitris Ν. Sakkas
Independent Researcher
dnsakkas@icloud.com




ABSTRACT

The investigation of piracy in the Middle and early Late Bronze Age Aegean is closely linked to contemporary maritime
activity. In that context, the active incorporation of Crete, in the ­beginning, and then of the Greek mainland in the
­international eastern Mediterranean system established maritime networks and intensified communications and the
 circulation of goods among the aforementioned areas. In addition, the architecture of some contemporary coastal settle-
 ments, and particularly the presence of fortifications together with iconographic evidence indicate other-than-peaceful
 contacts as well. From this point up to the identification of piratical activity, however, lies a considerable distance. This
 paper examines this distance through different types of archaeological evidence. After outlining the major maritime net-
 works in the Aegean of the Middle and early Late Bronze Age, the present work discusses material evidence and several
 case studies that have been interpreted as indicative for piratical activity, and which thus afford the evaluation of the
 phenomenon of piracy in the area and era under consideration.




INTRODUCTION

According to the definition that was introduced and adopted by the A.P.Pir.A. project, the term piracy refers
to the seaborne robbery through some sort of ship, and also to the looting of a sunk ship even if this activity
is taking place directly from the coast, both motivated by personal profit (Samaras, this volume). This paper
is a brief review of the case studies associated with piracy in the Aegean of the Middle Bronze Age (MBA)
and the early Late Bronze Age (LBA), the Old and the New Palace period, and, also, the Final Palatial period,
in Cretan or Minoan terminology. The challenge of exploring a series of case studies with the corresponding
evidence is developed in three parts. The former roughly presents the context of maritime communications,
the major sea routes and the dominant networks in the area and era under study. The second part reviews the
actual case studies that have been interpreted as indicative for piratical activity by previous research – each one
is established on a different sort of evidence, so that they provide the opportunity not only for an up-to-date
consideration, but also for an evaluation. This is the subject of the final part, which explores in detail the best
documented case study for identifying piracy, in order to conclude with a reassessment on piracy in the MBA
and early LBA Aegean.
· 100 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



THE CONTEXT: MARITIME ACTIVITY IN THE MBA AND THE EARLY LBA
AEGEAN

In the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE, during the MBA and the early LBA, initially Crete and a­ fterwards
the Greek Mainland witnessed the emergence of the political economies, which also affected the coast of western
Anatolia, not to mention the islands of the archipelago. The establishment and the evolvement of the Minoan
and the Mycenaean palatial systems were accompanied by the intensification of the maritime contacts between
Crete and the Mainland with eastern Mediterranean and Egypt: the “maritime exchanges in the Mediterranean
were rather limited in the earlier part of the 2nd millennium, and started to increase in the course of the 18th
century BC only to evolve into a proper network for the circulation of metals, other raw materials and finished
luxuries by the 17th century BC” (Papadimitriou and Kriga 2016, 12). This integration of the Aegean into the
eastern Mediterranean world system was analyzed, among others, through a tripartite model (Sherratt and
Sherratt 1991, 358, 367–70): the early contacts in prepalatial Crete, with the exchange of low bulk raw m
                                                                                                        ­ aterials
for luxuries, were followed first by the adoption of life style and technology for the limited linkage with the
network in the Old Palace period, and then by the actual participation in the period of the New Palaces; the
latter presupposed the reorganization of the agricultural production in order to support manufacturing of the
products that were necessary for the participation in the network, whether the growth and the increasing scale
of contacts requested and forwarded products to the new periphery of the Greek mainland, in areas such as
Laconia, Messenia and the Argolis, where the new centers of power were about to emerge.
     Long before the transformation of the agricultural production, however, other transformations are ­evidenced
in the fields of the settlement patterns and the ship technology with the employment of the sail, which further
affect the maritime communications as well; it is worth exploring at some point how this shifting is related to the
acquisition of raw materials and more particularly metals. Specifically, only one of the three prepalatial A
                                                                                                           ­ egean
maritime networks survived in the period of the Old Palaces. Apart from the former that was developed in
the northwestern Aegean with the coast of Macedonia and Thessaly, as also that of Euboea and central Greece,
the second started from Aegina in the west and after crossing the Cyclades it reached the coast of western
­Anatolia to the east, while the third one included Crete and the Peloponnese through the settlement of Kastri
 on Kythera, according to the distribution of Middle Minoan (MM) IA pottery (Broodbank 2000, 351, 354, fig.
 120). The second, horizontal network collapsed during the MM IB period, simultaneously to the foundation of
 the Old Palaces in Crete. There from, a dendritic network that was developed through the Cyclades in order to
 reach the Greek mainland, actually reflected the counter course of raw materials and particularly metals to the
 ­production centers of Crete (Broodbank 2000, 356, fig. 121). This network remained active during both the Old
  and the New Palatial period, with major stations initially in the Saronic gulf and later in the Cyclades and the
  Dodecanese, as it is mentioned below.
      Apart for these interregional networks, maritime contacts in local scales are evidenced through, among
others, the assemblages of three shipwrecks that are assigned to the period under consideration. The ­assemblage
from the Minoan shipwreck at Pseira in the gulf of Mirabello is dated to the Old Palace period (MM IIB),
­according to the nearly 140 pots that comprised its cargo (Hadjidaki-Marder 2021), in their vast majority
 ­products from the surrounding area of the wreck, which “opens a new window into the nature of regional
  trade along the north coast of east Crete during MM II” (Nodarou 2021, 61). The assemblage recovered at
  Şeytan Deresi (Bass 1976; Margariti 1997), which included 17 complete and fragmentary vases that are assigned
  to the New Palace period, the Late Minoan (LM) I (Margariti 1998), is now interpreted as deriving from “a
  small, local craft capsized, spilled out its cargo and floated away” (Bass 2005, 31), so that the site is no longer
  ­considered as that of an actual shipwreck. The third shipwreck is different in nature and scale and it lacks any
   documentation, since its location is only indicated by the 19 Cypriot copper ingots from the sea area of Kyme
   (Svoronos 1906, 168–72; Sapouna-Sakellaraki 1984, 158, fig. 2b; Banou 1988; Stos Gale et al. 1997, 109–12),
   which are most likely assigned either to the New or even to the Final Palatial period, and they are therefore
   ideally ­combined in spatial and temporal terms with the Stafylos’ tomb on the island of Skopelos (Platon 1949).
D. N . S A K K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                          · 101 ·




The future ­research will contextualize the Pseira and Şeytan Deresi assemblages within the small worlds of the
Mirabello gulf in eastern Crete and the Gökova gulf, immediately south of the Latmian gulf with the major
site of Miletus ­(Tartaron 2013: 272–6). On the other hand, the Kyme find is rather situated in a branch of the
aforementioned dendritic network, which established ports initially in the Saronic and later on in the western
Cyclades, as it is mentioned below.




THE EVIDENCE: TIME UNITS AND CASE STUDIES

In the earlier and the middle part of the MBA, which roughly correspond to the period of the Old Palaces on
Crete, the settlement at Kolonna on Aegina stands apart, first of all due to “the most impressive fortifications
in the Aegean world after those of Troy” (Rutter 2001, 126; see also Gauss 2018, 52–6, figs. 5.4–5.6; 2019, 60–1,
figs. 8–9, 66, figs. 13–15; Samaras forthcoming). The fortifications of Kolonna IX and a contemporary series
of ship representations on matt-painted jars were considered indicative for the identification of the site with a
“nest of pirates” (Basch 1986, 429). Although an earlier hoard of the Early Helladic III period with finds from
different origins (Felten 2007, 15, fig. 5) is not opposed to that interpretation, and this is further the case for
the also coming from Kolonna, later and possibly contemporary to Town X, “Aegina Treasure” (Higgins 1987;
­Simantoni-Bournia 2003; Fitton et al. 2009), Kolonna is currently understood as an outstanding residential
 center with an early elite. ­Minoan and Minoanizing pottery and a potter’s wheel, as also additional evidence,
 including among other a ceremonial stone hammer and a mason’s mark (Hiller 1993; Kilian-Dirlmeier 1997;
 Gauss 2006), ­document the relations between the Kolonna and the Old Palatial Crete and even led to the hy-
 pothesis that the site might represent the earlier state outside Crete (Niemeier 1995).
       The outstanding role of Kolonna in the MBA is also evidenced by the elite burial in the earlier so far shaft
grave (Kilian-Dirlmeier 1997; Rutter 1999), which produced the oldest assemblage of weaponry, jewelry and
vases for drinking, pouring and transportation, an assemblage that is elaborated in the later shaft graves (Rutter
2001, 140). Furthermore, it is documented by the recent excavation of a monumental building with possible
­administrative character (Gauss et al. 2011; Tartaron 2013, 220). This evidence, along with the unprecedented
 distribution of Aeginetan pottery in the coast of Thessaly and central Greece, and also in the Saronic and the
 ­Argolic Gulfs, the Cyclades and Crete (Gauss and Knodell 2020), question the identification of Kolonna as
  a pirate nest. Instead, Kolonna, which is currently regarded as the core of the “small world” of the Saronic
  gulf (Tartaron 2013, 213), developed maritime activity that brought the latter closer to other, not-so-small
  worlds north- and mainly southwards. In that context, it is not surprising that at this site firstly the shifting
  of ship ­representations from the area of a mere symbol to that of an event or concept, likely associated with a
  ­narrative circle, is identified (Emanuel 2021, 132), and that at Kolonna the maritime activity is directly com-
   bined with warlike pursuits (Rutter 2001, 130), two fundamental elements in the composition of the identity of
   the emerging elites.
    During the subsequent period of the New Palaces, the dendritic communication network that was based on
Crete intensified its presence in the southern Aegean and more particularly in the connection of the D
                                                                                                     ­ odecanese
islands with western Anatolia and the Cyclades with the Greek Mainland. Better documented are the sites
­developed along the western Cyclades, Akrotiri on Thera, Phylakopi on Melos and Ayia Irini on Kea (Davis
 1979, 146), situated within a day’s sail of each other (Cherry and Davis 1982, 340). The presence of distinctive
 “Minoan” elements in several aspects of material culture and their implications on the corresponding social
 practices, including ritual, that was initially debated between the model of “Minoan” colonies and that of the
 indigenous process, has lately become the subject of more complex questions (Davis 2008, 202).
    Minoanization, “the adoption in places beyond Crete through whatever means, of ways of doing things that
originated directly or indirectly within this island” (Broodbank 2004, 46; see also Girella et al. 2016), was so
intense in the case of Kythera that actually made that island indistinguishable from Neopalatial Crete, and this
· 102 ·                              T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



was possibly also the case for Karpathos (Broodbank 2004, 69). In both instances the process left a clear imprint
in the landscape. Although the ­presence of farmsteads with Minoanizing material culture is considered indic-
ative of a “steady out-migration from Crete” (Broodbank 2004, 69), the future research will demonstrate if the
transformation of the landscape in these islands signified the reorganization of agricultural production, as was
also the case in the Cretan c­ ountryside, according to the aforementioned model of Andrew and Susan Sherratt
(1991, 367–70). Needless to say that, if the ­Minoanized landscapes of Kythera and Karpathos indicate their ac-
tual incorporation to the system of Crete, alternative ­scenarios are mobilized for Thera and particularly Melos
and Kea (Davis 2008; N ­ iemeier 2009), whose c­ ountryside lack such evidence, although studied in great detail.
Among these ­scenarios, and not opposed to the relation of maritime and warlike pursuits noted at Kolonna, is
“power at a distance […] probably exercised by a combination of elite linkage and the classic hegemonic strategy
of violence, perhaps in the form of seaborne raiding, as witnessed in a West House wall-painting, the so-called
Siege Rhyton from Mycenae, possibly the Knossos “town mosaic”, and earlier images on matt-painted pottery
at Kolonna, rather than through the establishment of permanent control infrastructures and mechanisms to
regulate tribute flow” (Broodbank 2004, 72).
    This evidence advances the discussion toward issues of iconographic interpretation. The Knossos town
mosaic (Foster 1979, 99–115; 2008, 178–79; Waterhouse 1994), the miniature frieze from the West House in
Akrotiri (Marinatos 1973; Televantou 1994), the Siege Rhyton from Shaft Grave IV of the Grave Circle A at
Mycenae (Sakellariou 1975; Papadopoulos 2019) and also the fragmentary steatite vase from the sanctuary of
Apollo Maleatas in Epidaurus (Papadimitriou 1950, 194–210, fig. 10; Sakellariou 1971; ­Lambrinoudakis 1975,
172–73, fig. 149a) were initially considered as reproducing narrative compositions from the life in coastal towns,
public gatherings in the cases of the MM and LM finds, instead of violent events in that of the early Mycenaean
ones (Sakellariou 1981, 538). Although the former were enriched with the miniature frieze from the north-
eastern bastion at Ayia Irini on Kea (Morgan 2020), the final publication of the miniature frieze from the West
House in Akrotiri demonstrates beyond doubt the warlike aspects of the composition and establishes its direct
associations to the Epidaurus and the Mycenae rhyta (Televantou 1994, 331–38). Sufficient evidence supports
that all three finds reproduce the same iconographic circle and could even refer to a single event (Televantou
1994, 331–33), which corresponds to coastal raids, including possible piratical activity (Morgan 1988, 153).
      Regarding that Aegean “siege” iconography and particularly the Mycenae rhyton, however, which is
r­ ecognized as reproducing a generic theme, it was plausibly questioned whether “the richly buried individual in
 Grave IV at Mycenae have ordered a precious item to be made for him showing nothing more than a ­piratical
 raid”, so that seaborne raids were rather interpreted in the context of the acquisition of goods and supplies
 (Papadopoulos 2006, 134–35; 2019, 409). In that direction, albeit through a more complicated course, also
 points the hegemonic strategy of violence that was mentioned above, which could generate genuine repre-
 sentations for reproduction in the period and the area under consideration. After all, the linkage between the
 ­aforementioned ­iconography and the Aegean elites is evidenced through both the specialized production cen-
  ters and the ­consumption ­patterns of the finds themselves.
    Therefore, the surviving iconography of the New Palatial period in the Aegean documents seaborne raids
and the consideration of the nature of this assignment by the current research brings the discussion in the
essence of the topic for identifying piratical activities. If piracy was an enterprise for the direct acquisition of
personal profit, then it stands apart from the hegemonic strategy of violence, which, even without exercising,
intended to control an area in order to secure regular flows; this conceptual distinction raises the question of
whether it is possible to distinguish between these incidents and how the latter can be documented in the MBA
and the early LBA Aegean.
     Actual evidence for addressing this issue derives from the next time unit, that is the period after the
­destruction of the New Palaces and before that of Knossos, the Final Palatial period in Cretan terms, which
 demarcates the chronological limits of the present consideration as well. In that period, at the end of the Late
 ­Helladic (LH) II or early in the LH IIIA period, at the last quarter of the 15th or the first quarter of the 14th
D. N . S A K K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                     · 103 ·




c­ entury BCE, is dated the earlier, so far, reference to Mycenaeans in the Hittite archives. It is the often-cited text
 that is known as the “Indictment of Madduwatta” (Beckman et al. 2011, 69–100, AhT 3), that was dictated to a
 scribe by the Hittite king Arnuwanda I and refers to incidents that took place in the reign of his father, T­ udhaliya
 I/II. The latter had installed Madduwatta in a kingdom of western Anatolia, possibly close to the area of A    ­ rzawa
 (Beckman et al. 2011, 98). The Hittite king reminds to his client ruler that, although he was rescued more than
 once from Attarissiya, a man from Ahhiya(wa), he then joined him and together with an unnamed ruler of
 Piggaya they raided Alashiya (Cyprus).
    The incident is cited towards the end of the document AhT 3, in paragraph 36, and reproduces earlier
­correspondence, which according to Beckman (et al. 2011, 94–5) is translated:

              [The report] of Mulliyara: “I gave [the tablet to Madduwatta (saying)]: His Majesty said thus […]:
              ‘Because [the land] of Alashiya belongs to My Majesty, [and the people of Alashiya] pay [me tribute]
              – why have you continually raided it?’” But] Madduwatta said thus: “[When Attarissiya and] the rul-
              er [of Piggaya] were raiding the land of Alashiya, I often raided it too. But the father of His Majesty
              [had never informed] me, [nor] had His Majesty ever informed [me] (thus): ‘The land of Alashiya is
              mine – recognise it as such!’” “If His Majesty is indeed now demanding back the civilian captives of
              Alashiya, I will give them back to him.” And given that Attarissiya and the ruler of Piggaya are rulers
              independent of My Majesty, while (you), Madduwatta, are a servant of My Majesty – why have you
              joined up with [them]?

      Maduwatta is accused by Arnuwanda for joining the two other individuals, since he is actually a client ruler
  to the Hittite king, in contrast to his allies who are independent (Gilan 2013, 53–4). Attarissiya ­concentrated a
great deal of attention: this ruler or warlord of Ahhiyawa is generally recognized as a high-status ­Mycenaean
and, although his role remains ambiguous, it is widely accepted that he was installed in western Anatolia and
that he had a considerable fighting force at his command, which included infantry and chariots (Kelder 2004–
2005). Also, a fleet or some sort of access to ships, according to his involvement in the raid on Alashiya, for
which it is also argued that: “Such raids would be entirely consistent with the image presented in the Homeric
epics of ­Mycenaean plundering enterprises conducted through the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean regions
(and may well account for much of the wealth that was accumulated in the Mycenaean palace states). On this
­occasion, a Mycenaean warlord called Attarissiya, a ruler of Ahhiya, extended his military operations in western
 Anatolia to piratical raids off the southern Anatolia coast. Opportunistically, he appears to have c­ oordinated
 his operations against the cities of Alashiya with his former enemy Madduwatta. Both benefited from the
 ­partnership.” (Beckman et al. 2011, 99).




THE REASSESSMENT: PIRACY IN THE MBA AND EARLY LBA AEGEAN

Attarissiya’s involvement in the raid against Alashiya is therefore considered a piratical action (Cesarano 2008,
41–5, 93) and deserves further exploration, even if its identification required the spatial expansion of the r­ esearch
area, in order to include Cyprus, and it further occurs in the expiration of the period under ­consideration.
­However, it is argued below that the main significance of the text for the assessing piracy in the early LBA
 ­Aegean lies not that much in Attarissiya’s involvement to the raid that caused the indictment of Madduwatta, as
  to that of the latter person. Moreover, that the evidence that derives from the reviewed text should be considered
  rather as analogical instead of direct.
     First of all, it is safe to argue that the accusation by the Hittite king against Madduwatta for raiding Alashiya
is established on two arguments. The former considers the claim that Alashiya was under Hittite control –
­although this was possibly not the actual case according to Beckman (et al. 2011, 99); the latter that Madduwatta
 was a client ruler and thus a vassal to the Hittite king. The very combination of these aspects renders the raid
· 104 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



against Alashiya a politically not acceptable military action, as far as Madduwatta is judged from the point of
view of the Hittite king Arnuwanda. This, however, is not the case for the remaining two participants to the
raid, the Mycenaean Attarissiya and the unnamed ruler of Piggaya, at least according to the existing evidence. In
other words, this politically unacceptable action, which was meant to be signified as piratical in a later context,
considers exclusively the client ruler to the Hittite king, and is not evidenced for Madduwatta’s independent
allies. In these terms, it can be assumed that this same event, the raid against Alashiya, likely represents piratical
activity for one of the participants and an act of war for the remaining two.
    The difficulty of distinguishing between war and piracy has already been noted and previous considerations
on piracy in the Bronze Age Mediterranean in general and the Aegean specifically did not proven particularly
fruitful. Baruffi (1998, 10) argued that, although “coastal raiding and piracy were also significant factors during
the Bronze Age, as they have been during sporadic periods in the Mediterranean ever since. […] war and piracy
were so closely linked that it was not always clear when an enemy action was to be treated as one or the other”.
In the same vein, for the Aegean and for the periods before the composition of the Homeric poems and that of
the poems themselves, de Souza (1999, 18) argued that “piracy is so closely related to warfare in both aims and
methods that they are virtually undistinguishable” (see also de Souza 1999, 16, 21). This argument was debated,
however, by Samaras (2015, 191), who introduced two key-points for distinguishing between the issues of war
and piracy that puzzled Baruffi and de Souza: (1) while war is a political activity, piracy is an economic one,
and (2) instead of the war’s official aspect, piracy is rather an unofficial enterprise for personal benefit, so that
“despite their resemblance, war and piracy are two entirely distinct concepts” (Samaras 2015, 191).
     Returning to the aforementioned text and reviewing it under these principles, it is now demonstrated that
the raid mentioned in the “Indictment of Madduwatta” actually represents the violation of the political status
due to the economic motivation. Also, that this enterprise further violated the established official relations, a
practice that even if not itself informal, lies out of the formal process. In these terms, the essential element that
differentiates the perception and defines the nature of the event-raid is the relationships between the four LBA
macro-agents, on the one hand, and with the subject of the raid on the other; the fact that both the accused,
Madduwatta, and Alashiya were formally under the control of the accuser, Arnuwanda, while this was not
­actually the case for the remaining two participants, Attarissiya and the unnamed ruler of Piggaya. Therefore,
 the distinction between war and piracy in that case presupposed the consideration or even the reconstruction
 of the relationships among the involved individuals that was enabled by the surviving text.
     Although the archaeological record of the MBA and the early LBA Aegean lacks such solid evidence
and in order to retrieve it we had to turn eastwards, the field of the relationships is at least promising for the
­consideration of piracy. Here too, one or more dominant powers established special relations with a series of
 settlements, including nearly all the sites which yielded the evidence that supported the case studies previously
 discussed. It is therefore argued that the secure identification of piratical activity can be attempted through the
 reconstruction of relations among sites and, if possible, among individuals as well, while, if this consideration
 demonstrates the limitations of the archaeological record, then the sequel of the A.P.Pir.A. project might be
 developed as an interdisciplinary one.




CONCLUSIONS

In the previous parts of this paper and following a brief presentation of the context of maritime contacts and
networks in the MBA and early LBA Aegean, a series of case studies for piratical activity was critically discussed.
It was argued that archaeological evidence previously interpreted as indicating piratical activity in the study area
and era should be reconsidered. In the case of architecture, that the fortifications of Kolonna, even if combined
with early ship representations, are currently understood in association to the site’s outstanding role in the
Aegean of the Old Palace period, where evidently the maritime element is for the first time in the period under
D. N . S A K K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                           · 105 ·




consideration associated with the martial one. In the case of the iconography of the period of the New Palaces, it
was argued that, although it reproduces seaborne raiding events, the latter possibly indicate activities other than
piracy. On the other hand, the textual case study of the Hittite record known as the “Indictment of Madduwatta”,
not only produced evidence for the secure identification of a piratical event, but also demonstrated what was
perceived as piracy by the LBA hierarchical societies and its close affinities with warfare. On the basis of this
evidence, it was argued that particularly promising for the identification of case studies for piracy in the MBA
and early LBA Aegean might similarly require the consideration and the reconstruction of relationships among
sites and even among individuals, especially macro actors.
