Insecurity at Sea and the Fortified Sites of the 13th/12th
­c enturies BCE on Crete


Leonidas Vokotopoulos
Independent Researcher
leonvok@gmail.com




ABSTRACT

The 13th/12th centuries BCE saw the appearance of large walled sites on Crete – a major change for an island p­ reviously
distinguished by the scarcity of fortifications. The use of these sites was brief; therefore, they were the outcome of partic-
ular circumstances – those prevailing around the 1200 BCE collapse. This paper examines three fortified sites that are
distinguished by their proximity to the coast, in order to determine if they aimed at countering ­seaborne raids or were
established by groups that carried out such acts. Regarding Kato Kastellas, a site near the bay of Zakros, the topography
is not suggestive of a pirate base. Kato Kastellas probably provided refuge to the inhabitants of the s­ urrounding area – or
to settlers that came from the sea. The fortified promontory of Elias to Nisi is near the d ­ efensible settlement of Vrokastro
but does not seem to have served as its port. Instead, it was probably established earlier, p­ ossibly by people involved in
sea raiding. The fortification on the island of Dia was hitherto dated to the Early Bronze Age; however, it should rather
be placed in the 13th century BCE. Given the importance of Dia for seafaring and the concurrent decline of Knossos, the
enceinte may tentatively be ascribed to bands of sea raiders who attempted to turn that island into a pirate base.




THE CLOSING STAGES OF THE LATE BRONZE AGE ON CRETE: 		
A BLEAK TIME AND A DIFFICULT PLACE TO LIVE

The demise of the Mycenaean administrative centers at the transition from the 13th to the 12th century BCE
resulted, inter alia, in significant changes in settlement patterns – namely, in the near abandonment of the
coastal zones and a concomitant massive relocation to the interior, often at defensible sites (on the causes of
the destructions and their outcome, see e.g., Dickinson 2006, 43–56; 2010; Middleton 2020; Maran 2022). The
evidence from mainland Greece gives the impression of a sudden, largely unanticipated collapse. In the case of
Crete, though, the relevant phenomena unfolded earlier and at a slower pace (Preston 2008, 318; Cunningham
2017, 389–90; Langohr 2017a, 24–5; Driessen and Gaignerot-Driessen 2023, 119, 125–26). Thus, the habitation
of Palaikastro and Zakros, the main centers of the easternmost part of the island, ended at the close of Late
Minoan (LM) IIIA or early in LM IIIB at the latest (Cunningham 2017, 355, 359, 373–74; Macdonald 2018,
322–23; Platon 2022a, 325; 2022b, 67–8). Further to the west, the occupation of coastal settlements continued
during the first part of LM IIIB: Mochlos and Sissi were abandoned around the middle of the 13th century BCE
(Soles 2008, 205; Langohr 2017b, 234–35), and the destruction of Malia also dates to this time (Driessen 2010,
567). Besides, the same century witnessed the decline of Poros and Kommos, the ports of the major centers of
Knossos and Ayia Triada (Dimopoulou-­Rethemiotaki 2004, 378–79; Rutter 2017, 275, 278). More importantly,
· 110 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



in LM IIIB the administrative centers of the island were well past their heyday (see Preston 2008, 318; on Ayia
Triada, see D’Agata 2017, 306). Only Kydonia retained its significance – but not necessarily for long, given that
its palace was destroyed around the middle of this period (Andreadaki-Vlazaki 2022, 196, 199).
    In sum, the evidence suggests a decline, destruction and/or abandonment of the major centers of Crete –
settlements with a long history that may have held a special significance for the inhabitants of the island. The
abandonment of the coasts indicates pervasive insecurity at sea (Nowicki 2000, 224–25, 228; Langohr 2017a,
24). However, the threats did not affect solely this zone and tensions were not necessarily entirely exogenous – as
is suggested by Kalamafka, a LM IIIB site of difficult access in the gorge of Aposelemis, which may have served
as a hideout of bandits (Kanta and Kontopodi 2017, esp. 99–100; see also Driessen and Gaignerot-Driessen
2023, 125 – where a use as a refuge is proposed; nonetheless, the topography and the finds would not exclude a
ceremonial use related to the initiation of young males and hunting). It is not entirely ­certain if the ­depopulation
of the coasts was coeval with the establishment of defensible settlements at the i­nterior. Nevertheless, the be-
ginning of the latter phenomenon can indeed be placed in LM IIIB, given the presence of such pottery at the
excavated sites (Cunningham 2017, 390; Langohr 2017a, 24–6). In any event, the profound transformations
that occurred on Crete in the 13th century BCE can be regarded as a harbinger of the processes and events
that ­resulted in the collapse of the core of the Mycenaean world itself –namely, of the palatial centers of the
­mainland– at the transition to the 12th century BCE.




THE FORTIFIED SITES OF THE 13TH/12TH CENTURIES BCE

One of the most intriguing aspects of the closing stages of the Late Bronze Age (LBA) on Crete is the a­ ppearance
of large walled sites (on these, see Nowicki 2000, 226–27; 2011a, 363–64; 2011b, 439; Vokotopoulos and Mi-
chalopoulou 2018, 149, 158–63), given that in the preceding periods the island was distinguished by the scarcity
or even absence of fortifications: apart from some walled settlements of the late Prepalatial period and the guard
houses of the 1st half of the 2nd millennium BCE (Chryssoulaki 1999), proper fortifications were limited to
certain sites resembling small fortresses (Nowicki 2011a, 355–56) and to the enceintes of centers such as Malia
(Alexiou 1980, 17–9); these are few in number and only date to the Protopalatial period. The LM III walled sites
are usually designated as fortified citadels or acropoleis (see Nowicki 2000, 41, 227; Kanta et al. 2021). These
terms are misleading, as they imply that the sites were positioned next to urban centers – which was not the case
(Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018, 149 n. 2). Therefore, here the generic appellation fortified sites is used,
since it is descriptive and hence does not predispose to a specific function.
    Only nine such sites are currently known. They are restricted to the east half of the island, the only e­ xception
being Orne Kastellos (Fig. 1). Their topography varies. Thus, two sites are coastal, whereas the wall at K  ­ ophinas
was built at the foot of the peak of the Asterousia range. Nevertheless, most sites were positioned at the confines
of the coastal plains or hilly zones, keeping a safe distance from the sea. Many were placed strategically upon
important land routes and/or near sea-lanes, and they all commanded a wide view of their ­surroundings – in-
cluding the approaches to them. Interestingly, the sites were not positioned close to the urban and ­administrative
centers of the 13th century BCE. The only exceptions were the fortifications on Mount Juktas, which loomed
over the settlement of Archanes, and Elias to Nisi – a site in the vicinity of Gournia.
    As a rule, the sites crowned isolated heights or abrupt slopes that were defined in part by cliffs. The ­protection
of the sites relied to a large extent on their topography and morphology – that is, on the remote location, diffi-
cult access and steep ground. Fortifications were only erected at the sides that were relatively easy to reach. Their
length varied from ca 100 m, at Krousonas Kastellas, to 490 m, at Juktas. The walls were articulated in straight
segments, their thickness varying from 2.20 m, at Kastrokephala, to well over 5.00 m, at Εlias to Nisi. In any
event, they were stoutly built with boulders at the sides and a rubble fill in-between. Where needed, the latter
was kept in place by cross-walls. In most cases, the fortifications represent simple enclosures. Thus, bastions
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                      · 111 ·




                            Fig. 1. Map of Crete, showing the location of the fortified sites of the 13th/12th centuries BCE.




are only attested at Kastrokephala, whilst the gates had the form of narrow openings in the walls. The enceintes
lacked the offsets, corbelled galleries and elaborately arranged gates of the fortifications at the Mycenaean pala-
tial centers. Consequently, they cannot be compared to them in terms of the sophistication of their planning or
the work force required for their erection. Nonetheless, they followed the same principles in their construction
and defensive logic, and they still constituted substantial undertakings.
    The size of the sites ranges from ca 0.6 ha at Krousonas Kastellas to almost 11 ha at Elias to Nisi. However,
not much weight should be placed in these differences, given that the extent of the walled areas was largely
determined by the configuration of the ground. In contrast, of particular interest is the variation r­ egarding the
existence or not and the extent of building remains at their interior. Thus, large settlements ­developed at sites
such as Orne and Kritsa Kastellos, whereas elsewhere traces of occupation are few – if present at all. In any case,
even at the former sites a considerable part of the fortified area was not covered by buildings.
    So far, excavations have only been carried out at Kastrokephala and Orne Kastellos. The available evidence
suggests that both these sites were settled around 1200 BCE, only to be destroyed in the course of the first half
of the 12th century BCE (Kanta 2014, 186; Kanta et al. 2021, 751, 755). Pottery of the LM IIIC period is attested
at most sites. However, a LM IIIB date of some of them –or of their first use– should not be excluded (Nowicki
2000, 226–27; 2011b, 439; Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018, 163). All these “citadels” represent new
installations. Together with the scarcity of building remains, this suggests that the fortifications were the first
structures to be erected and, as such, they constituted the most essential element of the sites (Nowicki 2000, 226;
2011a, 363–64). In any event, their use was brief; actually, the evidence suggests that some sites were ­abandoned
in the course of the construction of their walls or soon thereafter (for Kophinas, see Nowicki 2000, 46).
     The fortified sites are usually discussed together with the defensible or “refuge” settlements, which ­constituted
the dominant type of habitation at many parts of the Cretan landscape from LM IIIC until the Geometric
­period. However, in spite of the common features in their topography, the “citadels” clearly differed from these
 latter in terms of their small number, large size, scarce building remains, brief use and, last but not least, in the
 very presence of fortifications, whose scale is indicative of the complex realities of the Bronze Age rather than
 of the coming Early Iron Age (Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018, 164–65). Consequently, they should
 be regarded as a distinct class, which was the outcome of specific historical circumstances – namely, of those
 prevailing on the eve of the collapse of 1200 BCE and in its aftermath. This being said, the differences between
 the individual sites imply that they did not necessarily serve the same needs (Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou
 2018, 165–67). Given their size, the majority of them were possibly intended to become the principal centers of
· 112 ·                                   T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                        Fig. 2. Kato Kastellas, the height and the fortification wall. Overall view from the northwest.



the respective regions – which did not eventually occur. However, others probably served as temporary refuges
for the surrounding populations – or they eventually came to be used as such. Accordingly, the fortifications
may have been commissioned by the authorities of the neighboring centers or by agents who only came into
prominence in the course of this troubled transitional period – such as local functionaries, fallen nobles and
their followers, former mercenaries and sea-raiders, or wandering groups of displaced people.
     This paper will discuss three fortified sites that are distinguished by their proximity to the coast in order
to determine the implications regarding the insecure conditions that apparently prevailed at seas – namely,
their potential relation to pirate activities or intrusions from the sea. Accordingly, this study will examine if the
­fortifications aimed at countering these phenomena, or were erected by the perpetrators of such deeds.




KATO KASTELLAS

The site of Kato Kastellas is situated at the east end of Crete, at the interior of the gorge that exits at the bay
of Kato Zakros. First explored by L. Mariani (1895, 294) during the initial stage of archaeological research on
the island, the site has been investigated in the context of the survey carried out in the region of Zakros by
the “Minoan Roads” research project (Vokotopoulos 1997–1998, 237–46, 248, 263–65; Vokotopoulos and Mi-
chalopoulou 2018, 158–63, 166. See also the discussion in Nowicki 2000, 46–8; 2018, 130).
    Kato Kastellas represents an extreme example of a “fortified citadel”: The site occupies a tower-like eminence
with precipitous sides, which is only joined to the north wall of the gorge by a low saddle (Fig. 2). Access to the
top was barred by a fortification wall with a length of ca 280 m and a thickness of 3.80 to 4.40 m. This imposing
structure was partly founded upon tall bedrock shelves, which added to its height. Halfway along its length
opened two narrow gates; the one to the east was blocked early on, possibly in the course of the construction of
the wall. One more gate was situated near the west end of the wall. Building remains only cover a small part of
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                          · 113 ·




the fortified area and are widely scattered. Thus, at the west end of the height, near its summit, stood an isolated
building of ca 150 m2; another such structure was erected near the gates, whereas the walls at the south part of
the site represent a larger, oblong edifice – or ­adjoining buildings placed in a row. Finally, a much smaller struc-
ture was situated at the east end of the height. All b
                                                     ­ uildings had a rectangular shell and their size was substantial,
with the exception of the easternmost one. Given that the site is not excavated, it is not clear if they represent
dwellings, or served specific functions. In this respect, the building to the east may have been used as an ob-
servation post, given that it offers a wide view to the lower reaches of the gorge. Accordingly, the abundance
of sherds from large pithoi around the building complex at the south side of the site implies that the storage of
agricultural produce and/or water was a major concern. In any event, in terms of their size and regular form the
buildings differed markedly from the small and simple, makeshift dwellings of the LM IIIA–IIIB settlement of
Kato Zakros (see Platon 2022a, 323). The LBA pottery of Kato Kastellas is scanty and generally undiagnostic.
Nevertheless, it is compatible with a dating in LM IIIC – although it is also probable that the site, or its initial
use, dates to LM IIIB.
    The mountains that flank Kato Zakros limit the view of the sea to the part extending due east. Furthermore,
the bay itself cannot be seen from the site. The approach from the shore necessitates an arduous walk of about
45 minutes. The most convenient route –if there is any– climbs the foot of Mount Traostalos and then follows
the north side of the gorge, before descending to the saddle. Alternatively, the saddle may be reached from the
bed of the gorge, by climbing the talus slope to the west of Kato Kastellas or the equally steep ravine to its east.
    The presence of a LM III fortified site near the bay of Kato Zakros, one of the few anchorages along the rocky
east coast of Crete, is of a special interest since the historical trajectory of this part of the island was significantly
affected by the sea (Chryssoulaki 2005, 84–5; Vokotopoulos 2007, 94). Thus, in the late Prepalatial period, small
settlements were established upon the steep hills overlooking the bays of this coast, their defensible form im-
plying an ambivalent stance towards the sea, which was evidently regarded as an area of opportunities as well
as a source of threats (see Sackett et al. 1965, esp. 278; Tzedakis et al. 1999, 326; Vokotopoulos 2000, 134, 140;
2007, 38–9, 71). The Protopalatial and Neopalatial periods witnessed the rise of two urban and administrative
centers, Palaikastro and Zakros, in spite of the fragmented terrain and limited arable land of this region or its
distance from the powerhouses of central Crete. The importance of these settlements stemmed from the fact
that they were positioned upon the sea route that linked the island with the east Mediterranean, constituting
major ports of call (Platon 1974, 228; Viviers and Tsingarida 2014, 167); actually, the evidence suggests that
in the late Neopalatial period Zakros served as the eastern port of Knossos (see e.g., Platon 1974, 228; Wiener
2007, 234–35; Vokotopoulos 2022, 61–2). In the 1st millennium BCE, the polities of Palaikastro and Zakros
were succeeded by Itanos, one of the rare Cretan poleis whose asty was on the coast. As in the case of its pre-
decessors, the economy of Itanos relied in part on maritime commerce and the city drew its wider significance
from its placement on the route to the east Mediterranean (Viviers and Tsingarida 2014, 169–73), eventually
becoming a Ptolemaic protectorate (Spyridakis 1970, 55–6). Itanos was deserted in the 7th century CE, in all
probability due to the onset of the Arab raids (Xanthopoulou 2004–2005, 1027). Likewise, from the 15th until
the late 18th century CE the wider region was largely abandoned and habitation was confined to the moun-
tainous interior precisely because of the constant threat posed by piracy (Rackham and Moody 1996, 198–200;
Vokotopoulos 2007, 15–6); this is confirmed by the accounts on the destruction of settlements (Noiret 1892,
520–21) and by the dense arrangement of the network of look-out posts that aimed at assuring the prompt
response of the Venetian authorities in the face of pirate raids or of an Ottoman invasion (Arakadaki 1997, esp.
72, 74–5 figs. 1a–b, 80 fig. 2d).
     In view of the above, the abandonment of the long-lived ports of Palaikastro and Zakros at the dawn of
the 13th century BCE is suggestive of a major rupture in the history of Crete, since it implies a contraction of
­maritime trade, if not rising insecurity at seas. In this respect, of particular interest is the establishment of a
 settlement on the steep hill of Kastri, over the ruins of Palaikastro, towards the middle of LM IIIB (Sackett et al.
 1965, 280–82; Cunningham 2017, 376–77, 386–87, 389). This site may represent a last attempt to maintain over-
seas connections. However, given that the defensible settlements of the closing stages of the LBA were normally
· 114 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



positioned inland so as to avoid the threats from the sea, the coastal location of Kastri would rather suggest that
its inhabitants contributed to the insecure conditions of the period – either by providing a safe haven to sea
raiders or by an active involvement in such activities (Nowicki 2001, 29; 2018, 135; Hitchcock and Maeir 2018,
5–6; Driessen, this volume). The same cannot be said of Kato Kastellas, though. Diachronically, pirate bases
were positioned on defensible locations near major maritime routes, as was indeed the case of this site; however,
pirates invariably chose places near the shore in order to strike timely any passing vessels and protect their own
ships from attacks by their victims or rival parties (Samaras 2015, 192; Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018,
165). It is clear that Kato Kastellas did not meet these prerequisites (contra Hitchcock and Maeir 2018, 6; see also
Nowicki 2001, 27). The opposite option, that of a fortress built not by outlaws but by a pre-existing authority
–namely, a polity situated elsewhere on the island– so as to safeguard this remote region, cannot be accepted
either: the regular form of the buildings does point in this direction, yet a military installation aiming to curb
incursions from the sea would have to be placed on the bay itself.
     It would then be more reasonable to consider the walling of Kato Kastellas as an outcome of both the ­volatile
conditions at seas and the internal dynamics of this region. Thus, the site could have served as a refuge for the
inhabitants of Kato Zakros in case of threat. Alternatively, it may represent an attempt of this community to
resettle at a safer place without abandoning its ties to the sea (as suggested in Platon 2022b, 68). The above
entail a construction of the fortification at the transition from LM IIIA to LM IIIB, much earlier than the
­establishment of the excavated sites of the same class. Such a dating should not be excluded, though, on account
 of the ­prevalence of insecure conditions well before the collapse of 1200 BCE (it should be noted that this view
 differs from that expressed in Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018, 166). However, it is still possible that
 the site was settled after the abandonment of Kato Zakros, in the course of LM IIIB or at the transition to LM
 IIIC. In the 13th century BCE occupation shifted to the hilly interior, and was in all p­ robability scarce and dis-
 persed. Therefore, in case of a late dating the site would have provided protection to these scattered habitations.
 A drawback of this hypothesis is that the access from the hinterland is only possible by crossing the bed of the
 gorge – the route any enemy coming from the sea would have followed to penetrate the area. Furthermore, it is
 doubtful if the remaining inhabitants of the region had the organizational capabilities and the means to erect
 the fortifications (Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018, 166). Thus, another ­option would be that the site was
 founded by a group of immigrants, who decided to settle on this desolate height precisely because it was difficult
 to reach from the potentially hostile hinterland, but also due to its ­relative proximity to the sea – the route of
 escape, in case of failure of this endeavor.
     In sum, the available evidence does not weigh in favor of one of the aforementioned hypotheses. In any
event, the use of Kato Kastellas was brief, as is suggested by the small quantity of the pottery and the sparse
­architectural remains. In the course of LM IIIC, if not at its start, habitation was transferred to neighboring
 ­Lenika – a defensible site that was situated inside the same gorge, but offered easier access to the fertile ­hinterland
  (Vokotopoulos 1997–1998, 247–56, 263–69). As a result, this settlement proved to be more long-lived, lasting
  until the Geometric period or even beyond its end (see Vokotopoulos 1997–1998, 256; Platon 2022b, 68).




ELIAS TO NISI

The walled settlement of Elias to Nisi was investigated by the Vrokastro Survey Project (Hayden 2001; 2004a,
138–39; 2005, Site Catalogue, 24–6; see also Gaignerot-Driessen 2016, 305–6; Nowicki 2018, 132). The site is
located at the south side of the gulf of Mirabello, to the west of Gournia – the most important center of the 2nd
millennium BCE at this part of the island (for the LM IIIA–IIIB occupation, see Watrous 2012, 66–7; Watrous
et al. 2015, 439–43; Gaignerot-Driessen 2016, 351–54). Unlike most other LM III “citadels”, it is situated on the
coast – specifically, on a two-pronged promontory (Fig. 3). To its southwest rises the steep peak of Vrokastro
– the site of one of the most extensively investigated LM IIIC–Geometric defensible settlements (Hall 1914;
Hayden 1983; 2004a, 141–42; 2005, 184–86; see also Nowicki 2000, 107–9; Gaignerot-Driessen 2016, 308–11).
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                              · 115 ·




         Fig. 3. Elias to Nisi, the east prong of the promontory. In the background, the west side of the gulf of Mirabello. View from the southeast.



Vrokastro was not the only such site in the area: in LM IIIC it was flanked by a chain of settlements, situated on
the hills and ridges that oversee the coast (Hayden 2004a, 148–49, 153; 2005, 236). Elias to Nisi and Vrokastro
are close to each other and intervisible (Fig. 4). Nevertheless, because of the difficult terrain, the climb from the
promontory to the summit of Vrokastro requires about 40 minutes.
    The sides of the promontory are precipitous. However, to the north a narrow cove is formed between its
prongs, which can provide shelter to a few small vessels (Hayden 2001, 64 fig. 3, 69 fig. 6, 80). Across the neck
of the promontory stretched a 350 m-long fortification wall. This structure was distinguished by its substantial
width, which reaches 5–6 m. According to B. Hayden (2001, 70 fig. 7, 73; 2004a, 138, 360), its superstructure
consisted of a series of box-like compartments that were filled with rubble. However, the walls separating the
presumed compartments were not freestanding, since they only had one face; consequently, they represent
mere cross-walls. It seems, therefore, that the enclosure at Elias to Nisi did not differ from those of the other LM
III fortified sites in its construction and form (Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018, 160). The LM IIIA–B
sherds eroding out of the deposits upon which the wall was founded provide a terminus post quem for its erec-
tion in the 13th century BCE (see Hayden 2001, 68, 75–6; 2004a, 139). The most extensive traces of occupation
are located at the east side of the promontory, above the cove, covering an area of 2.25 ha. The pottery suggests
successive periods of use, a part of it dating to LM IIIC and the Early Iron Age (Hayden 2001, 66–8, 71; 2004a,
138–39). Building remains associated with LM III pottery were also detected at the west side of the promontory
and on the highest point of the east prong; the latter seem to represent an isolated structure, possibly a watch
tower since this spot offers a wide view to the coastline and the open sea (Hayden 2004a, 139; 2005, 24, 26).
    According to B. Hayden (2001, 80–1; 2004a, 153, 155–56), Elias to Nisi and Vrokastro had a symbiotic
relationship – that is, they complemented each other since they served different functions: Vrokastro con-
stituted the main settlement, whilst Elias to Nisi served as the port of both that site and those in the sur-
roundings. To this line of thought, the topography of Vrokastro indicates the prevalence of insecure con-
ditions in the 12th century BCE, but these are only a part of the picture, the fortified port suggesting that
the ties to the sea –and hence to the wider world– were actively maintained. Hayden (2004a, 139) did not
exclude an occupation of Elias to Nisi for only a part of the year – presumably, during the sailing season.
· 116 ·                                              T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




          Fig. 4. Elias to Nisi, the height of Vrokastro as seen from the site. In the foreground is the fortification wall. View from the north/northeast.
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                        · 117 ·




It is difficult to reconcile this view with the existence of the enclosure, though: if nothing else, this would have
necessitated the constant presence of a garrison to prevent the seizure of the port by enemies. As the closest
parallels to this dual settlement system, pairs of sites representing the asty and port of specific Cretan poleis were
cited, such as Lato and Lato pros Kamara (Hayden 2004a, 155–56). However, the ports were later additions,
since they only developed in the Hellenistic period – an extrovert time, during which the economy and poli-
tics of the Cretan poleis became increasingly tied to the affairs of the wider Aegean and Mediterranean worlds
(Coutsinas 2011, 247–48). Accordingly, the modern ports of many Aegean islands appeared much later than the
main settlements, which were usually positioned on defensible locations further inland: the development of the
coastal settlements went hand-in-hand with the rise of interregional maritime commerce and the suppression
of piracy. In contrast to the above, the 12th century BCE did not represent a time of widening horizons but of
political fragmentation, instability and decline. Consequently, the hypothesis of an upper and lower settlement
system does not seem credible. Besides, given the manifestly insecure conditions of the period, the split into two
nuclei of habitation would not have enabled an effective response in case of attack; the walling of the port but
not of the main settlement would not make much sense either.
     It would be more reasonable to assume that, instead of being complementary, the two sites expressed
­different realities and contrasting dynamics. In this regard, it is probable that they were not founded simulta-
 neously. One option would be that Elias to Nisi was established later than Vrokastro, during the brief revival
 of the middle stage of LM IIIC, representing an attempt by the inhabitants of the latter site to resettle near the
 sea in order to take advantage of the rise in maritime circulation. However, such a venture would have been
 particularly risky, given that conditions remained unstable; hence, it is not likely to have occurred. Given that
 the size of the fortification points to the realities of the period before the collapse, it is more probable that Elias
 to Nisi was the first site to be established. The earliest activity on Vrokastro may date to the close of LM IIIB,
 yet occupation only started on a significant scale at the onset of LM IIIC (Hayden 2004a, 127, 149). Therefore,
 the fortification of Elias to Nisi should be dated to the 13th century BCE or around the transition to the 12th
 century BCE at the latest.
     In theory, the walling of Elias to Nisi could have been an initiative of neighboring Gournia. In the Final
Palatial period, this settlement retained the status of an administrative center (Watrous 2012, 66–7; Watrous et
al. 2015, 443). However, only a fraction of the site was reoccupied after the LM IB destructions (Watrous 2012,
66). Moreover, survey evidence indicates that its hinterland was depopulated (Hayden 2004b, 235; Haggis 2005,
79–81; Watrous 2012, 65–6); it is even probable that this phenomenon became more intense in the 13th century
BCE, given that in the area of Vrokastro, at least, LM IIIB is elusive (Hayden 2004a, 133). It is therefore doubtful
if this center could provide the resources and the workforce for the construction of the wall at Elias to Nisi; be-
sides, if the need was felt to protect the population, one would have expected the authorities to fortify Gournia
itself. Accordingly, it is difficult to envisage the enclosure as a collective undertaking of the communities of the
area: The LM IIIA–IIIB sites in the surroundings were small to begin with (Hayden 2004a, 132–33), and the
dominant trend in the 13th century BCE was the relocation to the interior, not the foundation of new settle-
ments upon the shore (on the scarcity of LM IIIA–IIIB coastal sites in the area of Vrokastro, see Hayden 2004a,
149; 2004b, 238 fig. 17.5). In this regard, it is not without interest that Elias to Nisi was relatively easy to access
from the sea but not on the landward side, due to the presence of the cove and the fortification, respectively.
    In view of the above, it would be reasonable to assume that the people who occupied this site differed from
those inhabiting the surroundings in terms of their background and occupations. In other words, they were
probably incomers and/or bands of locals that viewed the turbulent conditions reigning at sea as an opportu-
nity rather than a problem, making their living by plundering the coasts of Mirabello and by preying upon the
ships sailing along the route that joined north-central Crete with the east Mediterranean (Vokotopoulos and
Michalopoulou 2018, 165; see also Nowicki 2001, 31; Hitchcock and Maeir 2018, 6). An involvement of the
inhabitants of Elias to Nisi with piracy was proposed by Hayden (2004a, 139) as well, who also considered the
increase in settlement during LM IIIC as indicating the influx of a new population in the area – namely, the
Dorians (Hayden 2004a, 155; 2004b, 240). This was regarded as having occurred gradually, starting in late LM
· 118 ·                                           T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




      Fig. 5. Dia, the cove of Ayios Georgios and the promontory of Korakia as seen from the highest part of the latter. View from the west/northwest.



IIIC and the Subminoan period – the time of the appearance of corbel-vaulted tombs and cremations. However,
the major rupture signaled by the walling of Elias to Nisi may indicate that this phenomenon was initiated much
earlier, towards the close of the 13th century BCE.




KORAKIA

The last case to be examined concerns the enceinte at the west end of Dia, an island situated off the north coast
of central Crete. This site has not been included among the LM III “citadels” thus far, given that it is c­ onsidered
to be earlier in date. The fortification was detected by C. Kritzas, in the course of the ­underwater survey he
carried out together with J.-Y. Cousteau (on these investigations, see Kritzas 1988a; 1988b, 10–1), and was first
discussed by S. Alexiou (1980, 19–20) in his seminal study on the “acropoleis” of Prepalatial and Protopalatial
Crete. Previously, A. Evans (1921, 298) had noticed “blocks of an early wall close to the sea” at this part of the
island; however, he also mentioned the presence of terraces and level areas on the upslope side, which implies
that he did not refer to the fortification (contra Alexiou 1980, 20); instead, these remains should be ascribed to
the habitation of the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE that extended to the northeast (see Kopaka 2012, 438,
447, 449). The site has recently been reinvestigated in the context of the surface survey conducted on Dia by the
University of Crete (Kopaka 2012, 446–47, 453).
     The fortification wall is situated on Korakia, the rocky promontory that defines from the west the ­sheltered
cove of Ayios Georgios – one of the four embayments formed at the south side of Dia (Figs. 5–6). The ­promontory
is in effect a steep slope that rises to the west and then drops into the sea forming a sheer cliff. The inclination of
the ground is smoother only at the tip of Korakia. The wall extends across the promontory on an east–west axis
(Kopaka 2012, 446, 460 figs. 14–5). Just before reaching the edge of the cliff, though, it turns to the northwest,
stretching along the bedrock outcrops that rise over the precipice, and then makes an abrupt turn to the west,
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                         · 119 ·




                       Fig. 6. Korakia, the promontory and the fortification wall. Satellite image (modified from Google Earth).



ending at the top of Korakia (Fig. 6). The changes in direction evidently aimed at including this specific spot in
the enclosed area, since it offered a wide view to the coast of Crete and the open sea. The fortification, whose
preserved length reaches ca 250 m, consisted of straight segments built in the megalithic technique, with large
blocks at the faces and a rubble core (see Alexiou 1980, 20, pl. 8; Kopaka 2012, 446). The width of the wall is
2.70 m on average. A widening at about the middle of its length may indicate a gateway; this would have been
a narrow passage, formed between two parallel segments of the wall. To the east, an oblong structure extends
along the inner side of the fortification. This may represent a buttress or –what is more probable– a staircase that
led to the battlements. The abundance of pottery at the highest part of Korakia suggests intense frequentation,
yet architectural remains are apparently lacking (Kopaka 2012, 447) – a picture which is compatible with a use
of the area as a lookout. Near the probable staircase are two contiguous rooms or small buildings that abutted
on the wall. Apart from them, no buildings seem to have existed within the enclosed area. Nevertheless, the
presence of a nucleus of habitation at the end of the promontory should not be excluded, given the relatively
thick deposits extending around the modern chapel of Analipsis (see Kopaka 2012, 466 fig. 29).
    On the basis of surface pottery, Alexiou (1980, 20) surmised that the fortification is Prepalatial in date;
furthermore, he stated that the wall was related to the prehistoric fortifications of the Aegean, citing those of
the Cyclades as examples. The ascription to exogenous influences or agents is not quite what would have been
expected, given that this view was expressed in a study aimed at deconstructing the myth of the peaceful nature
of Minoan civilization by providing the first systematic discussion of the defensible sites of the Cretan Bronze
Age. It may be guessed that Alexiou came to this conclusion due to the location of Dia between Crete and the
Cyclades, and also because the sites he studied largely lacked defenses. Besides, the fortifications of Prepalatial
Crete known to this scholar did not resemble that of Dia in their form and size (see Alexiou 1980, 11–3). It is
nevertheless surprising that he did not notice the similarity of Dia’s wall with the one of Juktas, dated by himself
to LM III, even though this latter was discussed in the same paper (Alexiou 1980, 14). The dating to the Early
Bronze Age (EBA) was retained by K. Kopaka (2012, 446 n. 15, 453), who explicitly referred to a connection
with the Cyclades.
· 120 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



    In the first half of the 3rd millennium BCE, the links between Crete and the Cyclades were strong: the
islands provided obsidian and metals, as well as valued goods such as liquids transported in jars or marble
figurines, eventually exercising considerable influence on Crete (Wilson 2008, 82–3, 89–90, 98–9). Given that
seafaring and trade were of crucial importance to the EBA Cyclades, it is fairly probable that the movement of
these products was largely carried out by the islanders (Wilson 2008, 90, 99). Dia would surely have been used
as a stepping stone during these voyages, providing respite and fresh water to the crews of the longboats (see
Kopaka 2012, 437–38). However, in spite of the evidence for Cycladic settlement elsewhere on Crete in Early
Minoan (EM) I (see Wilson 2008, 82, 86–7), it is hard to envisage such an installation on Dia. If nothing else,
the main gateway for the goods from the islands was situated on the coast opposite Dia, that is at the port of
Poros, as is indicated by the substantial quantity and variety of the Cycladic or Cycladizing products at this site
(Dimopoulou-Rethemiotaki et al. 2007, 88–92, 94; Wilson 2008, 82–3, 89–90). Furthermore, the intensity of
the contacts suggests that the relations between the islanders and the inhabitants of Crete were largely amicable.
Consequently, a fortified outpost on Dia would have been superfluous.
      The earliest Cycladic fortifications date to the Final Neolithic (Televantou 2008, 44–5), whilst in the
EBA walled settlements abounded on the islands (see Doumas 1990, 92; Marangou 1994, 471–72, 475–76;
­Sotirakopoulou 1997, 536; Angelopoulou 2014, 20; 2016–2017, 145). With the exception of Markiani, though,
 whose fortifications were constructed in Early Cycladic (EC) I and early EC II (Marangou 2006, 84, 86–7; Ren-
 frew 2006, 248), the excavated sites belong to late EC II (Angelopoulou 2016–2017, 139) – that is, they postdate
 the intensive interactions with Crete, whose heyday is placed in late EM I and EM IIA (Wilson 2008, 82, 90).
 Besides, the fortified sites of the Cyclades were densely occupied, whereas at Korakia building remains are
 scarce – if present at all. In any event, the enceinte of Dia differed significantly from those of the islands (for the
 morphology and construction techniques of Cycladic fortifications, see Bossert 1967, 57–8; Marthari 2017, 65
 [Kastri]; Plassart 1928, 14, 16–7; MacGillivray 1980, 4, 7 [Kynthos]; Angelopoulou 2014, 20, 27, 65–6 [Korphari
 ton Amygdalion]; Marangou 2006, 81–6 [Markiani]). Thus, it did not have bastions or an outwork, features that
 were typical of EC fortifications (Angelopoulou 2014, 65–6). On the other hand, it was more massive, given
 that in the Cyclades curtain walls were as a rule thin – not more than 1.70 m in width (see Bossert 1967, 57;
 ­Marangou 2006, 81 n. 11; Angelopoulou 2014, 20. The probable fortification wall at Spedos was slightly thicker,
  reaching 1.90 m: see Renfrew et al. 2022, 23–4). Last but not least, the enceinte of Dia represents a much larger
  undertaking than the Cycladic fortifications, whose walls did not exceed a length of about 70 m (see Bossert
  1967, 57; Marangou 2006, 81) – much less than at Dia. In sum, the presumed Cycladic connections of the en-
  ceinte on this island are not confirmed by the available evidence: the wall does not belong to the same ­tradition
as the EC fortifications and was not influenced from them either; therefore, it cannot be ascribed to sea-traders
or settlers originating from these islands, or to Cretan masons following the relevant prototypes. Accordingly,
the wall does not resemble the early fortifications of Crete, given its large size, but also because of its megalithic
walling and arrangement in straight sections – features not attested at Prepalatial walled settlements (for such
sites, see Vokotopoulos 2000, 139–40; Alusik 2016, 55). Consequently, a dating to the EBA is highly improbable.
    A more plausible hypothesis would be that Dia was fortified in the Middle Ages. Specifically, the wall may
have been built after the establishment of the Emirate of Crete, in the context of the successive attempts of
the East Roman Empire to retake this island. After all, Dia is mentioned repeatedly in the relevant sources.
Thus, the island provided refuge to Photeinos, co-leader of the first campaign, after the defeat of the Byzantine
army (Makrypoulias 1999–2000, 348), while in the expedition of 949 CE Dia served as the last stopover of the
Byzantine fleet on the route to Chandax – and the same must have been the case before (Christides 1984, 176;
Chaniotis 1992, 125; Makrypoulias 1999–2000, 361; Yannopoulos 2011, 164). Furthermore, according to the
Life of Athanasios Athonites, in the final campaign of 960–961 CE the island was used by the fleet of Nikephoros
Phokas as a bridgehead before attempting the landing near Chandax (Christides 1984, 178). Besides, it may
be surmised that during the ensuing siege the coves of Dia were used as anchorages by the dromons, which,
according to Leo the Deacon, patrolled the sea so as to enforce a naval blockade (Theodosius Diaconus 2017,
11). If nothing else, the importance of Dia is confirmed by the significant quantity of Middle Byzantine pottery
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                     · 121 ·




yielded by the excavation of Cousteau and Kritzas in the cove of Ayios Georgios (Kritzas 1988a, 9). Thus, if the
fortification dates indeed to the time of the last campaign, it would have aimed at securing the grip on Chandax,
as well as at preventing a seizure of Dia by reinforcements to the besieged.
    The fortifications that covered temporary or unforeseen needs, such as those constructed by armies camping
in enemy territory or populations facing invasions, were usually makeshift and simple in form (Fachard 2016,
220–21; interestingly, the interior of such enceintes is often largely empty – as is the case of the site under con-
sideration). As a result, their construction technique and morphology may deviate considerably from the norms
of the relevant periods. By way of example, at Kastro tou Lazarou, a refuge settlement of the 7th century CE
perched on one of the highest peaks of Samos, the fortification is a mere rubble enclosure, the absence of towers
or elaborately arranged gates implying that it was constructed hurriedly – most probably, in the face of the first
Arab raids (Tsakos 1979, 11, 13–4, 16–20). In the case of Dia, a hasty construction may explain the absence of
towers or the fact that no mortar was used as a binding agent, yet it cannot account for the complete lack of
the characteristic traits of Byzantine fortifications. Thus, where the wall changes direction it does not follow an
arched course; instead, its sections join at obtuse angles. Accordingly, it is much thicker than the usual Medieval
fortifications of the same scale. Furthermore, the masonry is megalithic. Last but not least, the wall is well-built
– in other words, it was not erected under pressure. As a matter of fact, the aforementioned features are typical
of the Cretan fortifications of the 13th/12th century BCE, as is the scarcity of building remains in the enclosed
area. Consequently, the wall on Dia may well date to the later part of the Bronze Age. This is a working hypoth-
esis, given the apparent lack of LM III pottery, but on the basis of the available evidence it can be considered as
the most reasonable guess. Specifically, the erection of the fortification may be regarded as the outcome of the
strategic location of Dia and the dynamics created by the interplay between the political situation at the interior
of Crete and the unsettled conditions at sea in the 13th century BCE.
     Dia is a small island with few, infertile arable areas, and freshwater is scarce (Chaniotis 1992, 126; Kopaka
2012, 435, 441–42, 444–45). Nonetheless, and in stark contrast to the exposed and inhospitable north coast
of Crete, its coves provide safe anchorage since they are protected from the northerlies (Evans 1921, 298–99;
Kritzas 1988a, 8). Moreover, Dia faces the ports that served Knossos, the hegemonic center on Crete during
most of the 2nd millennium BCE, and then the successive incarnations of the capital of the island, from Rabdh
el-Khandaq to modern Herakleion. Consequently, in the past Dia was of particular importance for naviga-
tion as well as for the control of the opposite coast and, by extension, of the whole of Crete (Kritzas 1988b,
10; ­Chaniotis 1992, 125; Theodoulou et al. 2015, 622–23). Thus, this islet played a role in events of a major
­significance for the ­history of Crete: apart from its use during the Byzantine reconquest, Dia harbored the
 French fleet that attempted to help Candia at the last stage of its siege by the Ottoman army, and the squadron of
 the great powers of Europe that imposed the autonomy of Crete from that empire. Besides, the island intermit-
 tently served as a pirate lair, whilst in early Modern times it was used as an anchorage by large merchant vessels
 (Kritzas 1988a; Chaniotis 1992, 125–26). The proveditors and engineers of the Serenissima were conscious of
 Dia’s ­importance since they repeatedly stressed the necessity of fortifying the island, but to no avail (Chaniotis
 1992, 126). ­Evidently, they were not the first to envisage such a project.
    The survey of Dia has determined the presence of sites dating to the Middle Bronze Age, but the evidence for
the later stages of the 2nd millennium BCE is currently scarce, or elusive (Kopaka et al. 2022, 223; on the periods
of use, see also Kopaka 2012, 451–52). This is intriguing, at least as far as the early Neopalatial is ­concerned – a
time of intensive exploitation, if not dense occupation, of even the most marginal areas of Crete (see Driessen
2001, 54 fig. 4.2, 59, 63). A Minoan habitation site, whose use may have spanned many periods, was on the shore
at Ayios Georgios (Evans 1921, 298; Kritzas 1988a, 8; Kopaka 2012, 449) – as it might have been expected, since
that cove always served as the main harbor of Dia (Kopaka 2012, 449–50; Theodoulou et al. 2015, 621). However,
a substantial settlement such as those on the islets of Pseira and Chryssi (Betancourt 2012, 3–7; Brogan et al.
2019) does not seem to have existed on Dia, in spite of its larger size. In light of the above, an occupation during
the Final Palatial period and especially in LM IIIB should not be taken for granted, given that the ­hinterland of
Crete was rather thinly settled (Driessen 2001, 59–60, 64). If any habitations existed during that time, they must
· 122 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



have been both few and small – that is, their occupants would not have been numerous enough to build and
then man the fortification of Korakia. It can therefore be conjectured that the erection of this wall was due to an
external intervention – as is normally the case with outsized or elaborate defensive works on small, poor and/or
sparsely settled islands, given that they cannot provide the resources for such undertakings (Bevan and Conolly
2013, 191). In other words, the purpose of the enceinte was not the protection of the inhabitants –if there were
any– but the control of the cove of Ayios Georgios and of Dia itself.
     In theory, this initiative could be ascribed to Knossos. In that case, the fortification would have aimed at
preventing the occupation of Dia by hostile forces, such as sea raiders or the army of a rival polity. However,
this hypothesis presupposes that in the 13th century BCE Knossos was still a major palatial center, which is far
from certain (see e.g., Preston 2008, 310–11, 316; Hatzaki 2017, 71–2, 74; Driessen and Mouthuy 2022, esp.
73–5; Whitelaw 2022, 38–49). The surface survey of the valley of Knossos determined a drastic contraction of
the city in LM IIIB; nonetheless, Knossos was still one of the most extensive urban centers in the Mycenaean
world (Cutler and Whitelaw 2019, 15–8; Whitelaw et al. 2019, 7–8). Due to this, and by tentatively accepting an
early LM IIIB date for the latest Linear B tablets, T. Whitelaw (2022, 41, 46–7) concluded that Knossos remained
an important administrative center, whose control extended over large parts of central and western Crete (for a
similar view, see Driessen and Mouthuy 2022, esp. 75, 79 ; but see also Driessen and Gaignerot-Driessen 2023,
esp. 126–27). However, the excavations suggest anything but a flourishing city: habitation was scattered and
usually took the form of a partial reoccupation among the ruins of earlier mansions, whilst newly constructed
dwellings were simple and poor (Hatzaki 2004, 125; 2005, esp. 75–6, 91). In other words, the picture of LM IIIB
Knossos resembles that of the other centers of Crete in the r­ eoccupation phase after the LM IB destructions (see
e.g., Preston 2008, 314; Vokotopoulos 2019, 469). A  ­ dmittedly, the excavations have been largely restricted to the
core of the site, but they should be regarded as being representative of the whole, given that the investigations
at its port yielded similar finds (­ Dimopoulou-Rethemiotaki 2004, 378–79). Besides, the decrease in the number
and wealth of tombs is also consistent with a severe recession (Hatzaki 2017, 73). In sum, even if it is to be
­accepted that parts of the palace of Knossos were in use and a­ rchives were still kept in the first stages of the 13th
 century BCE, the wider picture indicates that, as stated by E. Hatzaki (2004, 125), this center was but a mere
 shadow of its former self. This is also suggested by the fact that no attempt was made to rebuild the palace on a
 grand scale after the LM IIIA2 destruction (see Whitelaw 2022, 44, 49). Knossos continued to tax its subjects,
 if only by default, and might have expected tribute from more distant centers – even though these would have
 been largely independent at that time. However, economic exploitation is not equal to military might. Conse-
 quently, Knossos may not have been able to control its territory effectively, much less to defend it (see Driessen
 and Mouthuy 2022, 78–80 – where a contraction of the territory of Knossos and a simplified ­administrative
 apparatus are proposed for early LM IIIB); accordingly, it is doubtful if this center could commission large
 defensive works as the wall on Dia. Besides, this would apply even more for the later part of that century,
 when Knossos was in steep decline (on the palace, see Whitelaw 2022, 49; on the lack of Linear B deposits, see
 Driessen and Mouthuy 2022, 75 table 1).
    If the enceinte was not built by Knossos, or a lesser center of the wider region for that matter, then those
who undertook this project may not have represented an established authority. Specifically, and in view of the
evidence for turmoil at seas, it can be surmised that in the later part of LM IIIB and at the transition to LM IIIC
Dia became a lair for bands of pirates or freebooters, who ambushed the ships heading to Poros and plundered
the plains and valleys of the north coast of Crete – areas that were rich, but without strong centers to protect
them. These groups may have been large and well-organized, as were those that wreaked havoc in the east Med-
iterranean at that time. Thus, and provided that their raids were indeed profitable and systematic, they may have
eventually decided to fortify the promontory of Korakia so as to turn Dia into a permanently occupied pirate
base (in this regard, see Jung 2018, 280 – where the presence of Sea Peoples’ strongholds on Crete is considered
probable; see also Bevan and Conolly 2013, 196 – where the existence of large fortifications on small, barren
islands is proposed as one of the material signatures of piracy). If this was the case, the wall could be dated to late
L . VO KO T O P O U L O S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                   · 123 ·




LM IIIB – the time of the destruction of Poros by fire (see Dimopoulou-Rethemiotaki 2004, 379), when even
Knossos may have been temporarily abandoned (Hatzaki 2004, 125; 2005, 86–7).
     However, it seems that the site never became a proper settlement. In this regard, it is of interest that the
­enceinte is preserved to a height of four courses at most (Kopaka 2012, 446) and the rubble from its collapse
 is not extensive. The above may imply that the superstructure of the wall was built with mudbricks – but this
 is unlikely: The preparation of the mudbricks would have necessitated a considerable amount of water, which
 does not abound in Dia. Thus, the evidence would rather suggest that the erection of the fortification was not
 ­completed – as was the case at Kophinas. Besides, a brief use is indicated by the scarce building remains.
    It appears, therefore, that the attempt to occupy Dia on a permanent basis was eventually abandoned – either
due to the limitations imposed by the arid and barren landscape or because there was not much left to sack on
the opposite coast, whereas raiding at other regions of the Aegean or the east Mediterranean may have seemed
more lucrative. Alternatively, the bands that used Dia as a staging area may have decided instead to settle on
Crete itself once they had formed a precise picture on its topography, the fertility of the land, and the limited
capability of the inhabitants to resist their attacks (on previous knowledge of the targeted areas as a significant
factor in phenomena such as incursions and population movements, see Anthony 1990, 899–904; Jung 2009,
79; 2018, 273–74). Such a turn of events is suggested by the example of Kastrokephala – a site placed at the west
end of the coastal plain opposite Dia: the material culture of this fortified 'citadel' is largely Minoan in character
(Kanta and Karetsou 2003, 152), but is also distinguished by strong Helladic and Italian connections; according
to the excavators, this implies that Kastrokephala was founded by groups originating from these regions.1 In any
event, the standardized form and regular arrangement of the buildings indicate a conscious effort to homoge-
nize a diverse population, which implies that the incomers were regarded as a constituent part of the nascent
community – if they did not hold an important position, indeed (see ­Vokotopoulos and Michalopoulou 2018,
167).




CRETE, PIRACY AND THE FORTIFIED SITES OF THE 13TH/12TH CENTURIES
BCE

Piracy is a varied and adaptable phenomenon, which according to the circumstances appears in different forms
regarding its intensity and range, or the motives, organization and origin of those actively involved (see e.g.,
Bevan and Conolly 2013, 187–89). Geography defines the coastal zones and islandscapes best suited to pi-
racy (Hitchcock and Maeir 2018, 4–5), but does not predetermine the role(s) of their inhabitants (Bevan and
Conolly 2013, 193–95). Thus, the same regions may alternately constitute pirate nurseries or the preferential
targets of sea-raids. For example, the flourishing of the small and rocky island of Antikythera in the Hellenistic
period was largely because it became a pirate base (Bevan and Conolly 2013, 189–92). Conversely, this strate-
gically placed island witnessed successive episodes of abandonment from the 7th century CE onwards; these
coincide with periods of insecurity at seas, which suggests that the inhabitants became the victims of pirate



1 Kanta and Kontopodi 2011, 130–33. Among the relevant finds, of particular interest are two locally made carinated cups of
sub-Apennine type. The presence of these vases could be ascribed to their exotic associations. However, given their rather simple
form and the lack of painted decoration, it is unlikely that they were viewed as prestige items; instead, it is more probable that
the people who used them were accustomed with the relevant sympotic practices, if they did not come from Italy itself. Also
significant is the substantial presence of built hearths of Mycenaean type, and of cooking vessels belonging to the LH III ceramic
tradition: since cooking techniques are embedded in wider cultural patterns, they are not particularly susceptible to change –
as opposed to consumption practices, which provide a more direct reflection of social dynamics; consequently, the sudden
appearance of exogenous habits in food preparation may well indicate the presence of migrants (see e.g., Jung 2011, 69). In the case
of Kastrokephala, the cooking utensils suggest that the inhabitants included mainlanders.
· 124 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



 attacks instead of being the perpetrators of such acts (see Bevan and Conolly 2013, 192). Regarding Crete,
 in the ­Hellenistic period piracy may have contributed significantly to the economy and wider importance of
 many of its ­poleis. ­Accordingly, after the Arab conquest in the early 9th century CE, the fleets setting sail from
 Crete ­devastated the coastal regions and islands of the East Roman Empire (Christides 1981; 1984, 162–63,
 165–67, 192; ­Yannopoulos 2011, 163), so much so that it was called θεόλεστος Κρήτη (“goddamned Crete”)
 by ­Constantinus P ­ orphyrogenitus (1830, 651.15). In the 13th/12th centuries BCE, though, Crete was in the
­opposite position.
    The progressive decline of the main ports and the abandonment of the coastal areas in LM IIIB suggest that
Crete became the target of systematic attacks from the sea – a situation that apparently continued in LM IIIC.
The causes of these developments, all the more so their precocious appearance in relation to the rest of the Ae-
gean, may lie in the lack of strong polities on the island during the later part of the 13th century BCE – if not
much earlier at certain regions. The geographical position of Crete at the crossroads of the sea routes that joined
the Aegean with the central and eastern Mediterranean would have also contributed to the frequency and scale
of the depredations; if nothing else, these routes were also used by the mercenaries who offered their services to
the states of both the Aegean and the east Mediterranean – groups that would have been prone to turn to piracy
and freebooting when in need or enabled by the circumstances (Samaras 2015, 192; Jung 2018, 285–86; Maran
2022, 240–41). Having frequented Crete and being aware of its riches and internal political situation, such bands
may have chosen the island as a target of their raids and a base for further attacks – and this may have occurred
on an even larger scale in the context of the displacements caused by the 1200 BCE collapse. In this regard, if
the hypothesis of a pirate base on Dia, right in front of the port of Knossos, is indeed true, this would signify a
reality radically different from that of the “Minoan Thalassocracy” of the Neopalatial period: instead of domi-
nating the seas, the inhabitants of once mighty Knossos were under the threat of a θεόλεστος Δία.

The Multiple Facets of the Seafarer in the Late Bronze Age
Aegean


Konstantinos Tsonakas
National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
kostastso00@gmail.com




ABSTRACT

The heyday of the Mycenaean palaces coincides with a period when international trade and overseas voyages increased,
due to the complex and centralized administrations that encouraged such actions. The Mycenaean palaces were part of an
international network linking Mediterranean elites, although there are lacunae concerning the agents who e­ ngaged in those
actions, their social identity, and the variety of seafaring activities that they could accomplish with their ­contemporary
technological means. The social background of the Mycenaean seafarer seemingly matches that of the palatial elite as the
prime agent of such actions, since the latter had the resources but also the motivation, which was the acquisition of exotic
goods, a common practice for the rulers of the Late Bronze Age. The need to obtain valuable resources may not have been
limited to peaceful means, like trade and gift exchange, but it could have involved violence, warfare, pillaging and piracy.
The main purpose of this paper is to try to approach seafarers and their affiliations, i.e., the palatial and non-palatial
agents. The difficulty in distinguishing between the last two intensifies even more when the line between warfare (which
would have been characteristic of the Mycenaean administration center) and actions related to piracy is blurred.




INTRODUCTION

The sea is a fundamental element of the Mediterranean civilizations and a primary agent in their cultural
­evolution. The Mediterranean Sea provided a comprehensive range of possibilities and a range of barriers that
 each civilization had to adapt and overcome (Panagiotopoulos 2011, 37; Broodbank 2013, 65–71, 87, 154–56).
 Bronze Age cultures developed largely independently and asymmetrically, but, through continuous ­seafaring
 and wayfaring, the Mediterranean Sea created an entangled environment that engaged all who took part in
 those movements or interacted with the mobile agents (the “travelers”) themselves (Van De Mieroop 2005,
 119; ­Panagiotopoulos 2011, 38–40). Each of those civilizations had a connection to the sea and their overseas
 ­inhabitants that is tentatively implied by the dispersion of artifacts (especially pottery), and shared t­ echnological
  ­innovations across the Mediterranean (Leidwanger and Knappett 2018, 3). Despite some similarities, not all cul-
   tural groups shared the same experiences on the sea, while some of them may have been shaped under the e­ ffect
   of maritime activities. The Mycenaean cultural group probably belonged to the latter category and through
   the connections they participated in over time, as with the Cycladic and Minoan palatial culture, they rose to
   represent the most dominant cultural trend in the southern Aegean during most of the Late Bronze Age (LBA).
  The treasures of the Shaft Graves in Mycenae and the other elite burials around the Aegean during the early
Mycenaean period (Late Helladic [LH] I–IIA, ca. 1700–1450 BCE), including certain “anticipations” of this
· 132 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



­ henomenon, as in the elite warrior burial from Middle Helladic (MH) Kolonna, dated to the 18th century BCE
p
(Driessen and Macdonald 1984, 66–7; Voutsaki 1999, 112–16), suggest the existence of an active and socially
distinguishable group that sought to obtain prestige goods and establish connections with other cultural groups
(Wright 1995, 69).
    Those early activities may have taken more violent forms, as seen in the variety of weapons and the ­martial
iconography that was preferred during the late MH and early LH period, in the 17th–16th centuries BCE
(Acheson 1999, 97). Furthermore, the number of fortified sites grew during that period (Maran 1995, 68–9;
Deger-Jalkotzy 1999, 122; Gauss 2018, 51; 2019, 64–5), which might be indicative of a turbulent phase. In
the following periods and simultaneously with the establishment of the first palaces in the Greek mainland
during the 14th century BCE, their scope and engagement in seaborne activities increased. During the LBA,
the ­Mycenaean cultural trends expanded throughout the Aegean and Ionian Seas, as reflected in the decorated
pottery styles and various finds, e.g., in Rhodes (Benzi 1988; Karantzali 2009, 355–57) and Zakynthos (van
Wijngaarden et al. 2021, 604–10). Moreover, administrative centers in central and western Crete enjoyed direct
overseas contact with the palaces of the Greek mainland, as indicated by the (inscribed) transport stirrup jar
traffic (Preston 2008, 311–12; Pratt 2014, 59, 74, 84–6; 2016, 42–6). Lastly, traces of Mycenaean influence and
possible occasional physical presence can be found in the eastern Mediterranean, like Cyprus and the Levant, as
well as in the central Mediterranean, e.g., in Italy, Sardinia and the coasts of the Adriatic Sea.
     The expansion and increase of Mycenaean pottery abroad can indicate a more intense interaction with the
sea and its people during the Palatial period (LH IIIA2–IIIB, late 14th and 13th centuries BCE). The mainland
palaces would have been the main factor in that kind of venture. Even so, direct commercial interests of the
Mycenaean elite are not clear on the palatial book-keeping records in the Linear B script (de Fidio 2001, 17–8),
which raises the question of whether other groups, perhaps to some degree independent from the palaces and
its elite, were active in this realm. Those groups, which we could characterize as non-palatial, would have had a
certain level of independence from the palaces and would not have had a strong presence in the palatial Linear
B archives. From the archival documents in the Linear B script, we observe multiple economic and social do-
mains that the palace was involved in, but that was just a fraction of the total economic activity. Even more, the
archives cover only a later period and different palatial centers (Palaima 2010, 358–9). The Linear B tablets also
reveal other possible social and administrative bodies, such as the da-mo (“community”), which in turn show
us the existence of independent or at least semi-independent agents other than the palatial ones (Shelmerdine
2006, 75). Moreover, based on the vital need of the Mycenaean elite groups to acquire prestige goods as well
as valuable raw materials, like copper and bronze (Wright 1995, esp. 68–70; Voutsaki 2001, 208–13), we could
propose that specific entrepreneurial individuals and groups might have emerged to meet those demands.
    Unfortunately, the Linear B tablets offer us limited evidence about maritime affairs (Palaima 1991, 274) and
in conjunction with the inherent difficulty of controlling naval trade and other seaborne activities (Broodbank
2013, 466; Monroe 2015, 7–8, 41–2; Sherratt 2016, 290–92), all of the above generates a realm of possibilities for
numerous non-palatial agents, who possibly had an interdependent relation with the palaces of the Mycenaean
or Eastern palaces. This level of interdependency is challenging to distinguish, while palatial and non-palatial
sectors could have overlapped (de Fidio 2001, 22–3).
    To study and understand the characteristics of the Mycenaean seafarers, we would need to utilize every piece
of evidence we have at our disposal. Detailed analyses have been conducted regarding maritime affairs by the
examination of contemporary iconography and written sources (Wachsmann 1981, 1995, 1998; Wedde 1999,
2001, 2005, 2006; Emanuel 2014, 2017, 2021), which we can utilize to investigate the people behind them. The
aim of this paper would not be to categorize certain groups rigidly as traders, mercenaries, pirates or military
personnel, but to assess the “fluidity” of their positions, as they could have been able to attain a variety of roles
(either overlapping or not mutually exclusive), depending on the circumstances and their needs.

THE SOCIAL POSITION AND THE ACTIVITIES OF THE MYCENAEAN
SEAFARER

The mainland palaces were developed by certain influential groups that managed through their actions and the
possession of prestige goods to assure their legitimate claims to power (Voutsaki 2001, 213; Killen 2008, 178–79;
Shelmerdine 2008, 145). Those groups, which were probably directed towards foreign and other peer groups on
the Greek mainland, utilized violent means to consolidate power (Wright 2008, 241–2, 245–6; Tartaron 2013,
64). However, we should not exclude peaceful ways that could also have been used, such as trade with overseas
regions.
       During that period (MH/LH I), we have evidence of Mycenaean pottery in several sites around the
­Mediterranean (van Wijngaarden 2002, 261–73). The non-systematic character of overseas contact is reflected
 in the disparity in their distribution and typology, perhaps suggestive of the opportunistic mobilization of
 ­certain independent groups who sought personal wealth (Wright 2008, 243). Those activities shaped the pala-
  tial centers of the subsequent period and, by bringing in the palatial Minoan traditions, the Mycenaean elites
  were able to start using more systematic and lucrative methods to support its administration needs, such as
  ­diplomacy through gift-exchange, while still being able to employ violent means, if necessary.
   The increase of Mycenaean artifacts in the Mediterranean regions was gradual, but as mentioned above, it
was already happening through non-systematic contacts. Those contacts set the foundations of the Mycenaean
palatial systems; one such example is the assimilation of Minoan traditions, whose civilization had dominated
the Aegean and had established a wide maritime network throughout the Mediterranean (Maran 2011, 284,
289).
    This proved effective, since Mycenaean pottery began appearing exponentially throughout the ­Mediterranean
during LH III. In some areas, like Cyprus and the Levant, Mycenaean products, especially painted pottery, were
seemingly highly valued (van Wijngaarden 2002, 275–80). In Cyprus, the influence of Mycenaean pottery and
possibly other perishable materials, such as wine, perfumes and textiles, may have played an essential role in
local strategies of status legitimacy and influenced Late Cypriote social practices. Their symbolic “weight” could
have been due to their impressive decoration in comparison to indigenous ceramics or other locally available
items, or it might have been a result of their exotic origin and the status of the Mycenaean seafarers, who might
have been traders themselves or acted as guards on trading vessels (Kristiansen 2016, 166–67).
     Another aspect we should examine is the fact that maritime activities gave even less influential, non-­
palatial groups an opportunity to participate in the development of LBA long-distance networks. The growth
of ­commerce and production would have attracted numerous groups independent or semi-dependent from
the palatial control, whose characteristics and significance have been examined by several scholars (e.g., Cline
1995, 278–79; de Fidio 2001; Monroe 2011, 94–6). In the Mycenaean world, those groups have not left any
clear archaeological traces, which has led to the interpretation that the movement of goods was under control
by the Mycenaean elites through a gift exchange system with peer groups (Voutsaki 2001, 211–12; Mee 2008,
esp. 363–64, 378, 382). That system would have acted as a way to acquire prestige goods and valuable materials
and would have helped in the establishment of diplomatic relations, resulting in the formation of alliances and
­further cooperation (Mee 2008, 382).
    There are, however, two problems with the interpretation of Mycenaean artifacts and pottery as evidence
for gift-exchange across the Mediterranean. Firstly, the distribution, quality and quantity of Mycenaean pottery
“abroad” are not sufficient for exchanges of such status. Secondly, the systemic frequency of gift exchanges may
not have provided a sufficiently reciprocal and stable supply of materials. However, a counterargument to the
second problem would be supplied by the content of the Uluburun cargo, which was able to cover multiple
palatial needs, such as payments and equipment with only its bronze oxhide ingots (Papasavvas 2021, 135–43).
Furthermore, the weapons found at the shipwreck site have suggested the theory that a particular group was on
board the ship and might have sought control over its cargo (Pulak 2005, 308; Bachhuber 2006, 354–55, 359).
· 134 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



    Considering the statements above, we may ask the following questions: to what extent were the palatial
agents involved in maritime activities, and what was the role of non-palatial agents in such activities? The
­Mycenaean palaces were able to influence maritime activity indirectly, since they had significant resources.
 One such example would have been the control of naval nodes, such as the one through the Dodecanese, so
 they could have watched over any ship sailing to or from Anatolia and protected them from natural and human
 dangers (Sherratt 2001, 218–24, 226–27). However, we cannot exclude that palatial agents would have acted as
 potential threat themselves, since they had an immediate interest in the cargo borne on many of those vessels
 (Panagiotopoulos 2011, 44–5).
     Another instance, where we have evidence for the interaction between palatial and non-palatial agents, is the
ta-ra-si-ja system (Killen 2001, 161, 175–76; 2008, 194–5). In several Linear B tablets, we find that specific term,
as well as some of its derivatives (a-ta-ra-si-jo “lacking/ without ta-ra-si-ja”), which describes an ­interaction of
economic nature between the palace as holder of raw material and specialized artisans, who were at least par-
tially unaffiliated with it (Shelmerdine 2008, 143). In the Linear B tablets of the Jn series from Pylos, we observe
the recording of bronze allotments of various quantities from the palace to independent or semi-independent
copper-/bronze-smiths (ka-ke-we) for them to be processed and returned in the form of ­finished products
(Ventris and Chadwick 1973, 508–11; Killen 2008, 194). If that interpretation is accurate, it suggests that the
Mycenaean palaces did not have total control over all stages of craft production, like metalwork, textile manu-
facture and wheel chariot production. Instead, the palaces cooperated with other agents (partly ­extraneous) to
advance their production.
    Following that logic, we cannot exclude the possibility of similar groups collaborating with the palaces without
them being under their exclusive control. Unfortunately, no such interaction concerning the sea ­activities has
been uncovered in the Linear B records. However, we know about the mobilization of South E         ­ uropean groups
into the East Mediterranean and that they influenced the Mycenaean material culture (­ Leidwanger and K    ­ nappett
2018, 1–3; Maran 2018, 225–26). Groups and individuals of different specializations might have ­traveled to and
from the Aegean, offering services and exchanging material goods (Kristiansen 2016, 172–80). The manner of
their interaction is unknown and presumably diverse based on the place and the period, but that kind of mobi-
lization could have been caused by more than just a few people of elite status. Conclusively, despite having the
full potential to engage in traveling and other seaborne activities, palatial agents may not have been able to fulfill
their needs on their own and may have resorted to cooperation and the a­ ssistance of other non-palatial groups.
    The co-existence of the palatial and independent or semi-dependent groups may have been the result of
the palatial agents taking over more responsibilities once the palaces had been established and the Mycenaean
administration focused on religion as a unifying factor, with maritime activities (especially long-distance) be-
coming de-prioritized (Wright 1995, 73–4; Deger-Jalkotzy 1999, 126–27). The effects of such a decision, as well
as the further expansion of the palaces, might have given rise to higher influx of more prestige and valuable
goods, which in turn mobilized an increasing number of groups to take on maritime activities (Monroe 2015,
45; Knapp 2018, 35). However, the evidence for such groups is scanty on the Linear B tablets; only a few related
occupational appellations can be identified, such as the e-re-ta (rowers) or the na-u-do-mo, the latter in the frag-
mentary tablets PY Vn 865 and Na 568, which can be related to the occupation of the “ship-builder” (Hocker
and Palaima 1990–1991). Nevertheless, due to the elliptical nature of the Linear B records, which were meant
for ­internal book-keeping purposes, we cannot know to what extent these individuals were palace-dependent
or not.
    Contemporary Near Eastern sources provide more information about groups related to maritime activities
and, in many cases, distinguish merchants from elite groups (Monroe 2009, 56–65; 2015, 11–2, 36–42, 45–6;
Knapp 2018, 113–14, 187–88). In the LBA Aegean, such distinction is rather obscure; while some studies have
focused on palatial and non-palatial contexts of economic activity (Halstead 1993; 2001, 38–50), the conclu-
sion of a collaboration between the palace and non-palatial agents is commonly reached (de Fidio 2001, 23–4;
Voutsaki 2001, 211), with the former assuming a dominant role in political economies of those regions in the
­


LBA Aegean where they were established.
