THE ACTIVITIES AND CAPABILITIES OF THE SEAFARERS

The social background provides valuable information about the people and their relation to maritime activities.
However, their background does not necessarily define their actions (Broodbank 2013, 465–66) and sometimes,
on the sea, each situation may become warped based on the perspective of each participant in it. The activities,
in which palatial and non-palatial agents might have been engaged in, provide little evidence for us to distin-
guish them. For example, warfare and piracy often share many characteristics and their perpetrators are often
accused of the latter instead of the former (Emanuel 2018; 2021, 23). In this regard, we should consider the
possibilities seafaring provided to each agent and how it enabled them to exercise both of those actions and
even more (Monroe 2015, 42–5). Still, the characteristics of each seaborne action may give us clues about these
groups. To do that, we may conventionally divide certain fundamental maritime activities into three s­ eparate
categories: (1) economic, (2) administrative / political, and (3) warfare. Also, we should clarify that those
­categories ­concern the activities and not their agents, who may have been involved in more than one category.
    Starting from the first category, trade is commonly viewed as the prime economic activity that involves
movement of any significant scale. Therefore, the existence of important political centers, such as the Cretan
and the Mainland palaces, is not the starting point of such activities; they are a continuation of similar ac-
tivities only on a higher and more systematic level concerning their demands. Tartaron (2013, 190–98) has
described the concept of the “Small Worlds” (see also Broodbank 2000; 2014, 52–6; Horden and Purcell 2000,
523; Beaujard 2011, 7–8, 19), a network of interdependent and (chiefly heterarchically) related communities,
whose development is parallel and interconnected. Specifically, regions like the Saronic Gulf (Tartaron 2013,
212–71; 2018, 73–82) were homes of multiple settlements, which had been subjects of a single or numerous
overlords over time. Nevertheless, despite any higher authority, the connection between those settlements re-
mained intact, at least on some level, due to their proximity and diachronic relation. In those microcosms, any
authority would have contributed only by expanding the horizons of those worlds through the development
of the appropriate infrastructure, whereby better control over the region could be gained. Therefore, people
already could accomplish such feats in some capacity, and any higher authority promoted and encouraged such
kind of activities (Kristiansen 2016, 160).
     The problem in tracking short-distance trade is its scale and potential complexity, which leaves us with
­minimal evidence as a result of the quantity and perishable nature of many products. On the other hand,
 long-distance trade has a higher energy consumption, so it should also have a similar output. To attribute
 trading capabilities in both the palatial and non-palatial agents, we will have to combine the theoretical frame-
 work of the “Small Worlds” with the diachronic communication of more prominent ruling centers. Thus, a
 network is generated between tangent “Small Worlds”, which were controlled and maintained by some insti-
 tutionalized authority/-ies, while allowing for certain opportunistic seafarers to traverse them (Monroe 2009,
 239). That could have given them a chance to escape the limits of their communities, as well as to advertise their
 seafaring skills, thus promoting cooperation with higher authorities. One example of such a development might
 have been the fishermen. The expertise that came with that and other similar professions were able to make a
 transition to long-distance trade and other maritime activities smoother.
      The second category consists of several activities requiring an organized administration center, whose
­subjects must accomplish specific actions to function and develop. A well-known example of such action is
 gift-exchange. This tradition was in effect during the LBA and was significant for any established elite group, as
 it functioned as a tool for maintaining their social status and enhancing their legitimacy. We can imagine the
 participation of several different palatial and non-palatial agents to accomplish such ambitious projects. Those
 exchanges might have been a seasonal event (Wachsmann 1998, 295–99) or part of a ritualistic process (Knapp
 2018, 196), like the ship procession of Akrotiri (Raban 1984, esp. 19), but required a significant organizational
 capability. To put that into perspective, the gift of the Pharaoh to the king of Alashiya, identified with the island
 of Cyprus, would need the cargo capacity of three ships at the size of Uluburun (Papasavvas 2021, 129). The
 transportation of such valuable cargo, the equipment, the crew and their long journeys in general required a
 high organizational skill, which was within the abilities of the LBA centralized states.
· 136 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



    From the Linear B archives, we have recordings of rowers on tablets PY An 1, An 610 and An 720, whose
context, although highly elliptical, may reveal the interest and the capability of the palace of Pylos on seafaring
ventures (Palaima 1991, 285–86; Wachsmann 1999). Unfortunately, as far as the Mycenaean non-palatial agents
are concerned, we cannot know for sure if they were also able to venture as far as the east or west Mediterranean,
but eastern recordings of their counterparts show us that even merchants could attain significant wealth, while
working within a similar ruling system, but also had some protection through some kind of legislative support,
thus making those expeditions possible even for non-palatial agents (Monroe 2015, 18–9, 23–4).
    By extension, we should consider other skills that would have been useful on such long journeys and gift
exchanges; an example is the presence of a mediator or a translator, either from the region whence the sea-
farers departed, a local at the place of destination or anyone knowledgeable enough to act in this capacity
­(Panagiotopoulos 2011, 41–3). Furthermore, considering the value of some shipments and the high risk in
 those journeys, we would expect the presence of armed guards and the employment of mercenaries was a
 common practice among Near Eastern rulers (Sandars 1985, 49–53). Consequently, we can assume palatial
 and non-palatial agents’ participation even on more significant ventures. How they were cooperating cannot be
 precisely known. Still, in the case of the Mycenaean palaces, the non-palatial workforce might have been under
 some forced or obligatory service, perhaps as a means of debt payment or acquiring land privileges (Killen 1983;
 2008, 171; Shelmerdine 2008, 147).
    Since the Mycenaean palaces had only a portion of the total production under their control, the emergence
and prosperity of several non-palatial individuals and groups were very likely. Even groups that were neither
traders nor palatial agents could have benefitted from such occasions, as we observe from the possible presence
of “multiethnic” groups from the Mediterranean but also from central European regions (Kristiansen 2016;
Konstantinidi-Syvridi 2021, 54–6), who might have traveled as mercenary groups (Maran 2018, 225–33) and
offered their services to the palatial centers in exchange of prestige and valuable goods. Conclusively, the palaces
might have been able to undertake the more daring ventures because of their resources and organization skills,
but that does not exclude the involvement of non-palatial agents. A sailing journey requires several individuals
and experts, possessing skills outside the confines of palatial control (at least as textually documented), thus
requiring cooperation with other extraneous groups. Even so, the palaces would be able to intervene and benefit
by promoting such situations, for example, by constructing and maintaining harbors and anchorages (Marazzi
2018, 99–105). Thus, palaces encouraged trade within their realm, which in turn enabled them to impose taxes
on the groups that utilize their infrastructures.
    The last category concerns seaborne hostile actions and violent tactics. The problem with such actions is
the distinction between organized warfare and acts of piracy, which include hit-and-run tactics, raiding, kid-
napping and undermining actions, while avoiding direct conflict (Emanuel 2018, 68–78; Knapp 2020, 144).
This problem is further intensified when trying to identify their perpetrators, since various groups (palatial and
non-palatial) could commit such actions within a period of human mobilization and intensive trade, primarily
through the gift-exchange system (Braudel 1973, 883–84; Broodbank 2013, 466; Knapp 2020, 143).
     De Souza (1999, 16–7) rejects the term piracy without the proper legislative framework, thus identifying
them all as acts of warfare by default during the LBA. However, Emanuel (2018, 73–4) argues that even without
proper definition, we can still distinguish the two of them by several distinct characteristics; for example, the
involvement of a state in such actions would make it an act of warfare. Furthermore, the operational scale is
essential, since pirates would usually utilize speed and avoid conflict, then war actions would have been con-
ducted on larger scales. For example, the famous relief of the battle with the Sea Peoples from Medinet Habu
implies the organizational level of a state-like authority (Wiener 1999, 411–12) and would not have had such
impact, at least as the one described by the Egyptian sources, if it was a minor pirate raid. Therefore, identi-
fying agents as palatial or non-palatial can be difficult given our current evidence. In this regard, a tablet from
­Amarna (EA 38) seems to suggest that participation of a state authority in raids was not impossible; in this letter,
 the king of Alashiya, referring to the Pharaoh, denied his involvement in raiding the coasts of Egypt, while also
K . T S O NA K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                     · 137 ·




complaining about his lands being overrun by Lukka (inhabiting perhaps the region later known as Lycia in
southwestern Anatolia) (Emanuel 2021, 94–5).
    Returning to the people amenable to such actions, we can look again at Wiener’s view (Wiener 1999, 411–
12) that large-scale raids required good organization. Without discounting the ability of independent agents in
the Aegean, the Mycenaean palaces were probably the only entities capable of conducting significant enough
raids that were able to damage other centers of similar or larger size. Conversely, less influential agents could
only operate on a more limited scale, without causing significant disruption at a broader level (Knapp and Man-
ning 2016, 122–23, 135; Knapp 2020, 155–56; contra Hitchcock and Maeir 2016, 256–60).
     The obscurity that veils the perpetrators of those hostile actions, either if those were considered piracy
or ­warfare, seems to be related to two significant factors. The first one is that the resources gained from
­accomplishing such deeds were essential in administration as much as in maintaining and improving social
 status. The second factor is the “flexibility” that a seafarer could have had. Those specific groups could utilize
 their skills and assume different roles depending on each situation. Mycenaean elite groups constantly needed
 valuable r­ esources (e.g., copper) and were also capable of launching naval expeditions (in consideration of PY
 An 610, see Tartaron 2013, 125–26). Consequently, actions like raiding and piracy, which could have provided
 the ­necessary materials, should not be excluded from the agendas of the palatial agents (Samaras 2015, 200).




THE IMPACT OF MARITIME TECHNOLOGY ON THE MYCENAEAN WORLD
                                                                                “Consider things, and you will have humans.
                                                           Consider humans, and you are by that very act interested in things.”
                                                                                                            (Latour 2000, 20)


In the previous sections, we focused on the human factor and its activities, observing interactions related to the
Mycenaean social organization, economy, and administration. However, the analysis of material culture might
give us additional insights into those human groups (Knappett 2006; Olsen 2010; Knappett and Kiriatzi 2016,
1–17). The close relationship between the human and the material factor allows us to interpret the Mycenaean
society and its activities not only on their own, but also as a result of the available technology that made them
possible. On the other hand, we can watch the development of that technology due to society’s demand for
better means to yield more gainful results in its endeavors.
    The technologies we could analyze are numerous, but we would limit ourselves to a single yet important
technology for this paper. Ships have been used and developed throughout human history; for the period under
consideration, extensive research on the LBA ships is already available in detailed analyses of iconographic,
archaeological and textual evidence (Casson 1994; Wachsmann 1995, 1998; Wedde 1999, 2000, 2005; Emanuel
2017, 2021). Drawing on Knappett’s (2006, 140) theoretical framework, we can examine the effect of the phys-
ical world on social institutions, human agents and their interactions. Therefore, we should first establish that
we have no clear or detailed depictions of the LBA ships for warships or trading vessels (Tartaron 2013, 57–8).
However, their lack of specialization may pertain to their capacity to work as both raiding ships and transport
vessels (Casson 1994, 65–8; Wedde 2001, 610–12). Even the oared galleys, a characteristic Mycenaean type of
vessel, which was probably of Greek origin (Wachsmann 1981, 209–13; Wedde 2005, 29), had a flexible nature
and additional uses other than to be used in warfare (Tartaron 2013, 58–9, 63). Therefore, by examining the ship
development, from the vessels depicted on the matt-painted jars from MH Kolonna on Aegina to the painted
pottery of LH IIIC (ca. 18th to 12th century BCE), we can see that oared-type vessels have been dominant in
the Aegean. Another evidence of those vessels’ flexibility is their inability to be used as weapons, in contrast
to the later Classical triremes, in which the projection on the keel at the bow side of the ship did not have the
strength to ram other ships effectively, but was probably used for landing the ship on the beaches (Wachsmann
1998, 344–46). On the relief from Medinet Habu, we can observe that the naval battle is done mainly by men
· 138 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



wielding hooks used to capsize the enemy ships (Wachsmann 1981, 216). With all of the above in mind, we can
suggest that the Mycenaean seafarers on board those ships were able to assume multiple roles depending on the
circumstances.
    For trade and transportation, they would have chosen their vessel by cargo capacity; for warfare or piratical
actions, they would have prioritized speed and crew size. Van de Moortel (2017, 267) also categorized the LΗ
IIIB–C ships into two types D1 and D2 based on the available iconography, with D2 types having a curved hull
possibly preferred as a trading vessel, and D1 types feature a straight bottom hull, which in that case favors
speed and it might be better suited for military operations. Despite such a categorization, both of those types
could have been used in both trade and warfare if needed (Van de Moortel 2017, 268). Therefore, we can assume
that any variant of the oared galley could potentially be used in multiple situations and for multiple purposes,
while the differences in their typology were based on the preferred use of the vessels in the context of their
original construction.
    Considering the characteristics of those ships and the general picture of the LBA in the Mediterranean,
­ ycenaean seafaring groups could have taken up multiple roles, disregarding the social position of each group
M
and individual. During the LH IIIA2–IIIB, Mycenaean palaces were already engaged in trading and they had a
significant interest in the exotic materials coming from the east Mediterranean, as well as other European regions
(Tartaron 2013, 20–30, 69). However, despite their central position in terms of the west and east ­Mediterranean,
the far richer eastern coasts were situated at the edge of the Mycenaean sphere of influence. Therefore, there
was a need for multifunctional types of ships that were able to accomplish long-distance journeys, protect
­themselves from dangers or even engage in hostile actions along the trading routes if needed.
    There is a relative scarcity of ship representations during the LH IIIA2–IIIB (Petrakis 2011, 218; Tartaron
2013, 59–60; Kramer-Hajos 2016, 128–41), which may indicate that maritime activity was not at the epicenter of
the palatial scope. An alternative hypothesis is that during their peak the Mycenaean palaces were without any
apparent internal or external disturbances and the need to express naval themes might have been secondary to
others. Without diminishing the effect of maritime activities during that period, it should be considered that the
Mycenaean elite could focus on administration, probably influenced by religion. That would possibly explain
the preference for other decorating themes, although there is no clear indication to support this suggestion
further.
      In the following period (i.e., the LH IIIC), the naval themes increased dramatically compared to the p ­ revious
periods. The warlike overtones become common in this period’s pictorial themes around the Aegean, with
depictions of naval battles, namely from Kynos (Dakoronia 2006, with further bibliography). Moreover, armed
or helmeted rowers or other figures on board are also some of the features that display similar naval activities
(Emanuel 2021, 320–23). The appearance of such a theme should not necessarily imply an increase in such
­activities, but a refocus on the significance of those actions and their perpetrators. The decline of the Mycenaean
 palaces would have resulted in further decentralization, especially in the peripheral regions of the Mycenaean
 sphere of influence (Tartaron 2013, 69–71). That would have led to the emergence of regional rulers, who
 would have risen to the occasion and prospered by using their naval skills and exploiting the waning power
 of the palaces to their benefit. This is showcased better in Wedde’s suggestion (2005, 33–6) of a “galley subcul-
 ture” centered on the ship captains and their crews, who sailed the Aegean Sea. Their activity might have been
 ­moderately suppressed by the Mycenaean palaces at their peak, but as of the end of their rule, groups using
  such vessels might have turned on palatial rulers, maybe even contributing to their final demise. Εlite-related
  themes, such as feasting, hunting and fight scenes, were popular on pictorial pottery during LΗ IIIC, perhaps
  suggestive of new elite societies, which valued military prowess (Kramer-Hajos 2016, 149–65) or perhaps capi-
  talized on associations with the palatial past (Crielaard 2006, 282–84). The oared galley made those acquisitions
  possible by any means, violent or non-violent, which led to the prosperity of groups probably unaffiliated with
  the ­palaces’ administrations.
    The LH IIIC iconography offers significant indications of the impact that those vessels had, as much as the
actions that they allowed (Samaras 2015, 193–95, 199–200). Those deeds could be considered either piracy
K . T S O NA K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                           · 139 ·




or warfare; however, this distinction might not have mattered as much to the LH societies. Interestingly, the
­Mycenaean period seems to close on a “circle”, which started partly through the initiative of some opportunistic
 elite groups and, towards its end, came to reflect a similar situation, namely through the intense war activity on
 the sea and the importance of warrior prowess in contemporary social practice.




CONCLUSIONS

The purpose of this paper has been to discuss some critical aspects of the identity and status of the people who
were crossing the Aegean during the LBA. Nevertheless, as shown by the discussion above, the evidence does
not point to a unique direction. On the contrary, the more we focus on these activities, the more we under-
stand that the sea was not only a place where ships sailed and goods moved through. Groups originating from
different backgrounds were able to sail the seas, each one of them bearing different agendas. The lack of total
control of the sea routes allowed those groups to accomplish various feats and assume multiple roles, potentially
interchangeably. Traders, mercenaries, warriors and pirates were able to interact with palatial and non-palatial
agents depending on the circumstances and the needs of each group.
     Detailed archaeological research and analytical studies of various categories of evidence (e.g., textual,
­iconographical) may enable us to identify certain factors, activities and networks that did affect or were affected
 by long-distance sea travel. The LBA seafarers were not necessarily representatives of their cultures, but they
 inevitably connected them through their own mobility, ideas and objects that moved with those groups.

Seeking Timber in the Pirates’ Lairs
The New Approach to Wenamun’s Report



Andreas L adas
National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
andreasladas2015@gmail.com




ABSTRACT

The Egyptians used cedar wood for the construction of both the sacred barks and the ships sailing in the ­Mediterranean
and the Red Sea. However, the lack of cedar and timber suitable for shipbuilding in general led Egypt to seek various ways
of securing the required quantity of wood. This is precisely the reason for the journey of the Egyptian priest Wenamun,
who was sent by the High Priest of Amun at Thebes to the Phoenician city of Byblos to procure the ­necessary cedar wood to
build the sacred bark of the god. During this journey, Wenamun was led into an action that could be described as piracy.
The present paper attempts to show whether the text with Wenamun’s adventures is a historical narrative, which offers
valuable information about the political, social and economic developments that took place in the eastern Mediterranean
during the end of the Late Bronze Age and the beginning of the Early Iron Age. It also attempts to identify the political,
economic and even psychological factors that contributed to Wenamun’s action of attacking a ship on the high seas and
stealing its silver. The main aim of examining this evidence is to determine whether Wenamun became, even temporarily,
a pirate.




INTRODUCTION

At the end of the Late Bronze Age (LBA) in the Levant, powerful empires, such as those of the Egyptians and
Hittites, coexisted with small kingdoms, which were mostly subordinate to some of the powers of the time.
Egypt succeeded in consolidating its position in the region. The construction of Egyptian temples in Byblos
and Egyptian-style fortresses in the Levant area, as well as the installation of an Egyptian governor in Byblos,
confirm that Egypt tried in every way to secure its interests and procure the necessary supplies (Stein 2017, 17).
    This situation was maintained until the 19th Dynasty (Sherratt 2003, 49–51), but changed significantly after
the fall of the Hittite empire and the gradual weakening of Egypt in the early 12th century BCE. The new sit-
uation in the Levant is reflected in an 11th century BCE text, the story of Wenamun. The eponymous hero of
the story, whose name is transcribed as WN-Imn, traveled to Byblos to obtain the necessary timber to build the
sacred bark of Amun. This paper discusses the historicity of Wenamun’s narrative and examines the depiction
of piracy as per this text. To approach these issues, it is necessary to re-examine the text in direct relation to the
social and political conditions developed in the eastern Mediterranean during the period of its composition, i.e.,
at the beginning of the 11th century BCE.

THE STORY OF WENAMUN: LITERARY TEXT OR HISTORICAL DOCUMENT?

According to the surviving text, an Egyptian priest, Wenamun, is sent by the High Priest of Amun at Thebes
Herihor to the Phoenician city of Byblos to acquire the necessary cedar wood in order to build the great noble
bark of the god of Karnak (Fig. 1). He initially found himself in Tanis, where he accepted the help of Smendes,
and from there he headed towards Dor, a coastal city at the foot of Mount Carmel, where the Tjeker lived, one
of the groups included in the heterogeneous group known as the Sea Peoples. Some scholars associated their
name with the term Teucrians, used by several ancient Greek and Roman authors to refer to the Trojans (e.g.,
Hdt. 2.114.2, 2.118.2–3, 5.13.2; Callim. Hymn 3.231; Verg. Aen. 1.248, 4.537, 12.824; for the Tjeker see Moreau
2003, 118, with further references).
    While Wenamun was in Dor, one of his crew members stole a significant portion of the gold and silver that
was intended for the purchase of cedar. To retrieve his lost wealth, Wenamun attacked a Tjeker ship and headed
for Byblos, where Zakar-Baal, the ruler of the city, refused to help him and asked him to leave immediately. After
several adventures, the hero of the story managed to secure the required timber. The ending remains unknown.
All we know is that the Tjeker pursued him and that Wenamun ended up in Alashiya (Cyprus), where he was
attacked, as the islanders tried to kill him. He finally escaped and headed to Hatiba, the princess of the local
kingdom, asking her to protect him and help him return home (Wilson 1969a, 26–8; for Hatiba and the possi-
bility of rule by women in LBA Cyprus see Middleton 2023, 102–7).
    The text with the story of Wenamun was discovered on a two-leaf papyrus (known as M120) in 1891, and
since then many different opinions have been expressed among scholars as to whether it is a purely literary text
(e.g., Egberts 1991, 57), an authentic account (e.g., Erman 1923, 225; Wente 2003, 116) or an administrative
report (e.g., Goedicke 1975, 4–5). More recently, Schipper (2005, 39–40) sought to reconcile these conflicting
views arguing that, although the story of Wenamun is a highly artistic literary work, the text incorporates a
wealth of historical knowledge.
A . L A DA S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                 · 147 ·




     This particular character of the text creates objections regarding its reliability, since a text in order to
be ­considered “historical” and not a “historic-fiction” narrative should be confirmed by other sources. The
­acceptance of this position has always been the cradle of disputes that have been formulated about Wenamun.
 Certain ­elements, such as the founding of Tanis by Smendes and his friendly relations with the high priest of
 Amun, are not attested anywhere else except in the text of Wenamun. At the same time, the acceptance of the
 Tjeker presence in Dor during the 11th century BCE requires a more careful review. Excavations conducted in
 the area by Ephraim Stern (Hebrew University of Jerusalem) in the period 1980–2000 concluded that the city
 was inhabited around 1150 BCE; however findings and stratigraphy have not yet confirmed the presence of
 the Tjeker in the specific area before the beginning of the 10th century BCE, where two settlements have been
 identified, one of the Tjeker and a later one of the Phoenicians (Nibbi 1996, 77–95). On the other hand, in the
 ­Onomasticon of Amenope, an Egyptian text dated from the late 20th to 22nd Dynasty, the exact place of resi-
  dence of the Sherden, Tjeker and the Philistines around Ako, Dor and the Philistine Pentapolis respectively is
  recorded (Stern 1994, 89).
    At the same time, the exact dating of the text was another issue that troubled academic circles until the last
decade or so. Most scholars have now accepted that the text was composed in the first half of the 11th century
(for a full discussion see Sass 2002, 248–49). In any case, the text of Wenamun deserves special attention as it
is the only, at least for now, written source, which renders in a way, perhaps literary, the political and social-­
economic status quo that had arisen in the eastern Mediterranean at the beginning of the 11th century BCE.
    The historical core of the text primarily lies in the reason for which the journey is made. Undoubtedly,
the sacred boats of Amun were made of cedar wood because of the religious character attached to that wood
(Meiggs 1982, 407). Understandably, since they also needed repairing from time to time, an interest in trying to
source cedar arose. Unfortunately, the archaeological remains that can confirm the use of cedar by the E
                                                                                                       ­ gyptians
are very limited. Specifically, we currently know of the 4th Dynasty Pharaoh Khufu’s boat (Jenkins 1980, 80;
Abdradou et al. 2022), the boats found at Dahshur (Creasman 2010, 113), as well as cedar planks found at Wadi/
Mersa Gawasis (Ward and Zarraro 2010, 30).
    The use of cedar wood by the Egyptians for the construction of both the sacred barks and the ships sailing
in the Great Green Sea, i.e., the Mediterranean, as well as in the Red Sea, is also confirmed by written sources
(Wilson 1969b, 227–63). The introduction of ash and meru timber as early as the 4th Dynasty period is men-
tioned in the fragmentary text of the Palermo Stele (Grimal 1988, 91–2). The mention of these two different
types of wood has led some scholars to associate the name ash with cedar (Rich 2016, 52–3). Although there
is much disagreement about this particular connection, the view of Chatonnet (2001, 43) can be accepted; he
argued that the terms meru and ash refer to coniferous trees suitable for shipbuilding, which Egypt was deprived
of. After all, as pointed out by the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus (19.58.3) and an Akkadian list of toponyms,
Lebanon was known for both cedar and cypress (Rowton 1967, 269).
     In most cases, neither the type of wood nor the use for which it was intended is specified. However, it
­appears that Egypt had very limited timber, which could not satisfy its needs, not only in shipbuilding but also
 in architecture. The Amarna letters confirm Egypt’s need to procure wood from other areas, such as Cyprus,
 since in the Troodos Mountains there were coniferous trees (pine and cedar) that could be used for shipbuilding
 (EA 35, 40; Moran 1992, 107, 113).
    Egypt did not consistently rely on legal trade to acquire the timber it required; in certain cases, procurement
was achieved through acts of looting. Such a case is referred on Kamose’s Second Stele, where, along with the
commemoration of his victory against the Hyksos, it is also pointed out that from the various ships in the port
of Avaris he secured various goods, among which were also various types of timber, without, however, them
being named (Knapp 2018, 105). In other cases, looting of entire ships with all their goods is recorded, as seen
in the chronicle of Thutmose III, which refers to the Pharaoh’s fifth campaign in the north (Breasted 1906, 196
§460). A similar incident is described in the chronicle of the ninth campaign of the same Pharaoh, which took
place in the 29th year of his reign. After the capture of two cities in the Zahi region and the surrender of another
· 148 ·                                             T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




          Fig. 2. Detail of the wall relief at Medinet Habu depicting Ramses III defeating the Sea Peoples in the naval battle of the Nile Delta (Oltau).



one in the Nuges region, the Pharaoh secured a quantity of wood, which is simply described as excellent without
specifying its species (Breasted 1906, 205 §490). Perhaps the Zahi region was known for its timber or for some
particular kind of tree and for this reason it is not mentioned by the writer of the chronicle.
     Moreover, Egypt tried early on to bring under its control areas of the Levant from which it could receive
as tribute, among other things, the timber it needed. In the record of the tribute paid by the region of Retenu,
which is located in Palestine, to the Egyptian Pharaoh, it is noted that among other things he gave logs of every
kind of tree that thrived in the region (Breasted 1906, 206 §491). Thutmose III created in the coastal cities
of the Levant, Beirut, Sidon, Tyre and Byblos naval bases which, together with small garrisons, maintained
Egypt’s control in the region, but at the same time supplied Egypt with the goods it did not possess (Gilan 2013,
51). During his reign, Byblos sent cedar to the Pharaoh as tribute (Winand 2011, 544), while on Ramses III’s
­funerary monument at Medinet Habu (Fig. 2) there are listed masts, sails and spars made of Phoenician wood
 (Liphschitz and Biger 1991, 168). Therefore, it seems that the supply of cedar from Byblos mentioned in the text
 of Wenamun is a historical truth.
     The choice of cedar by carpenters is still preferred today due to the properties it presents, and preference for
it in antiquity was by no means accidental. Specifically, woodworkers, when choosing the appropriate timber
for building a ship, are asked to take into account the hardness and density of the material, then its mechanical
strength along with its resistance to attack by fungi, termites etc., while the speed at which drying is achieved
should not be overlooked as well as the ease with which wood is processed (Meiggs 1982, 55; Damianidis 2013,
174–78). These elements should have been an a priori condition for the peoples of the eastern ­Mediterranean,
with the result that cedar had become one of the most valuable types of woods, as it shows moderate variability
in its dimensions, great resistance to biological attacks and moderate difficulty in its processing (­ Pavlogeorgatos
2012, 48–9; see also Pulak 2001; Liphschitz 2012; Ward 2013; Rich 2016). Unfortunately, the texts from
the eastern Mediterranean, the Aegean and the Near East do not offer the necessary information about the
­preference for cedar wood. Several centuries later, Theophrastus (Hist. pl. 5.7.1–5.8.1) informs us about the
 properties of the cedar of Lebanon.
A . L A DA S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                    · 149 ·




                                           Fig. 3. The route of Wenamun’s journey (map by the author).



    The element, however, on which we should focus on our attention is the route taken by Wenamun when he
sailed from Tanis and entered the Mediterranean (Fig. 3). The course he took is the usual route followed by a
ship when traveling from Egypt to Levant, as this course was facilitated by the sea currents flowing in the area.
Specifically, a current flowing from the Strait of Gibraltar, weakening near the Gulf of Sirte, was strengthened
by the waters of the Nile that flowed into the Mediterranean, following a course to the east, crossing the Syro-­
Palestinian coast and from there reaching the northeastern coasts of Asia (Antypas 2019, 64–5). Along this
route, there were also coastal cities with harbors and safe anchorages where each ship could stop. Three coastal
cities are marked along Wenamun’s route: Dor, Tyre and Byblos.
    In all three of these cities, harbors and port facilities have been identified that are consistent with the period
in which Wenamun’s voyage takes place. The excavator of the underwater area around the coastline of Dor
Avner Raban (University of Haifa) argues that these harbor facilities should be considered the first attributed to
one of the so-called Sea Peoples (see Stern 1994, 97–8). Tyre also maintained close trade and political relations
with Egypt due to its geographical location. This city from the end of the 11th century BCE began to acquire a
decisive role in international trade. After all, this is attested by several later sources of the Hellenistic and Roman
times, in which four different harbors are mentioned (Marriner et al. 2008, 1282). The Bronze Age port facilities
of the city have been identified on the northern leeward façade of Tyre (Marriner and Morhange 2005, 183–84).
Moreover, Tyre had a double port, one for conducting trade and one for docking warships (Woolmer 2017, 97).
Regarding the port of Byblos, the research project “Byblos and the Sea Project”, directed by Nicolas Grimal and
Martine Franchis-Allouche, confirmed the existence of a harbor during the Bronze Age at the southern foot of
the ancient city (Franchis-Allouche and Grimal 2016, 248–74).
     The course followed by Wenamun should also be examined in terms of time dimension. The length of time
it takes to get from point A to point B was and continues to be of particular importance to sailors even today.
According to the study by Crystal Safadi and Fraser Sturt (2019, 3–6), the time it took a ship to get from B
                                                                                                           ­ yblos
· 150 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



to Cyprus was directly dependent not only on the season, but also on the time of day the journey would start.
The aforementioned research demonstrated that the travel could be carried out during winter and that a direct
connection between Byblos and Cyprus was possible without one having to run a route along the coast of
­Syro-Palestine to Ugarit and thence to head east towards Cyprus. Besides, a similar course to that of Wenamun
 is also confirmed in one of the Amarna letters (EA 114; Moran 1992, 188–89), where Rib-Hadda, in order to
 avoid the ships of the Aziru, orders Amanmasa to cross the open sea from Byblos to Cyprus and from there go
 to Egypt.




EGYPTIAN OFFICIAL OR PIRATE?

Wenamun’s decision to rob a Tjeker ship reminds many of an act of piracy. The term piracy first appears in an
Attic inscription of the mid-3rd century BCE from Rhamnous (de Souza 1999, 3–4). However, it can be argued
that the concept of piracy predates the appearance of the term. For example, the term bandits was used by
Homer (ληϊστῆρες, e.g., Od. 3.73, 17.425) and Thucydides (λῃσταὶ, e.g., 1.8.1, 6.4.5) to refer to robbers of the
sea, i.e., pirates (LSJ, s.v. λῃστεία). In the eastern Mediterranean texts, there are several references to acts that
could be characterized as piratical (e.g., Ormerod 1924, 81–8; Sandars 1985; Derks 2016, 17–9; Hitchcock and
Maeir 2016; Kopanias 2019; contra de Souza 1999, 16–17). The Amarna letters reflect the insecurity existing at
sea and the danger faced by coastal areas, which were often attacked by groups, whose main objective was to
secure loot (EA 38; Μoran 1992, 111–12). At the same time, many inscriptions that accompany the reliefs with
the achievements of the Pharaohs point out the naval battles they fought to repel enemies attacking Egypt by
sea, with a typical example being the naval battle of Ramses III at Medinet Habu (Emanuel 2017, 63–70; Kopa-
nias 2021, 257–58; Fig. 2).
     Before proceeding with the characterization of Wenamun as a pirate or not, it is necessary to clearly d
                                                                                                           ­ efine
the context within which an act can be considered as piracy. The general observation that in war armies meet
and face each other on land or sea seems rather simplistic (Emanuel 2017, 33). Shelley Wachsmann (1998,
317–21), on the other hand, considers that in war there is involvement of the participating state with its troops
and vessels, which does not happen in the case of piracy (see also Emanuel 2017, 33–5). Philip de Souza (1999,
1), referring to the piracy of Graeco-Roman times, has characterized the pirates as “armed robbers whose
­activities normally involve the use of ships”. In the story of Wenamun, there is no involvement of any state
 power. Wenamun acted alone, made a decision by himself and put it into effect immediately, without waiting
 for approval of an official state authority. In Egypt, no one knew anything about the unexpected turn of events
 that took place at Dor and then off Tyre. Wenamun neither reported anything back to his superiors, nor asked
 for their guidance about what course of action he should follow. His action was financially motivated and done
 for personal gain; he had to complete his mission and return to Egypt with the required amount of cedar.
    The question inevitably arises, whether Wenamun could be classified as a pirate. It is a fact that, based on the
modern perception of pirates, as it began to take shape in recent times, i.e., after the so-called “Golden Age of
piracy” (late 17th – early 18th century CE), pirates are described as dangerous, marginalized groups, who plied
the seas with the aim of plundering territories, killing, capturing inhabitants in order to sell them as slaves or
to receive ransom for their release. For example, such an image of pirates is captured in The Travels of Reverend
Ólafur Egilsson, a 17th-century text describing the raid of pirates from Salé and Algiers on Iceland (Hreinsson
and Nichols 2008).
   At the end of the LBA and the beginning of the Early Iron Age (EIA), however, the identity of the pirate does
not seem to correspond to the one of a marginalized person, as it emerges from history and literature of the Early
Modern and Modern periods. The environment in which the sailor, the merchant, the seafarer moves is fluid
and full of multiple and unexpected risks. This element of the variability of conditions in the marine environ-
ment influenced and ultimately shaped trade relations and exchanges (Monroe 2011, 95). In this ever-changing
A . L A DA S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                     · 151 ·




and unstable environment, people move for different reasons but with the same goal, profit. Although there
were many dangers at sea, merchants gained much, as trade was already from the LBA a “heterarchical” activity
that was not only controlled by official state bodies but also by private individuals (Monroe 2015, 46).
    At the same time, the collapse of the great empires in the eastern Mediterranean and the Aegean at the end
of the LBA led to “an increase in political, social and economic fragmentation and liquidity” (Sherratt 2003, 53).
New social groups formed a new elite, which sought to establish itself, among other ways, through sea raids.
This new elite, members of which participated in the commercial networks controlled by the palaces in the
previous period, was now actively involved in trade but for their own benefit. Their involvement was achieved
either through trade (by controlling the already existing trade routes and markets) or through piracy. Therefore,
piracy should be understood as an “irregular, typically hostile, ongoing economic activity carried out for per-
sonal benefit and involving the use of ships, maritime mobility and plundering, at sea and along coastal areas”
(Knapp 2018, 36). The pirate was not necessarily an adventurer, a bandit, but could be a ship owner, a merchant
or even a government official, like Wenamun, who plundered when that was deemed necessary (Knapp 2020,
155).
     Therefore, what needs to be taken into consideration is under which circumstances a person can become a
pirate. In the Odyssey (14.191–359), the king of Ithaca, transformed into a beggar by Athena, tells Eumaeus a
fake story, as he presents himself as the son of Castor from Crete. He recounts that, just a month after his return
from the ten-year war in Troy, he sought new adventures; thus he and his companions went to Egypt for raiding.
However, this expedition did not have a positive outcome, because of a factor pointed out by the narrator
himself, which is directly related to human nature: “But my comrades, yielding to wantonness, and led on by
their own might” (Od. 14.262, trans. A. T. Murray, Cambridge, Mass., 1919). Namely, arrogance led O      ­ dysseus’
companions to raid the fields, to enslave young children and women, and to kill unsuspecting farmers and
­fishermen, until Pharaoh sent an army to confront the invaders.
     Wenamun’s transformation from the Elder of the Portal of the Temple of Amun to a pirate cannot be
­attributed to arrogance but to necessity that prompts him to such an act. The purpose of his journey was to
 secure the timber needed to build god’s great noble bark. His mission was going smoothly until he himself be-
 came the victim of a robbery. Wenamun’s decision to take a piratical action was not chosen from the beginning.
 At first, he appealed to the commander of Dor to help him find the amount that had been stolen from him,
 but Beder (or Bederi) refused to get involved, as the robbery had not been committed by any of his citizens.
 Without the help of any official authority, he decided to solve his problem by himself resorting to piracy, which
 was financially motivated and done for Wenamun’s own benefit. A possible failure would damage his prestige
 and it was highly likely he would be accused of very significant crimes. On the contrary, successful completion
 of his mission would further consolidate his position.
       For a better understanding of his act, some other factors must be taken into account. The text of
Wenamun dates to the 11th century BCE and captures the new political situation that has been formed in the
­Mediterranean. Cyprian Broodbank (2013, 394) has characterized the Mediterranean as “an anarchic, free-
 for-all zone for anyone with the skill, daring and funds to set out upon it”. The collapse of the Hittite empire, the
 emergence of new independent powerful centers on the Levant coast and the weakening of Egypt are evident in
 ­Wenamun’s text and can justify the state of uncertainty and instability that prevailed. He himself initially tried
  to follow the legal route by seeking the help of the official state authority. However, he realized that his status as
  a ­representative of Amun could no longer help him get out of his dead-end situation.
    Egypt during the 11th century BCE has lost the prestige it possessed in the past (Emanuel 2021, 197–200).
The presence of the Pharaoh through the emissaries of Egypt did not inspire any awe in the vassal rulers of the
Levant (Stein 2017, 17). Wenamun perceived this new reality the hard way, by personally experiencing it. When
he arrived in Byblos, he faced the prince of Byblos Zakar-Baals’ disparaging or even better hostile behavior,
since the ruler of the city refused to offer him any help. Instead, he was persistently asking him for 29 days to
leave, as the Tjeker were sailing off Byblos, and apparently he did not want to provoke them.
· 152 ·                              T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



    Byblos actively participated in the international trade network of the time and, as it can be understood from
the text, its ruler managed timber trade by controlling the entire process of logging, transporting logs to Byblos,
and also administering their sale. From the 12th to the 10th century BCE, the royal courts of the coastal cities
of the Levant controlled trade, often using the institution of the hubur, a type of trading cooperative. The com-
mander of Byblos stated that he had twenty ships in Byblos that are in hubur with Smendes of Egypt and also
that fifty of his coastal ships are in partnership with Urkatel, an enigmatic person who must have been some
powerful merchant (Woolmer 2017, 89). Byblos was no longer a tributary region of Egypt that was called upon
to offer Egypt the needed timber. Its ruler managed the trade and determined the conditions under which it was
conducted himself. What concerned Wenamun was how he would complete his mission, as his failure would be
an admission of his own incompetence, potentially affecting his prestige and position in the priesthood.




CONCLUSIONS

The text of Wenamun’s adventures has caused several disputes among scholars as to its historicity. There were
many who questioned the historical basis of the text, considering it to be a literary narrative with elements of
verisimilitude. However, the re-examination of the text that was attempted showed that the evidence presented
is confirmed by both the archaeological findings and the written sources from the eastern Mediterranean at the
end of the LBA and at the beginning of the EIA. The purpose of Wenamun’s journey, namely to procure cedar
from Byblos, is not a product of fiction, but seems to correspond to historical reality as Egypt did not have cedar
wood, which was necessary for shipbuilding. Also, the course followed by the Egyptian official is as expected as
the sea currents that sail in the area favor navigation. Furthermore, the mention of specific coastal cities, such
as Dor, Tyre and Byblos, confirms the historical core of the text, since they have been proven to have had a port
and port facilities and participated in the international trade network that had been formed at the beginning of
the 11th century BCE.
    At the same time, the narrative seems to reflect the political and social situation that had developed on the
shores of the Levant after the fall of the Hittite empire and the weakening of Egypt. The autonomy and power
the coastal cities in the aforementioned region had gained, affected the way that trade was as of then conducted
for Egypt, and more specifically the cedar trade. Byblos was no longer a vassal to Egypt; instead it was its ruler
who managed the cedar trade. This new reality turned Wenamun from a Priest of god Amun to a pirate in order
to complete his mission. The hero’s decision to attack and rob the Tjeker ship was a conscious action on his
part. It constituted a solution, undoubtedly unorthodox, but acceptable, which could be applied whenever the
circumstances dictated.
