Piratical Ships of the Aegean
A Comparative and Diachronic Approach of the Ships Used by the Pirates of the
Aegean during the Classical and Hellenistic Period



Ioannis Nakas
University of Haifa
jnak77@yahoo.com




ABSTRACT

The ship has always been the primary weapon and asset of every form of piracy. The ability of pirates to build, maintain
and man their ships would condition the success of any piratical endeavor, while the size and the type of these ships was,
in turn, determined by their owners’ needs and abilities. In the Aegean Sea, from the beginning of the history of piracy,
lighter and faster oared vessels were preferred, which were able to take advantage of their speed, as well as the r­ egion’s
geomorphology, moving swiftly between friendly and hostile coasts and islands, and offering the possibility of efficient
maneuvering and stealth. At the same time, their size was dependent on the ability of the piratical ­communities to support
their construction and manning. This paper explores the typology of the Classical and Hellenistic-era piratical ships in
the Aegean, as these are known through written sources and iconography, giving a comparative image of these ships and
connecting their use with practical issues, such as cost, manning and seaworthiness.




INTRODUCTION

Piracy has been one of the main features of the maritime cultural landscape in the Aegean Sea already since
Prehistory, as iconography, textual evidence and verbal tradition has documented, and has remained one of the
most important (and quite troublesome for many) occupations of the locals until the 19th century (Ormerod
1924, 13–4; Krantonelli 1985, 1991, 1998). The ramifications of piratical activity were numerous (political, fi-
nancial, social, symbolic), affecting nearly all aspects of life on the islands and coasts of the archipelago. Never-
theless, the practice of piracy required one essential tool and/or weapon, and that was the ship. The availability
of ships, their numbers, sizes, crews and seaworthiness dictated to a great extent the possibility of practicing
piracy in a successful way, as well as its impact on the communities that employed it (or suffered by it). It is
thus essential to have a clear view of the types of ships used by pirates throughout the ages, in order to fully
­understand and study the extent, form and impact of piracy both to perpetrators and victims.
   This paper deals with the ships that were used by pirates in the Aegean Sea during the Classical and H
                                                                                                        ­ ellenistic
period based on written sources, which form the bulk of evidence concerning piracy for this period, but also on
iconography, archaeology, experimental archaeology and ethnographical parallels. The period under study was
very important in the history of the Aegean and the Mediterranean in general, witnessing the development of
great naval powers, such as Athens or Rome, as well as an increase and better organization of piracy, especially
towards the end of the period (Tarn 1930, 129–41; Morrison and Coates 1996, 1–93). This study seeks to give
· 294 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



a diachronic approach of the development of piratical ships and the practicalities related with their use, such
as their seaworthiness, fighting power and logistics. This is an aspect of piracy that has not yet been sufficiently
explored in such a manner.




METHODOLOGY: POTENTIAL, PROBLEMS AND MAIN QUESTIONS

Piracy in the ancient world is a rather elusive subject of study (de Souza 1999, 2). The reason is simple: it was
predominantly (as has remained until today) an activity practiced in the margins of organized society and usu-
ally by small maritime communities, who had little interest or means in leaving proper documentation of their
activities. Piracy was, also, often interweaved with other, legal, activities, such as trade and warfare, r­ esulting in
the limits between the predatory/piratical economies and domination spaces or thalassocracies being obscure
and difficult to establish with precision in historiography (Bresson 2008, 214–19; for a discussion on the various
approaches on the issue, see Deramaix 2013, 359–87). Things become worse by the fact that the oared vessels
commonly employed for piratical activities in antiquity do not survive as shipwrecks in the region, due to their
light construction and lack of cargo to protect their wooden hulls (Wilson 2011, 33–9; Boetto 2012), and by the
fact that when galley images survive, there is no evidence to connect them to any piratical activity whatsoever.
And this is true also in the Aegean Sea, despite the richness in finds, both in the sea and on land, and iconog-
raphy.
    The only direct (to a certain degree) source of information concerning the ships used by the pirates of the
Classical and Hellenistic Aegean is, therefore, written evidence. The period studied here is, most probably, the
richest in terms of written documentation of nearly all aspects of contemporary life, with sources ranging from
historical texts to inscriptions and from poetry to graffiti. The methodology employed by this study is based
on the thorough examination of all written evidence available and their correlation with archaeological data,
iconography and historical parallels, in order not only to merely document the types of ships used by pirates,
but also to explore the practicalities and logistics of their employment and the ramifications these could have in
the practice of contemporary piracy. The basic questions this paper tries to answer concern the types of ships
used by pirates of the period studied, whether these were specially-built vessels or whether they were the same
as ships used in other types of maritime conflicts, whether these ships had a dual use for trade too, and, finally,
why did pirates choose specific types of vessels.




THE EVIDENCE

The Classical period
Despite the establishment of strong state naval fleets, such as the famous Athenian one, during the Classical
­period, piracy remained a constant threat to ship traffic and coastal communities (Ormerod 1924, 108–9;
 de Souza 1999, 43–96). The earliest references to piratical ships in the period come from two passages from
 ­Thucydides. In the first one, the historian describes how some Megarians, who conspired with the Athenians in
  431 BCE, would pretend to be pirates, using a small boat or akation, which they carried on a cart in and out of
  the city walls every night:

           “Every night for a long time back, under pretense of marauding [ὡς λῃσταί], in order to have a
           means of opening the gates, they had been used, with the consent of the officer in command, to carry
           by night a sculling boat [ἀκάτιον ἀμφηρικὸν] upon a cart along the ditch to the sea, and so to sail
           out” (Thuc. 4.67.3, trans. J.M. Dent, London and New York, 1910).
I . NA K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                   · 295 ·




    In the second passage, Thucydides describes the events in Sphakteria (425 BCE). He documents how
the Athenian general Demosthenes, preparing the defense of the islet, took weaponry “from a thirty-oared
[τριακοντόρου/triaconter] Messenian privateer [λῃστρικῆς] and a boat [κέλητος/keles] belonging to some
­Messenians who happened to have come to them” (Thuc. 4.9.1, trans. J.M. Dent, London and New York, 1910).
    The use of triaconters as raiding and plundering ships is also attested by Polyaenus, who reports that around
378 BCE Iphicrates raided the coasts of Phoenicia with one hundred such ships with great success (Strat. 3.9.63).
Although the reference does not describe Iphicrates’ actions as piratical, the use of these ships for a successful
raid implies that it was ideal for piratical use too (Casson 1971, 125). Around 350 BCE, Aeschines refers to the
ship epaktrokeles as a proverbial pirate ship, in which men with great lust and desire board as pirates to seek
their fortune: “these it is that fill the robbers’ bands [τὰ λῃστήρια], that send men on board the pirates’ boats [τὸν
ἐπακτροκέλητα]” (Aeschin. In Tim. 191, trans. C.D. Adams, London and New York, 1919).
     A new type of piratical ship, the hemiolia, which was a light galley that included a second file of oarsmen at
its center, appears in the 4th century BCE and a series of references in written sources underlines its importance.
It is first reported in the Etymologicum Magnum, at a reference roughly dated in the 4th century BCE, where
a Carian hemiolia, most likely belonging to pirates, is mentioned (450.38). Also, Arrian (Anab. 3.2.4) reports
that in 331 BCE Aristonikos, the tyrant of Methymna in Lesvos, sailed into the harbor of Chios with five pirate
hemioliai (ξὺν ἡμιολίαις λῃστρικαῖς πέντε) before being apprehended by Alexander’s troops and put to death
(Morrison and Coates 1996, 262).


The Hellenistic period
The conquest of the Aegean and Ionia by Alexander brought a short period of peace and safety in the seas,
which was, however, soon to finish, with the series of wars of the Successors, in which pirates took advantage
of the instability and were also employed by the rulers of the period as corsairs (de Souza 1999, 43–96). The
hemiolia continues to be firmly associated with piracy. Theophrastus, around 300 BCE, mentions the term as
the ­proverbial symbol of piratical threat, seen by cowards lurking behind each cape: “The coward, when he is at
sea, claims that p­ romontories are pirate ships [ἡμιολίας] (Char. 25.2, trans. J. Diggle, Cambridge, Mass., 2004).
Even in the 2nd century CE, Longus reports Carian pirates raiding the coast with a hemiolia (Daphnis and Chloe
1.28.1). In the early 3rd century BCE, the Rhodians counteract the piratical hemiolia by developing an improved
and larger version of it, the trihemiolia, one of the most successful warships of the period (Casson 1971, 130–31;
Gabrielsen 2001, 224; Pacheco 2020, 101). The trihemiolia was heavier and faster than the hemiolia by being a
full bireme along its whole length, but with a third file of oarsmen added at its center and, interestingly enough,
is never cited as a vessel used by pirates, but solely by official state fleets.
    About 200 BCE, another type of ship is reported as a pirate vessel. The lembos (λέμβος) is first mentioned
as the main vessel of the Liburnian pirates in the Adriatic, along with the later liburnae (Polyb. 2.9.1–2; Livy
45.30.12–15; see also Boršić et al. 2021), but is soon introduced in the Aegean too. In 197 BCE, Philip V sailed
to a parley at the Maliac Gulf in central Greece on a pristis (πρίστις, i.e., saw-fish), accompanied by five lemboi
(Polyb. 18.1.1). It is very likely that the lemboi and pristis (possibly a heavier version of the former) were
­similar to the liburna and were used for similar purposes, i.e., for piracy, raids etc. (Casson 1971, 25–6, 126–27;
 ­Morrison and Coates 1996, 263–64).
     The last heyday of piracy in the Aegean during the Hellenistic period was the Mithridatic wars (88–63 BCE),
during which the region became the main theater of a series of conflicts, both on land and in the sea ­(Morrison
and Coates 1996, 115–19). Mithridates employed and supported the Cilician pirates, who thus became p      ­ owerful
and numerous, greatly improving their military power and organization (App. Mith. 14.96; Ormerod 1924, 190–
247; de Souza 1999, 97–148). Initially, they employed relatively small ships, such as h­ emioliai and m
                                                                                                      ­ yoparones,
but they soon managed to build or acquire larger vessels, such as biremes (δίκροτοι), triremes and even, for the
first time, heavier cataphract vessels (Plut. Pomp. 24.4–5). The final defeat of Mithridates and his allies and the
· 296 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



occupation of Cilicia by the Romans brought practically the end of Hellenistic piracy (de Souza 1999, 149–224).




DISCUSSION

Typology of the pirate ships
The Classical and Hellenistic period saw the creation and development of multitude of galley types, each with
different size, crew and purpose (Morrison 1995, 68–77; Morrison and Coates 1996, 255–78). As it has become
clear, however, from the presentation of the evidence, the ships used by the pirates belonged to relatively small
types, fitted best for their uses within piratical activities. In this section, each ship type is presented and dis-
cussed according to its size and size of crew, from the smallest to the largest one.
      The akation (ἀκάτιον) and the lembos (λέμβος) appear to have been the smallest piratical ships used during
the period studied, since both terms mean boat or skiff in ancient Greek. The akation appears only once in
written sources in relation to piracy and in the peculiar circumstances of the Megarians using a skiff that can
be easily carried on a cart (see above), so it is very likely that it was not a term employed regularly for piratical
­vessels. It is also possible that the vessel was too small to accommodate any important attacking force to be
 useful in piratical activities. Lembos, on the other hand, appears much more often as a piratical ship in written
 sources. According to these references (as well as to others, which are not related to piracy), the term de-
 scribed various undecked small galleys with 16 to 50 oarsmen and was quite similar to the liburna, with which
 it ­operated side-by-side in Hellenistic Illyria (Ormerod 1924, 29; Morrison and Coates 1996, 264; Boršić et al.
 2021) and probably appears on the Illyrian coins of the 2nd century BCE (Höckman 1997, fig. 1.2–3, 5–6). It is
 possible that the liburna was introduced in the Aegean by the so-called Tyrrhenian pirates, who had expanded
 their operations there in the 2nd century BCE (Ormerod 1924, 127). A unique example of a lembos most likely
 survives in Pisa (Boat C): the well-preserved vessel was a small undecked galley with six pairs of oars, a single
 mast and a cutwater, that could have been used for various activities, such as espionage, raids or simply for
 ­ferrying passengers within harbors and estuaries (Bonino 2010; Olaberria et al. 2023).
     The triakonter (τριακόντορος) was one of the simplest and lightest types of galleys employed in the Aegean
and known already from the Geometric period (Ormerod 1924, 29; Casson 1971, 44–5). It was a light, undecked
monoreme galley with 15 benches of oarsmen, arranged in single files on the sides of the ship. It was most
­probably equipped, like almost all oared vessels of the period, with a cutwater at the bow. It is unknown whether
 such a small vessel could also employ a ram in battle, being probably too light to withstand the tensions created
 by ramming. It had limited space both for provisions or loot, as well as for extra marines and, as described by
 Polyaenus for Iphicrates’ raid in Phoenicia (see above), oarsmen doubled as fighters. Thanks to its small size and
 corresponding draft, a triakonter was not only swift, but it could also approach shallow waters and estuaries and
 be hauled on beaches and required a smaller crew. There are no known depictions of this type of ship during
 the period studied.
    The myoparo (μυοπάρων), which means mouse in ancient Greek, is known as one of the ships used by the
Cilician pirates in the early 1st century BCE, but little is known about its size and form. A unique image of it
survives in the 3rd-century CE ship mosaic of Althiburus in Tunisia, where a series of ships are depicted, along
with their names (Gauckler 1905, 134–35, fig. 16; Duval 1949; Redaelli 2014). It appears to have been similar
to the lembos described above: a small, undecked oared vessel (Ormerod 1924, 30; Casson 1971, 132, fig. 137).
     As its name suggests (κέλης, i.e., racehorse), the keles (celes in Latin) and its diminutives (κελήτιον) or
­variations (ἐπακτροκέλης) were swift oared ships, ideal for piratical use. Very little is known about this ship,
 which appears in the Althiburus mosaic as a small, simple galley. It was most likely very similar to the lembos
 and the myoparo, whereas the epaktrokeles must have been a larger version of it (Ormerod 1924, 30; Casson
 1971, 161–62, fig. 137).
    Probably the pirates’ favorite ship, the hemiolia (ἡμιολία) was a two-banked, undecked variation of a
I . NA K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                  · 297 ·




t­ riakonter or a pentekonter (Ormerod 1924, 29; Coates 1995, 139–40; Morrison 1995, 73–4; Morrison and
 Coates 1996, 317–18, fig. 73). It had 30 to 50 oarsmen arranged in two superimposed files but, in contrast to
 larger vessels such as biremes or triremes, the second file could only be accommodated in the wider central
 part of the hull (hence the name that means one-and-a-half). It has also been suggested that a hemiolia had a
 slenderer hull compared to the similar liburna, because it used a rowing outrigger (apostis), which allowed more
 efficient rowing, without widening the hull itself (Morrison and Coates 1996, 317–18). Thanks to its low length-
 to-beam ratio, it was an easily maneuverable ship, especially when compared to the much slimmer triremes or
 heavier galleys, and could accommodate marines, whereas a light deck protected the rowing crew. It is estimated
 it could reach a speed of 7½ knots, less than a trihemiolia or a trireme but more than a liburna (Morrison and
Coates 1996, Appendix D). It is possible that the hemiolia was developed as a pirate ship in Caria, since it is
related by written sources with Carian pirates (Morrison 1995, 73).
    The bireme, the trireme and the cataphract appear only once in relation to piratical fleets, and that is in the
fleets of the Cilician pirates that allied with Mithridates in the early 1st century BCE. All three types were widely
employed by contemporary and earlier naval fleets, and they were relatively heavy vessels, with crews of 100
to 200 people, whereas the cataphracts were even heavier (usually tetreres’/fours or penteres’/fives; Casson 1971,
123, n. 94), with closed superstructures in order to protect their rowing crews (Morrison and Coates 1996,
255–57). Nevertheless, these cannot be considered common pirate ships, since they only appear within this his-
torical framework, when the Cilician pirate cities developed, thanks to the wealth accumulated through raiding
and the support by Mithridates, proper naval fleet.


Evolution of the pirate ships
According to the written sources discussed above, in the Classical and Hellenistic Aegean there seems to have
been an evolution from simpler and lighter to more elaborate and heavier piratical ships. The earliest ships em-
ployed in piracy were the small triakonters and keletes, which were relatively small vessels. The operation of great
naval fleets during the 5th and the early 4th centuries BCE in the Aegean most likely prevented pirates from
building, capturing or buying larger ships and limited them to the simplest galleys they could afford, which also
fitted their purposes better. The rising of piracy within the endemic warfare of the Successors after Alexander
boosted the size of piratical ships and that is when the hemiolia appeared, a larger and heavier ship, which was
no match for the much larger Hellenistic galleys in terms of fighting power, but was much faster and easier to
handle and hide. Smaller vessels, such as myoparones and lemboi, continued to be used, although the hemiolia
became the “trademark” of the pirates of the period. Finally, as Cilician piracy reached its peak –with the organi-
zation of a proper “pirate state”, the acquisition of enough resources, but also the need to deploy stronger vessels
to fight the naval fleets of the Romans– we witness a surge both in the number and in the size of vessels em-
ployed, and for the first time triremes and cataphracts appear (Morrison 1995, 73; Morrison and Coates 1996,
115–19). This period, however, is unique in the history of ancient piracy and most probably no ship heavier
than a hemiolia was ever properly used for any piratical operations in the area during the ­Graeco-Roman an-
tiquity. It is not surprising that also in much more recent periods, like the 16th–19th centuries, ships of similar
dimensions, such as the fusta, the galliota, the felouka or the mistico, were used in the Aegean by the local pirates
(Ormerod 1924, 26–8; Krantonelli 1985, 341–49; 1991, 425; 1998, 286–88).


Fighting techniques and employment
There is little to no evidence in written sources about the techniques used by the piratical vessels during the
­period studied and ancient authors hardly ever describe how pirates employed their vessels in battle. Pirate
 ships always belong to oared types, as would be naturally expected, since the ability to move without the help
 of wind and to achieve great speed was an essential part of ambushing, raiding and evading pursuing ships.
 ­Ramming could have also been employed in battle, but it is quite likely that this would have been possible only
  by relatively large and sturdier vessels, such as hemioliai or triremes (Coates 1995, 133–34). It should also be
· 298 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



noted that capturing an enemy ship would be much more profitable for pirates, who could reuse it or sell it.
There is no reference to the existence of marines (ἐπιβάται) on pirate vessels. In smaller vessels, where there was
also little space for extra troops, the rowing crew could easily double as marines too, but larger ones should have
had a number of marines (hoplites, archers etc.) onboard in order to tackle enemy ships in sea battles, as well as
hostile forces on land. A useful weapon would have also been catapults, which were a common feature of Hel-
lenistic warships, but there is no reference to their use by pirates. The large piratical fleets of the Cilician pirates
were, most likely, organized in the models of other contemporary naval powers, with larger vessels manned by
large numbers of well-armed and trained marines, were equipped with rams and catapults, and were employed
like every other proper naval fleet of the period, particularly when joining forces with rulers like Mithridates,
but there is no direct information about how these fleets were organized and used.


LOGISTICS OF THE PIRATE SHIPS

A vital element of the operation of piratical fleets or single vessels that often eludes the attention of scholars is the
logistics related with it. Every ship requires certain resources to be constructed, equipped, manned, provisioned
and maintained, especially the oared vessels, which not only needed much larger crews (oarsmen, ­marines
etc.), but also constant maintenance, in order to remain in fighting condition (Coates 1995, 132; Dotson 1995,
217). The ability of a community or state to maintain a fleet (or in the cases of small islands even a single ship)
depended on the availability of resources, monetary or not.
    A major issue must have been the provisioning of timber, which was often scarce in the arid Aegean islands
and would have had to be imported or ships to be constructed in areas, where there were natural forests, such
as the coasts of Asia Minor (Morrison and Coates 1996, 354). Although these practices were common in the
naval fleets of the period (e.g., the Athenians would construct triremes in Macedonia; Borza 1987, 39), it is
doubtful whether pirates had the abilities to fund such endeavors, keeping in mind that local timber would also
have to be used for the rest of the regional fleets, consisting of merchant ships, ferries or fishing boats. It is not
surprising that the largest piratical fleets were the ones employed by the Cilicians, who had direct access to an
extended mountainous hinterland that would easily provide material for galley building.
    The same logistic problems would have existed for the rest of the shipbuilding material. Metal was employed
for the nails (bronze or copper), although the extent of their use in galley hulls remains unknown (Coates 1995,
131), as well as for anchors (iron, lead or bronze; Kapitän 1984, 36–43; Votruba 2014, 78) and possibly for
seathing (lead; Kahanov and Ashkenazi 2011). Rigging equipment (ropes, sails, pulleys etc.) was also essential
for navigation, since all ancient galleys would regularly hoist sails and avoid rowing when wind was favorable
(Casson 1971, 229–38; Dotson 1995, 220). Finally, special protective primers or other types of paint were im-
portant to protect the wooden hull from rotting and from shipworms, but also to decorate them (Galinier and
Nantet 2020, 60–8), whereas in one case it is reported by Philostratus that scout and pirate ships would be
painted blue for camouflage (Imag. 1.19; cf. Casson 1971, 212, n. 48).
    The light, undecked galleys of the period, required regular maintenance, especially during the winter months,
to remain seaworthy, as well as specialized personnel to undertake such tasks. It is thus not surprising that pi-
rates preferred relatively small ships, which were easier to build and maintain. Piratical communities, being,
most probably, small and functioning in the margins of society and in remote and poor regions like some of
the small Aegean islands or Cilicia, were unable and unwilling to maintain proper galley fleets (Ormerod 1924,
14–5, 142–43). Furthermore, for communities, where piracy was a “part-time” occupation of poor farmers or
mariners who had turned to it out of necessity, as Aristotle describes (Pol. 1256b; Gabrielsen 2013, 141; Pacheco
2020, 99), the maintenance of oared vessels was an extra burden, since, due to their lack of space that could be
used to transport cargos, these ships could have no dual use as warships and merchantmen and any income
supplied by them would be strictly related to warfare, raids or piracy (merchant galleys were not ­unknown, but
they are not reported in relation to any piratical activity; Casson 1995, 117–23).
    The maintenance of galleys in the ancient world was also commonly related to the construction and o
                                                                                                      ­ peration
I . NA K A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                  · 299 ·




of shipsheds and slipways, where galleys were hauled and maintained usually during the winter months (on the
ancient shipsheds, see Blackman and Rankov 2013). There have been many simple, single slipways carved on
the shores of various small Aegean islands or of the mainland, which could have been used by pirate commu-
nities to shelter and/or hide their vessels (their size corresponds not to triremes or larger vessels, but to smaller
ships such as the ones employed by pirates; Baika 2013, 248–49) and allow for a swift launching when prey was
in sight. Nevertheless, there has been no firm evidence connecting any of these naval installations with piracy
and these could as well have been outpost for squadrons of small, swift coastguard vessels (φυλακίδες νῆες or
navis speculatoria) that are known to have operated along the coasts in antiquity.
    Another important issue related with the logistics of piratical ships was provisioning. A hemiolia, with a
crew of 50 oarsmen, plus five other crewmembers, would require considerable daily provisions of water and
food to be able to operate. Each oarsman would consume 2.1 to 6.6 liters of water per day (­ depending on the
temperature and the amount of rowing involved) and 4,000 to 5,000 kilocalories (Dotson 1995, 219–20). It is
doubtful that such a vessel could carry water for more than a couple of days in the sea due to the limited hold
underneath the rowing benches, and thus would require regular stops for provisioning. ­Furthermore, it would
not spend nights in the open sea, seeking instead shelter in protected bays and beaches (Tarn 1930, 124; Casson
1971, 89–90). Piratical ships, therefore, had a rather limited operational radius, unless they were supported by
allies or managed to control their illegal activities and act as regular vessels.
   One final, logistical and human resource deficiency of piratical fleets was their manning. Not only they
required an experienced and trained rowing crew, which would also double as fighters, but it was a task that
had to be undertaken by the fittest members of the community and, at the same time, was a rather dangerous
occupation. The loss of a piratical galley at sea would mean the loss of many of the youngest and most dynamic
members of the community. Taking into consideration that the coastal communities of the Aegean (at least the
ones from the smaller islands and coastal settlements that were most likely to harbor piracy) were relatively
small (Reger 1994, 51–5), the operation of piratical ships would have been an activity done with great caution
and care, especially towards the precious tools of piracy, i.e., the ships.




CONCLUSIONS

This brief examination of the sources concerning piracy in the Classical and Hellenistic Aegean shows that
the ­pirates of these periods tended to use small, light and swift ships for their endeavors. Their favorite ships
appear to have been the triakonter and the hemiolia, which they preferred for their small size, speed and
­maneuverability. Smaller ships, such as the lembos or the keles, were also employed. Larger units, such as tri-
remes or cataphracts, were only used in the occasion of the heyday of Cilician piracy in the early 1st century
BCE, when pirates expanded their sphere of operations, along with their resources and funding, but this was a
unique event. The choice of smaller vessels was not only due to their qualities concerning speed, small draft and
stealthiness (Ormerod 1924, 26–8), but was also imposed by the nature of piracy, which operated in the fringes
of society and states of the period, and considered relatively small communities of limited means, for which
ships were precious as tools and weapons but also difficult to obtain, man and maintain. Finally, there seems to
have been no type of vessel specially designed and built for or by pirates, who would adopt and use the vessels
most ­suitable for their activities and deploy them in accordance with their needs.

Seascapes and the Athenian Relationship with the Sea in Cult
and Vase-Painting


Eleni Manakidou
Aristotle University of Thessaloniki
hmanak@hist.auth.gr




ABSTRACT

Iconographic patterns and themes depicting the sea and its world have a diachronic, though relatively limited, presence
in Attic vase painting. At the core of these are the ship representations, often accompanied by various other features (e.g.,
dolphins, fish, waves) and human figures, composing aspects of seascapes in a variety of pictorial contexts. In Geometric
pottery of the 8th century BCE, ships participate in multi-figured narrative scenes (e.g., warfare, departure, sailing, ship-
wreck) as early as the Middle Geometric II, although most of them belong to the Late Geometric I. In Protoattic pottery
of the 7th century BCE, the known depictions of ships are impressively limited and do not allow the identification of
specific nautical scenes. The ship representations in the 6th century BCE Attic black-figured pottery have certain common
features in terms of rendering of their parts and accessories. Regardless of the vase shape and the subject of the scenes, the
ships are always placed in their natural context, i.e., the sea, sometimes individually and sometimes in pairs or groups
(from four to six). There are three vase shapes usually chosen for ship depictions: lebes, kylix and volute krater, in order of
frequency (less often in amphorae, hydriae, oinochoai, plates). Almost all these vases are associated with the symposium
and date from the last quarter of the 6th and the first twenty years of the 5th centuries BCE, apart from three earlier
representations in the second quarter of the 6th century BCE. Among the numerous votive offerings in Greek sanctuaries,
the evidence stands out, mainly from literary and epigraphic sources and less from archaeological finds, for the dedication
of ships, whole or parts of them, and ship models on the occasion of war or trade successes. For Athens, naval victories
against the Persians were the main occasion for such dedications. Moreover, the Athenians’ relationship with the sea is
evident in certain ritual events associated with it as part of the polis’ official festivals.



                                                                            In memory of an invaluable colleague and friend

                                                when the statues fall silent / and the myths concur / the voices / vibrate […]
                                                                                       and suddenly reveal the eternal secrets

                            Nikos Engonopoulos, The Voices (“The Returns of the Birds”, trans. D. Connoly, Athens, 2007).



The Acropolis of Athens is about 8 km from the bay of Phaleron, the nearest coastline where the city’s harbor
was located until the beginning of the 5th century BCE. The port was accessible by a broad wagon road (ἁμαξιτή
ὁδός), the Phaleric Road, which more or less overlapped with today’s Faliron Street. At its junction with Spyros
Dontas Street, there was probably the “Alade” gate (ἅλαδε, IG I3 84, lines 34–35) or eastern Phaleric gate, which
designated the beginning of the course of the Phaleric wall (458/7 BCE, Thuc. 2.13.7) to the coast of Phaleron
(Taxiarchi 2009; Theocharaki 2020, 42–4, 229 n. 10, 267–68). There was also a western Phaleric gate, the
· 304 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



s­ o-called Southern gate, at the foot of the Muses Hill, on today’s Erechtheion Street (Theocharaki 2020, 248–50).
 In addition to the importance of the city’s first harbor, for its economic development as early as the time of Solon
 at the beginning of the 6th century BCE (Haas 1985), we must also consider the early presence of the maritime
 element in the religious life of the Athenians and its reflection on Attic vase-painting. Below, we will discuss
 some cultic events and various representations, showcasing the Athenian connection to the sea.


CULTIC CONNECTIONS WITH THE SEA IN ATHENIAN RELIGION

The procession called “ἅλαδε ἔλασις” (group walk and ride to the sea) ended in Phaleron on the third day (16th
of the month Boedromion) of the Eleusinian Mysteries, comprising the ritual cleansing of the worshippers
(μύσται) in the sea and of the piglets for slaughter brought along for the celebration. Another procession during
the celebration of the Plynteria would also arrive at Phaleron, where the xoanon of Athena Polias would be
washed into the sea by the washers (λουτρίδαι), two girls of the genus of Praxieridai (on the 25th or 26th/27th
of the month Thargelion, depending on the chronological order with the Kallynteria). The xoanon was thus
cleansed from any impurity, thanks to the antiseptic properties of the salt water. Ritual baths of xoana, mainly in
rivers, are also known for other deities related to fertility and women across the Greek world (such as Artemis,
Hera, Aphrodite). However, in Athens, the day of the Plynteria had a special significance, as it was ἀποφράς
(unlucky, fateful), and thus with the bathing of the goddess in the sea and the return of the clean xoanon to the
temple normality was restored to the city (Burkert 1977, 134, 347–48; Parker 1996, 307–8).
    Near the coast of Phaleron was the sanctuary of Athena Skiras (Paus. 1.36.4; a similar one also in Salamis:
Hdt. 8.94.2), which was the ending point of the Oschophoria procession (Burkert 1977, 385; Parker 1996, 309–
11). This was another fertility festival, a ritual associated with the return of Theseus from Crete – apart from
the connection with Dionysos and the Salaminian people. Another Attic festival, the Kybernesia (Parker 1996,
315), was indirectly connected with Theseus –as well as with Salamis– and with the foundation of two heroa in
Phaleron for the captain Nausithoos and the prowman Phaiax, who were sent by the Salaminian Skiros to assist
Theseus’ journey to Crete (Plut. Thes. 17.6). It is therefore plausible that the Kybernesia was a naval celebration
for the captains and crews of ships, who played an important role in the economic and military power of the
city. The heroic cult of Frontis at Sounion (Parker 1996, 35) also falls into the same category, if we accept the
existence of his heroon in the sanctuary of Athena in Sounion.
    To conclude this brief overview, I would like to mention two ship-wagons that stand out in the cultic life of
the city and emphasize its close relationship with the sea: first, the ship-cart depicted on some late black-figure
skyphoi (BAPD 465, 4319, 4321; Morrison and Williams 1968, 116; Basch 1987, 227–8; Fritzilas 2006, 10, 15–8,
264), in the context of Dionysian processions and in connection with the introduction of the cult of Dionysus
Eleuthereus in Athens (Burkert 1977, 166, 254, 257–58). Second, the ship-cart that carried up to a certain point
the woven peplos of Athena in the procession of the Great Panathenaia to the Acropolis (Fritzilas 2006, 31;
Williams 2007, 149; Wachsmann 2012). Boat races (νηῶν ἅμιλλα) consisting of ephebes from different tribes
competing against each other became an athletic event of the Panathenaea at a much later time.




IMAGES OF SHIPS (AS WHOLE OR IN PARTS) IN ATTIC POTTERY

The ship representations on Attic Geometric vases are well known and have been studied from various
­iconographic and typological aspects (first by Kirk 1949; then by Morrison and Williams 1968, 12–42; Ahlberg
 1971; Basch 1987, 161–87; more recently by Haug 2012, 296–307; see also Petrakova 2013, 154–55). Ships are
 involved in multi-figure scenes as early as Middle Geometric II (800–760 BCE), although most belong to Late
 Geometric I (760–735 BCE). In the few Middle Geometric examples, such as a skyphos from Eleusis (Athens,
 National Archaeological Museum 920: Morrison and Williams 1968, 32–3 no. Geom. 38) and a krater in New
E . M A NA K I D O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                          · 305 ·




York (MMA 34.11.2: Morrison and Williams 1968, 31–2 no. Geom. 25), the warlike character of the scenes is
evident, and in addition to hoplites with shields of the Dipylon type, there are individual archers in the land
and sea combats (Moore 2000). In contrast, on Late Geometric vases, ships are depicted in considerable detail,
both in battle scenes (though not always as a naval battle between opposing ships) and in other neutral (i.e.,
non-combat) scenes in the friezes and in the space under the double handles. The latter consist of “departure
scenes”, with figures boarding the stationary ship and “sailing scenes” with rowers in action and sometimes fish
accompanying the ship – the rendering of the sea with wavy lines is very rare. Noteworthy is the quasi-realistic
depiction of the movement of the rowers and other crew members (pulling ropes, hoisting sails), the perspective
in the depiction of two rows of oarsmen and the fact that their military status is only indicated in a few cases.
Because most of the vases survive only in fragments, the figure of the helmsman has not been preserved in many
cases; he is discernible in a few examples, while in others it appears that he was not depicted.
    Regardless of the subject depicted and the different opinions about each interpretation as realistic, mythical/
epic/heroic or generalized (Haug 2012, 299: “Verhandlung männlicher Rollenbilder”), the interest and admira-
tion for shipbuilding, the use of ships and the knowledge of navigation are undeniable (Wallinga 1993, 33–41).
Ultimately, all these examples indicate the existence of various kinds of ships during the 8th century BCE (to-
gether with the know-how that this implies) and their multiple roles in the social and economic life of Athens.
    In the last quarter of the 8th century BCE, ships are central to a new and unusual iconographic theme,
that of the shipwreck. Although some elements are depicted, as in the Munich oinochoe (Antikensammlungen
8696: Hurwit 2011) –e.g., the castaways wear helmets, only one has survived on the overturned keel of the ship–
the mythological background of the scenes remains undefined (cf. the evocative, vivid description of the final
shipwreck in the Odyssey 12.286–290 and 12.409–417). Indeed, on the krater from Pithekoussai (Ischia, Museo
Archeologico di Pithecusae: Morrison and Williams 1968, 34 no. Geom. 32; Basch 1987, 187–88), the drama of
the scene is heightened by the size of the fishes and the unclear condition of survivors, though one figure is de-
picted swimming. These scenes offer for the first time a different perspective from that of the earlier Geometric
iconography, which now relates to the dangers of navigation, caused by natural phenomena or anthropogenic
factors. Thus, we have indirectly new pictorial evidence of the ever-increasing sea travel and maritime traffic of
the time. At the same time, the Homeric poem is a key source of valuable information (Od. 5.244–260 [on ship-
building], 2.212–213, 3.323 and 9.126–129 [on knowledge or lack of knowledge of navigation and sea routes]),
attesting to the nautical experiences of the first adventurous seafarers.
     In the 7th century BCE, the known depictions of ships in Protoattic pottery are impressively limited and do
not allow the identification of specific maritime scenes. Interestingly, almost all of them come from sanctuaries
and from the area of the later Athenian Agora (Basch 1987, 202–4; Haug 2012, 301–2, 307–8; Doronzio 2018,
20–1). In the two best preserved examples, ships are depicted quite concisely, mostly following the previous
Geometric tradition, as we see on the votive pinax of the Analatos Painter from Sounion (Athens, National
Archaeological Museum 14935: Morrison and Williams 1968, 73–4 no. Arch. 2; Doronzio 2018, 22; Arrington
2021, 215–16) and on the votive krater of the Checkboard Painter from the sanctuary of Heracles at Thebes
(Archaeological Museum 43360; Aravantinos 2010, 146–47). On the pinax, the presence of fully armed hoplites
with round shields refers to a warship, while on the krater the oarsmen sit in compartments and wear dotted
clothes, and an archer is seen disembarking. In both cases, the helmsman (κυβερνήτης, captain) is depicted on
a larger scale, and so are the steering oars, which are highlighted in this way. We probably have war-like scenes
on a few other vase fragments with warriors in ships. Perhaps the current rarity of similar representations is
­accidental, as shown by the finding of two Protoattic miniature louteria with ship depictions in a child’s jar
 burial (Arrington 2021, 138–39, fig. 4.30, pl. 9; Arrington et al. 2021, 245–48, figs. 11, 13). However, they cannot
 be compared with the ships depicted on the Western Greek Aristonothos’ krater (Basch 1987, 233–34, fig. 482;
 Arrington 2021, 78–80, fig. 3.16, pl. 6), dated from the second quarter of the 7th century BCE, despite certain
 “Protoattic” features of the latter, or with ships on East Greek plates (Basch 1987, 241–3; Attula 2006, 116–17,
 pls. 60–1).
· 306 ·                                        T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




            Fig. 1. Detail (ship), black-figure lebes, Exekias, Rome Villa Giulia Museo Etrusco di Villa Giulia 50599 (photo by the author).



     The depictions of ships in the 6th century BCE on Attic black-figure vases have certain common
c­ haracteristics that will be discussed below, regardless of the type of vases and the exact subject of the represen-
 tations (Morrison and Williams 1968, 84–6, 91–115; Basch 1987, 204–32; Petrakova 2013, 157–8; Münds 2017 ;
 Mackay 2022). What is also common is the setting in which they are participating, whether they are individual
 ships, pairs or groups of ships (their number ranges from four to six). They are always placed in their natural
 environment, i.e., the sea, the surface of which is indicated by continuous wavy lines that distinguish it from the
 ships, while the frequent depiction of fish, especially dolphins, completes the ideal image of the seascape. The sea
is rendered as a black mass, perfectly in keeping with the “wine-dark sea” of the written sources (οἶνοψ πόντος,
attested in the Iliad and the Odyssey; Münds 2017, 41), and is the limit to which the vase would have been filled
with wine, in order to give the impression of the ships’ swaying. Matching the unstable movement of the ships
was of course the instability of the drinker during the banquet, which increased as the drinking progressed.
    There are three main vase shapes that display ship depictions: cauldrons (lebetes), cups and volute kraters, in
order of frequency. Almost all these sympotic vessels date to the last quarter of the 6th and the first twenty years
of the 5th centuries BCE, most of them towards the end of the 6th century BCE. Only two representations of
Kleitias are earlier (BAPD 300000, 300740), with mythological themes and a scene on the shoulder of a hydria
(probably a mythological scene too: Paris, Louvre E 735: BAPD 300789), which date to the second quarter of the
6th century BCE (570/60 BCE). Sporadic ship scenes can be found on amphoras, oinochoai, column kraters, a
phiale and a plate (Münds 2017, 44; add also, BAPD 310, 2420, 5549, 9586, 10088, 9023202, 9027000).
    It so happens that the earliest known lebes with a row of ships (Fig. 1) is an inscribed vase of Exekias found at
Cerveteri, commissioned by an Epainetos to be donated to a certain Charops (or, according to another view, to
Heracles Charops, who was worshipped in Boeotia), as can be seen from the incised inscription written before
firing on the shoulder of the vase (Rome, Museo Etrusco di Villa Giulia 50599: BAPD 310402; Münds 2017, 39;
Rocco 2018). Perhaps the new iconographic scheme with the row of ships on the inside of the rim (here there
are five), as well as the glossy all-black exterior of the vase can be attributed to the inventive Exekias, which is
also true of other innovations by the same potter with regard to vase-shapes, such as the version of the type
A cup (BAPD 310403; Fritzilas, this volume), perhaps the calyx krater, as well as some iconographic themes
(Manakidou 2022).
    Almost all ships are depicted at sea, flat and elongated (νῆες μακραὶ; Morrison and Williams 1968; Morrison
1980, 14–21), with the bow and stern accentuated and often decorated with spread sails and with one or two
rows of oars (μονόκροτος, δίκροτος). Of the crew, the helmsman holding the steering oar(s) stands out and is al-
ways depicted, while the oarsmen are at best depicted as black dots and are often omitted. The oars are drawn in
a row in outline and their number varies from thirteen to twenty-four. Without aiming to be precise in ­depicting
E . M A NA K I D O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                              · 307 ·




                                  Fig. 2. Black-figure pinax, Berlin Antikenmuseum F 831 (photo by ArchaiOptix).



a particular type of ship and depending on the number of given oars, the larger ships could be penteconters
(πεντηκόντοροι) and the smaller triaconters (τριακόντοροι). From written sources, we know that these two
types were also in use in other Greek cities during the 6th century BCE (Wallinga 1993, 66–102; Spartans: Hdt.
1.152.2, 1.163.2; Phocaeans: Hdt. 1.164.3; Battus from Thera sailing to Cyrene: Hdt. 4.156.2). The same ­applies
to the trireme, which was the invention of the Corinthian shipbuilder Ameinocles (Thuc. 1.13.2–3) at the end
of the 8th century BCE, when he built four warships for Samos. In the same passage, Thucydides m  ­ entions that
the Corinthians with their fleet cleared up piracy and thus their city gained large profit as a hub of land and
sea trade, becoming very powerful. However, depictions of ships in Corinthian vases are very few and appear
mainly in some black-figure pinakes from Penteskoufia (Fig. 2) dedicated to Poseidon (Morrison and Williams
1968, 87–9; Basch 1987, 234–9; Palmieri 2009; Hasaki and Nakas 2017), at a time when the production of
­pictorial pottery at Corinth was beginning to gradually decline under the predominance of Attic painted vases.
    Herodotus mentions a lot about the naval power of Samos during the tyranny of Polycrates, and Thucydides
reports that the Ionians followed the development of the navy during the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses (Hdt.
3.39.3–4, 3.122.2; Thuc. 1.14.2 on Polycrates and Phocaeans who defeated Carthaginians in a naval battle). He
further narrates that, only shortly before the expansion of the Persians, the Sicilian tyrants and the Korkyraeans
acquired triremes (τριήρεις) in large numbers; these were the most powerful fleets in Greece before Xerxes’
campaign (Thuc. 1.14.3). The Aeginetans and the Athenians, and perhaps some other cities-states, had small
fleets, and most of their ships were equipped with fifty oars. Only later, when the Athenians clashed with the
· 308 ·                                  T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                       Fig. 3. Black-figure lebes, Manner of Antimenes Painter, Malibu, J.P. Getty Museum 92.AE.88.



Aeginetans and the danger of a Persian invasion was removed, did Themistocles persuade them to create a fleet
(Wallinga 1993, 148–64).
    Although most Attic black-figure vases depict warships (only three examples with trade ships are known),
there are no examples of triremes. Their tropis (τρόπις, the ship’s keel) ends on the bow in a ram, which is most
often in the form of a boar’s head and rarely a dolphin’s head, while apotropaic eyes may be depicted to the sides
of the prow (Carlson 2009). The rudders are visible at the stern and the aphlaston (ἄφλαστον, the upward curved
end of the stern with figure-shaped decoration) has the shape of a bird (or swan). A few representations on
cups show the ladder (or ladders) of the ship. Only one cup (by Nikosthenes potter, Paris, Louvre F 123: BAPD
301239) depicts two ships in full sail side by side. Also, in addition to the helmsmen with their steering oars,
we see the bow officer (πρωρεύς) standing behind the stem post. However, the depiction of hoplites t­ogether
with ships is rare. In one case we have the unusual scene of four naked bearded men who have folded the sail
and have tied it with red bands, while another younger man with himation stands nearby (cup Heidelberg
­University 25.8: BAPD 2178).
    Most black-figure representations on cauldrons (lebetes) and volute kraters are attributed to the Antimenes
Painter and his workshop (Fig. 3; BAPD 5166, 10090, 19547, 30701, 30975, 320144, 320211, 320212, 340494,
9025825, 9026113) and to painters of the Leagros and Golvol Groups (BAPD 579), while the cups are associ-
ated with the Leagros Group, the workshop of Nikosthenes and the Lysippides Painter (BAPD 479, 275113,
230722, 302377, 320001, 9050808). All the above date to the last quarter of the 6th century BCE, testifying
the predominance of ship depictions in friezes inside the rim of the vases and to the preference of potters and
buyers –especially from the aristocratic elite– for this iconographic theme during that period. According to
Mackay’s assumption (2022, 223–26), the increased interest in this kind of vase scenes was perhaps partly due
to Peisistratos’ nautical exploits
   A volute krater and a band cup with representations of ships (Fig. 4) are of particular interest, as they were
found together as grave gifts in a tomb in the cemetery of ancient Thera in Sellada (Thera, Archaeological
­Museum 1773, 1774: BAPD 5049, 5405; Münds 2017, 41–2, fig. 1). These two vases form a kind of “symposium
E . M A NA K I D O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                 · 309 ·




                         Fig. 4. Detail (ship), black-figure volute krater, Thera Archaeological Museum 1774 (photo by the author).




                                           Fig. 5. “Bilingual” cup, London, British Museum 1843,1103.29 (E 2).



set”, both in terms of use and iconography. Both bear the name of their owner (incised inscription: Τιμόστενος),
while on both vases the pictorial scenes reflect the interests, social status and perhaps the occupation of the de-
ceased with the sea. Among the most impressive depictions of seascapes in Attic vase-painting are those occu-
pying the interior of cups (Fig. 5), where, in addition to the frieze of ships, there is the possibility that the subject
chosen for the tondo of the cup may also have a connection with the world of the sea, such as Poseidon on a
seahorse (Paris, Louvre F 145: BAPD 4390), or the same god battling with the Giant Polybotes (see above, cup
from Thera). The tondo scene may also be related to the symposium, as in some “bilingual” cups with youths
carrying pointed amphoras (Fig. 5; London, British Museum E 2: BAPD 202287).
· 310 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                                Fig. 6. Black-figure cup, London, British Museum 1867,0508.963 (B 436).

    The best-known representation with a pirate warship (ἡμιόλια; Casson 1958) and a merchant ship (στρογγύλη
ναῦς, ὁλκάς; Morrison 1980, 51–8) is found on a late black-figure cup (London, British Museum B 436: BAPD
479). It is worth mentioning some interesting details, such as the fact that the sail of one ship is spread out and
the other is furled (Fig. 6), and that the warship has two rows of oars with different number of rowers on one
side and four sailors engaged in unfurling the sail (Basch 1987, 222–24). Also, visible under one handle is the
forward half of another ship with an eye depicted on the bow.
    Mythological scenes with ships (Fig. 7), and perhaps a few of daily life, do not appear often on Attic vases
until the late 6th century BCE (Neckamphora, Mannheim, Reiss-Engelhorn Museum CG 343: BAPD 11; Neck-
amphora Daybreak Painter, London, British Museum B 240: BAPD 5; Oinochoe Keyside Class, London, British
Museum B 508: BAPD 303254), except for the three earlier ones from before the mid-6th century BCE, which
I mentioned above. Another interesting case is the depiction of the prow as shield device (ἐπίσημα) on hoplite
shields, one of the many iconographic motifs chosen for the decoration of round shields on vases.
    In Attic vase-painting of the 5th century BCE, scenes from the world of the sea are few and far between.
A few marine creatures are depicted as secondary elements, mainly dolphins and fish (more rarely Tritons,
seahorses), designating the seascape, occasionally accompanied by chariots of astral deities flying over the sea
(BAPD 223, 13479, 206531, 212985, 213417, 213469, 361416, 43179). On red-figure vases, depictions of ships
are very rare and limited to certain mythological scenes. In these cases, usually only the bow or stern of the ship
is depicted as “part taken for the whole” (pars pro toto). The only known representation of a whole ship is on a
Late Archaic red-figure stamnos of the Siren Painter with Odysseus and the Sirens, where the sea is indicated as
a uniform mass with diluted paint (Fig. 8; London, British Museum E 440: BAPD 202628). The same rendering
of the sea is found on the other side, as three Erotes fly over it.
    On some red-figure vases the aphlaston is depicted in the hands of Athena or Nike and then it is obvious
that the maritime power and the naval victories of the city are implied. Indeed, all relevant representations
date to the second quarter of the 5th century BCE, in the aftermath of the Persian Wars (Miller 1997, 33,
39). The presence of statuary types of these two deities holding the aphlaston –sometimes also a mast and a
yardarm or Nike on a ship’s prow (Fig. 9)– on late red-figure vases (bell krater Nikias Painter: BAPD 217479)
and late ­Panathenaic ­amphoras (Williams 2007, 148–49; e.g., BAPD 303133, 303151, 303155, 303156, 303159,
303162, 303166, 303167, 9033910) indicates their association in the collective memory with successes at sea
(e.g., against the pirates in the Aegean in the years of Lycurgus’ tenure, 338–326 BCE) that were the hallmark of
Athenian state policy.
E . M A NA K I D O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                          · 311 ·




                            Fig. 7. Black-figure neck amphora, Daybreak Painter, London, British Museum 1848,0619.2 (B 240).




SHIPS AS VOTIVE OFFERINGS OF THE ATHENIANS

From literary and epigraphic sources mainly, and less so from archaeological material, we know of ship
­dedications, whole or parts of them, as well as ship models, on war or commercial successes on collective
 and individual level (Frielinghaus 2017). Small ship models, of clay, bronze or wood, are not so common vo-
 tive offerings (e.g., bronze lamp in the form of a ship from the Erechtheion, with the inscription “sacred for
 Athena”: Basch 1987, 228–30; Wachsmann 2012, 248–55), although some have been found in sanctuaries of
 various ­deities other than Poseidon (such as Hera at Samos and Perachora, Aphaia at Aegina, Apollo at Corinth,
 Pelops at Olympia and elsewhere; Frielinghaus 2017, 32–3). Offerings also include depictions of ships on votive
 pinakes, mainly painted and more rarely in relief (such as the trireme on the “Lenormant” votive relief, found
 near the Erechtheion; Athens, Acropolis Museum 1339: Morrison and Williams 1968, 170–72; Pritchard 2021,
 412–15). On the contrary, in the Hellenistic period there is more evidence and there are many depictions of
 ships, both in monumental form and on various categories of objects (statues and reliefs, coins, jewelry etc.).
   A rare offering in the Greek sanctuaries were the warships themselves, which were dedicated in the Archaic
and Classical period as “victory ships” (νικητήρια), i.e., they were keepsakes of naval victories (Frielinghaus
2017, 24). The difficulty in transporting and finding a suitable place, as well as in protecting and maintaining
these vessels, made of delicate and perishable materials, were decisive factors in the limited presence of actual
· 312 ·                                 T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                          Fig. 8. Red-figure stamnos, Siren Painter, London, British Museum 1843,1103.31 (E 440).



ships in the sanctuaries. In every respect, the keeping of a captured ship as a war booty was something very
special. We know from written sources that among the various ἀκροθίνια (ἀκροθίνιον: the topmost part of the
heap and offered to the gods, first-fruits), dedicated by the Greeks after the naval battle of Salamis, were three
Phoenician triremes as spoils and monuments of war victory (Hdt. 8.121.1; Kourta 2021, 70, 130 O12, 161 Φ55):
One ship was dedicated to the sanctuary of Poseidon at Sounion, another to Poseidon’s sanctuary at Isthmia,
and the third to the sanctuary of Ajax at Salamis. It is no coincidence that Phoenician ships were also depicted
by Polygnotus in his monumental painting of the Battle of Marathon, which was displayed in the Poikile Stoa
at the Athenian Agora (Paus. 1.15.3). On similar occasions, the Athenians after their victory in the naval battle
of Naupactus in 429 BCE, followed one year later by the Spartans for another victory, dedicated a trireme (Fig.
10) to the sanctuary of Poseidon at cape Rion, along with a trophy (Thuc. 2.84.4, 2.92.5; Kourta 2021, 70, 161
Φ56–57).
    More often, however, various parts of ships, mainly ἀκρωτήρια or ἄκρα κοσμήματα (i.e., aphlasta, akroprora)
and rams, are mentioned as the most common offerings in commemoration of a naval victory (Frielinghaus
2017, 24–5). This custom was old and quite widespread in Greece, according to written sources. Pausanias
(1.40.5) mentions that the Megarians dedicated a bronze ram to the temple of Zeus in Megara, for their victory
over the Athenians in the early 6th century BCE during the naval battle near Salamis (Kourta 2021, 161 Φ58).
Also, the Aeginetans entrusted akroteria of ships to the sanctuary of Aphaia after their naval victory over the
Samians towards the end of the 6th century BCE, as Herodotus mentions (Hdt. 3.59.3; Kourta 2021, 71 n. 451,
161 Φ59). For the Aeginetans, who led the naval battle of Salamis, Apollo himself demanded that they make a
special tribute to Delphi and they commissioned a bronze mast bearing three golden stars (Hdt. 8.122.1; Kourta
2021, 71, 131 O17, 162 Φ60).
E . M A NA K I D O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                · 313 ·




                                     Fig. 9. Panathenaic amphora, London, British Museum 1873,0820.370 (B 610).




    As we can see, it is interesting that the votive offerings for naval victories were not only dedicated to s­ anctuaries
of Poseidon, but also to sanctuaries of Zeus (mainly in Olympia), Athena (on the Athenian ­Acropolis) and Apollo
· 314 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                                       Fig. 10. Model of a trireme, Munich, Deutsches Museum.



(at Delphi). In fact, for a statue of Apollo, which was a panhellenic tribute on the ­initiative of ­Themistocles after
the victories at Artemision and Salamis, Herodotus mentions that the god held an ἀκρόπρωρον in one hand
(Hdt. 8.121.2; Kourta 2021, 35, 118 Π7, 152 Φ24) and, according to the oracle recorded by Pausanias for the
same statue (10.14.5), this must have come from a Persian ship (Kourta 2021, 151–52 Φ22).
    We know of other statues of Apollo being commissioned at Delphi for naval victories, although we have
no further information about their appearance (Kourta 2021, 35–6). This was the case for the Massaliotes re-
garding their victory in a naval battle against the Carthaginians (around the middle of the 6th century BCE),
the Peparethians for the capture of two Carian ships, apparently during the Persian wars (first quarter of the
5th century BCE, since the Carians were allies of the Persians and major ship-suppliers to the royal fleet) and
the Epidaurians, who contributed substantially with their ships to the naval battles against the Persians and to
land battles. Also, the Athenian trireme commander Lycomedes, the first to capture a Persian ship, dedicated
the ship’s “ensigns” (παράσημα), perhaps a kind of emblems, to the sanctuary of Apollo Daphnephorus at Phlya
(Plut. Them. 15.3).
    Indicative of the dedication of similar monuments from the entire city is the inscription on the stylobate in
the Stoa of the Athenians at Delphi: “Ἀθεναῖοι ἀνέθεσαν τὲν στοὰν κα̣ὶ τὰ ℎόπλ̣[α κ]αὶ τἀκροτέρια ℎελόντες
το͂ν πολε[μίο]ν” (Syll.3 29; see also Paus. 10.11.6; Kourta 2021, 116 A17, 150 Φ16, 163 E2; Fig. 11). In addition to
the stoa (Kourta 2021, 27, 75), these are spoils dedicated by the Athenians after the triumphal battle at Mykale
and the capture of Sestos (479/8 BCE); the word ὅπλα (Kourta 2021, 28, 72, 132 O18a) has been interpreted
as ropes of ships or floating bridges that Xerxes had built over Hellespont, while the word “ἀκρωτήρια” as the
figure-heads (aphlasta or akroprora) of enemy ships: “They are also dedicated the figure-heads of ships and
bronze shields” (Paus. 10.11.6, trans. W.H.S. Jones, Cambridge, Mass., 1935). Some scholars assume that the
construction of the Athenian stoa is related to the victory at the river Eurymedon (470/69 BCE, also a double
victory there, in land and sea) and that it was part of Pericles’ building program (i.e., after 456 BCE).
    Regardless of which victory we accept as the occasion for the dedication of the Stoa of the Athenians and
the discussion on the date of its erection, with this monumental tribute to the Panhellenic sanctuary at Delphi
and with the foundation of the First Delian League (478/7 BCE), Athens asserted its political power and naval
dominance in the Aegean φόβῳ ῥοθίου καὶ νεῶν δεινότητος, i.e., “through fear of the splashing oars and of the
E . M A NA K I D O U • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                         · 315 ·




                                             Fig. 11. Stoa of the Athenians at Delphi (photo by B. Werner).



awe-inspiring sight of ships bearing down” (Thuc. 4.10.5, trans. C.F. Smith, Cambridge, Mass., 1920).

Tyrrhenian Pirates and Dionysus
The Iconography of an Ancient Story of Piracy



Stamatis A. Fritzilas
Academy of Athens – Research C enter of Antiquity
sf ritzilas@academyofathens.gr




ABSTRACT

The present study examines, through selected monuments from the Archaic to the Roman era, the iconography of the
myth of the abduction of Dionysus by Tyrrhenian pirates. The Homeric Hymn to Dionysus refers to the abduction of
the god by the pirates and their punishment for this lawless act because they tried by force to keep him as their captive.
Tyrrhenian pirates, identified by modern researchers with the Etruscans who lived in Italy or the inhabitants of Lemnos,
considered him the son of a king and captured him to demand a ransom from his parents. Through a series of miracles
based on symbols of his religion, Dionysus completed the circle of his revenge by transforming the impious pirates into
dolphins. The story of the Tyrrhenian pirates allowed Greek and Roman writers and artists to present their version of
this episode. The pirate ship at sea and its crew play a central role in the pictorial renderings of the subject. By studying
this mythological episode, the plausible elements and historical ramifications are sought in relation to the phenomenon
of piracy, as it exerted a timeless effect on ancient art and religion, each time allowing imagination and faith to provide
distinct approaches to oral or visual narratives.

INTRODUCTION

The Mediterranean Sea was the first broad geographic area, where piracy took on the features of a mass
­phenomenon. As a means to acquiring material wealth and slaves, it was utilized by almost all the peoples
 that settled on its shores during antiquity: the Sea Peoples, the Tyrrhenian marauders, but also the Greeks,
 who, along with classical civilization, produced some of the most fearsome pirates in the known world. An
 ­interesting composition of reality and fiction may be observed in the myth of Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian
  pirates, which is commonly found both in ancient literature and in the pictorial arts.
    The story of Dionysus is full of journeys and peregrinations to spread his cult, and cruel treatment meted
out in irrational fury to those who opposed it, as was the case with Lycurgus, king of Thrace, Pentheus, king
of Thebes, as well as the Tyrrhenian pirates. Notwithstanding the diversity of the modern theories governing
research into myths, there is often a historical reality that triggers each myth, however abstract and fanciful its
plot may be. Therefore, it is often possible to look for chronological limits and geographical boundaries within
the evolution of the myth.
