THE TYRRHENIANS: THE ETHNIC NAME AND THEIR PLACE

The name Tyrrhenian Sea is attributed to that part of the Mediterranean, which is off the southwestern coast of
Italy and all the way to Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily. The ethnic name Tyrrhenoi (Tyrrhenians) was used by the
ancient Greeks to denote non-Greeks in general and pirate people in particular (LIMC 8:154–5, s.v. Tyrsenoi).
In ancient written sources, the term “Tyrrhenian” is found for the first time in the end of Hesiod’s Theogony:

           And Circe the daughter of Helius, Hyperion’s son, loved steadfast Odysseus and bore Agrius and Latinus
           who was faultless and strong: also she brought forth Telegonus by the will of golden Aphrodite. And they
           ruled over the famous Tyrsenians, very far off in a recess of the holy islands (Hes. Theog. 1011–1016,
           trans. H.G. Evely-White, Cambridge, Mass., 1914).

In Attic Greek, they occur as Τυῤῥηνοί (Turrhēnoi), in Ionian as Τυρσηνοί (Tursēnoi), and in the Doric dialect
as Τυρσανοί (Tursānoi) (LSJ, s.v. Τυρσηνός).
     The term Tyrrhenoi is also used in Greek to refer to the Etruscans. The ancient Greeks used the place name
 “Tyrrhenia” to denote the land of the Etruscans on the western shores of the central part of the Italian ­peninsula.
 According to Strabo (e.g., 2.1.40, 2.5.19, 2.5.29) and Ptolemaeus (Geog. 3.1.1), the term Tyrrhenian Sea was
 related only to the middle part of this broader maritime region, as opposed to its northern (Λιγυστικόν, i.e.,
 the Ligurian Sea) and southern (Σικελικόν, i.e., the Sicilian Sea) parts. The Etruscans or Tyrrhenians were an
 ancient people, who lived in a land called Etruria by the Romans or Tyrrhenia by the Greeks. They developed an
­impressive civilization of some significance, especially from the 8th century BCE onwards.




PRESENCE OF THE TYRRHENIANS IN THE AEGEAN

According to the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, which is discussed in more detail below, Tyrrhenians pirates
wanted to take Dionysus away from the Greek world and sell him to barbarians who lived either in the west or
northwest (Hyperboreans), the south (Egypt) or the east (Cyprus). In Euripides’ Cyclops (10–22), Sicily is men-
tioned as the area of operations of these marauders from Tyrrhenia (γένος Τυρσηνικὸν / λῃστῶν). The presence
of Tyrrhenians in the Aegean is also attested to by several written sources. Thucydides (4.109.4) reports that
in the old days the Tyrrhenians lived in both Athens and Lemnos. Myrsilus of Methymna, a 3rd-century BCE
author, states that the Tyrrhenians were originally from Italy, but they had migrated to the Aegean region, and
ever since that time they became known as Pelasgians (FGrHist 477 F8–9). In the 1st century CE, Dionysius
Halicarnassensis (Ant. Rom. 1.28.1–4) claimed that the Tyrrhenians were not of Pelasgian origin, but lived in
Italy instead (Kobakhidze 2008, 74–7).
     The island of Lemnos has become the focus of numerous debates and arguments ever since the discovery
of the famous inscribed stele of Kaminia in 1884, which depicts a warrior holding a spear. The stele has two
long texts incised on the front face (around the figure of the warrior) and on one of its narrower sides, written
in Greek letters but in a non-Greek language, most probably closely related to Etruscan (Lehr 1942–1945;
Di ­Cesare 2024). Herodotus considered the inhabitants of Lemnos to be Pelasgians (e.g., 4.415.2–5, 5.26.1).
The same author informs us that the Pelasgians of Mountain Hymettos, who, driven away by the Achaeans,
­settled on Lemnos, other islands of the Aegean and the shores of Asia Minor (Hdt. 6.136.2–140.2), were called
 ­Tyrrhenians (Hdt. 1.57.1–3).
    The Tyrrhenians of Lemnos, who were directly related to the Pelasgian Tyrrhenians, must have migrated to
the north Aegean region at the beginning of the 1st millennium BCE (De Simone 1996, 39–84). They rapidly
evolved into a great maritime power and are rightly credited with being the first to use the naval ram. Sources
after the 5th century BCE refer to the inhabitants of Lemnos as “Tyrrhenians”. Numerous pieces of evidence,
S . F R I T Z I L A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                      · 321 ·




combined with Thucydides’ testimony, lead to the plausible conclusion that the Tyrrhenians mentioned in the
Homeric Hymn may also include the inhabitants of Lemnos (see Greco 2010, 3–180). One cannot, however,
ignore the reputation of the Tyrrhenians of the west, i.e., the Etruscans, as pirates (Sassatelli 2004). It is not
improbable that Etruscan merchants had settled on Lemnos and occasionally engaged in piracy. From the 5th
­century BCE onwards, Lemnos was considered to be a possession of Athens; this might explain the Athenian in-
 terest in the myth of the transformation of the Tyrrhenian marauders and, possibly, hint at its Attic ­provenance
 (Chudziński 1886, 9).




TYRRHENIAN PIRACY

 Despite the great civilization of the Tyrrhenians, the ancient Greek written sources refer mainly to their intense
 pirate activity (e.g., IG II2 1629, line 223; IG XI.2 148, line 73; Syll.3 1225, line 8; Diod. Sic. 15.14.3; Strabo 5.2.2,
10.4.9; Aristid. Or. 44.570). One of the better-known Tyrrhenian pirates was Postumius, who went raiding at
the head of a flotilla of twelve pirate ships in the 4th century BCE and was captured in Sicily. Timoleon, the
­Corinthian general and politician who was sent to Sicily to rid the local Greeks of tyrants and Carthaginians,
 executed Postumius, whose raids had been playing havoc with the local sea lanes of communication:

               Timoleon himself seized and put to death Postumius the Etruscan, who had been raiding sea traffic
               with twelve corsairs, and had put in at Syracuse as a friendly city (Diod. Sic. 16.82.3, trans. C.H.
               ­Oldfather, Cambridge, Mass., 1954).

However, the Tyrrhenian pirates are mainly associated with the well-known myth of Dionysus, both in ancient
written sources and in the arts (e.g., James 1975; Paleothodoros 2012).




ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN THE
­A NCIENT WRITTEN SOURCES

The myth of the abduction of Dionysus by the Tyrrhenian pirates is mainly known from three ancient written
sources: the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus, the Metamorphoses of Ovid (3.564–691) and the Dionysiaca of Nonnus
(31.86–91, 44.231–252, 45.105–168). Brief references to the myth may also be found in Euripides (Cyc. 10–22),
Apollodorus (Bibl. 3.5.3), Hyginus (Fab. 134), Seneca (Οed. 449–466) and Philostratus the Elder (Imag. 1.19).
Oppian also mentions the transformation of men into dolphins by Dionysus (Halieutica 1.650).
   The earliest hint of the Dionysiac myth with the Tyrrhenian pirates may be traced to the Late Archaic pe-
riod. The first reference to the appearance of the Tyrrhenian pirates is in the seventh dithyramb of the Homeric
Hymns, which is dedicated to Dionysus, probably dating from the late 6th or early 5th century BCE:

               Presently there came swiftly over the sparkling sea Tyrsenian pirates on a well-decked ship — a m
                                                                                                               ­ iserable
               doom led them on. When they saw him, they made signs to one another and sprang out quickly, and
               seizing him straightway, put him on board their ship exultingly (Hymn. Hom. Bacch. 6–10, trans. H.G.
               Evely-White, Cambridge, Mass., 1914).

    According to Apollodorus, mythographer of the 2nd century BCE, when Dionysus decided to sail from
Ikaria to Naxos, with the aim of initiating the local inhabitants into his cult, he chartered a Tyrrhenian pirate
ship (Τυρρηνῶν λῃστρικὴν τριήρη) to ferry him to the island (Apollod. Bibl. 3.5.3). The Tyrrhenians accepted,
but their ulterior motive was to sell him into slavery in Asia (Romizzi 2003, 352 n. 1; Emilio-Ioannidou 2017,
· 322 ·                                             T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




Fig. 1. Ancient Etruscan kalpis attributed to The Painter of Vatican 238. Formerly in the Toledo Museum of Art (inv. no. 82.134), now repatriated to Italy (photo
                                              by M. Daniels, courtesy of the Toledo Museum of Art, January 1992).


140). When Dionysus became aware of the plot, he transformed their oars into serpents, filled the ship with ivy,
immobilized it in its wreaths, and made invisible flutes sound. The pirates lost their minds and dove into the sea,
where they were transformed into dolphins:

               And wishing to be ferried across from Ikaria to Naxos he hired a pirate ship of Tyrrhenians. But when
               they had put him on board, they sailed past Naxos and made for Asia, intending to sell him. Howbeit,
               he turned the mast and oars into snakes, and filled the vessel with ivy and the sound of flutes. And the
               pirates went mad, and leaped into the sea, and were turned into dolphins (Apollod. Bibl. 3.5.3, trans.
               J.G. Frazer, Cambridge, Mass., 1921).




 ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN THE
­A NCIENT ARTS

The most significant depiction of the myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates in south Italian vase-painting appears on
a Late Archaic black-figure Etruscan kalpis, formerly in the Toledo Museum of Art, Ohio (inv. no. 82.134) and
now repatriated to Italy (Fig. 1). It is attributed to The Painter of Vatican 238, a follower of the Μicali Painter
S . F R I T Z I L A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                             · 323 ·




Fig. 2. The so-called “Dionysus Cup” by Exekias, ca. 540/530 BCE. Attic black-figure kylix; from Vulci. München Staatliche Antikensammlungen, inv. no. 8729
                                                                   (photo by M. Kabel).


(Rassmusen and Spivey 1986, 2–8). The main subject is painted on the body: six pirates are transformed into
dolphins as they dive into the sea, which is rendered with a running counterclockwise spiral. The figure on the
left is human from the waist up, while its lower part is a dolphin’s tail. All other figures of pirates in the process of
transformation have human legs and the torso of a dolphin. This detail may be interpreted more as the depiction
of two different types of metamorphosis, one beginning at the legs, the other at the head. The figure at the far
right has its legs bent and overlapping with those of the figure to its left. All other figures have their human legs
bent at various angles, which, as modern researchers have correctly observed, may be taken as an attempt on
the part of the vase-painter to portray different snapshots of the pirates falling into the sea. An ivy stem is visible
along the left edge of the panel, possibly an indication of the presence of Dionysus. In any event, this kalpis is
the earliest illustration of the myth in Italy depicting the transformation of the Tyrrhenian pirates into dolphins
(Paleothodoros 2012, 459–60).
    The myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates, as described in the Homeric Hymn, has been associated by modern
research with the scene painted in the tondo of the kylix of Exekias in Munich, Staatliche Antikensammlungen
(inv. no. 8729), depicting Dionysus sailing the seas (ABV 146.21; BAPD 310403; Isler-Kerényi 2007, figs 104–7;
Paleothodoros 2012, 462–4, fig. 51). The god is lying within the ship, much like a symposiast, holding a cornu-
copia in his right hand, while dolphins are dancing all around (Fig. 2). Four dolphins follow along the course
of the ship, while three others move in the opposite direction. Research has shown that the Munich cup by
Exekias illustrates the myth of the Tyrrhenian pirates, since the god is clearly associated with the dolphins. This
association is further enhanced by the presence of a small white dolphin in the bow, as well as in the stern of the
ship. Images of Dionysus sailing the seas, whether accompanied by dolphins or not, also appear on other vases
painted in the late black-figure style, some of which have been commented upon in detail by Paleothodoros
(2012, 463–5).
· 324 ·                                             T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




          Figs. 3a–b. Details of the frieze from the Lysikrates choragic monument (fig. 3a: photo by G.E. Koronaios, fig. 3b: photo by G.E. Koronaios).



    The next notable representation of the Tyrrhenians pirates may be found in an Attic monument of the
second half of the 4th century BCE. We refer to the contiguous frieze in the well-known choregic monument
of Lysikrates (334 BCE), above the architrave of which there is a relief sculpture depicting the clash between
Dionysus’ retinue and the pirates who attempted to capture the god, before he turned them into dolphins (Er-
hard 1993, 10–11, figs. 1–4; Figs. 3a–b). It is the best-preserved choregic monument of antiquity, situated on the
S . F R I T Z I L A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                        · 325 ·




  Fig. 4. Young Dionysus transforming Tyrrhenian pirates into dolphins. Mosaic from a Roman villa. Bardo National Museum, Tunis (photo by DrRachT).



ancient “Street of the tripods”, and was erected in 335/334 BCE, during the archonship of Euaenetus, in order to
carry on its top the bronze tripod that would have been awarded as a prize for victory in the dramatic contest
(Ridgway 2001, 15–8, figs. 1–3).
    It may plausibly be deduced that the subject of the frieze of the choregic monument derives from a dramatic
performance, for which Lysikrates won the tripod. The story is the transformation of the men into dolphins in
the presence of Dionysus and his entourage. The artistic requirements have modified the myth to a significant
degree. The incident takes place not in a ship, but on the shore. To be sure, the vignettes differ from the myth
as presented in the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus. Dionysus is depicted on the frieze in the shape of a man, not in
that of a lion, as in the hymn. He is shown not aboard a ship, but sitting on a rock by the sea, next to a panther.
The satyrs of the thiasos celebrate over a krater of wine, when they are attacked by the unsuspecting pirates,
who expect to collect a ransom in exchange for the god. In other parts of the frieze, the satyrs react to the as-
sault. They hold down the pirates, beating them with thyrsi. A satyr brandishes a thyrsus to strike at a prostrate
marauder. Another satyr raises his arm in supplication, while a third one chases after a terrified pirate. Some
marauders have survived and jump into the sea, where they turn into dolphins, beginning with the head, while
the transformation has not yet reached their torsos and limbs. Other pirates dive into the sea, almost completely
transformed into dolphins (Erhard 1993, 16–37, pls. 1–19).
     The frieze records the Dionysiac episode on a monument that was erected on the occasion of a dramatic
contest, possibly a satyr play. The satyrs who chase the pirates punish them in various ways, tying their hands
­behind their backs as captives. They probably represent the chorus of actors sponsored by Lysikrates. Other
 landscape features, such as rocks, trees and large craters, are interspersed between the human figures, ­delineating
 the conventional boundaries between the land and the sea. Given the limited height of the frieze, one cannot
 comment upon the rendering of the Tyrrhenian pirates’ facial features and expressions. Their muscle structure
 is conveyed with very little in the way of details, in a somewhat impressionistic fashion. What we have here is a
 frieze that belongs to a choregic monument, i.e., not a public project, but an offering by a private citizen on the
 occasion of a theatrical play.
    Among Roman art works depicting Dionysus on a ship and the transformation of the pirates into dolphins,
we may mention the excellent 3rd-century CE mosaic pavement from Thugga (modern Dougga), Tunisia, pre-
served in the National Bardo Museum (Yacoub 1995, 173–4; Fig. 4). It is depicted the warship with Dionysus
and ­Tyrrhenian pirates sailing in sea. Portrayed as an adolescent, the god is accompanied by an elderly Silenus.
Two pirates, terrorized by the god, are already in the water, turning into dolphins. One is being snatched by the
foot by a leopard, which appears ready to devour him. Two small boats are on either side of the divine ship. One
of them is carrying three men, probably fishermen, and the other a couple of Cupids.
· 326 ·                                             T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




Fig. 5. Part of the Filarete Door at Saint Peter’s Basilica in Rome with the bas-relief depicting Dionysus and the pirates (photo by https://stpetersbasilica.info/
                                                               Interior/DoorFilarete/DoorFilarete.htm).


     The mosaic in question recalls a description by Philostratus the Elder (Imag. 1.19) of an ancient Greek
painting at Neapolis (Naples), which depicts a Tyrrhenian pirate vessel attacking a sacred ship of Dionysus
and his Maenads. The transformation has already begun and the god’s ship is covered in ivy and vines. The
­introduction of a naval battle motif is obviously a later invention, when the myth was incorporated into other
 tales that recounted Dionysus’ warlike mien.




ΤHE MYTH OF DIONYSUS AND THE TYRRHENIAN PIRATES IN EARLY
MODERN AND MODERN ARTS

The Dionysiac myth remained popular after the end of antiquity and up to modern times. A bas-relief depicting
Dionysus’ ship and the punishment of the pirates adorns the main bronze door of Saint Peter’s Basilica in Rome
(Suffi 1998, 26–31; Glass 2012, 549; Fig. 5); the subject is based on an episode from Ovid’s Metamorphoses of
Ovid (3.656–691). It was commissioned for the Old Basilica by Pope Eugene IV (1431–1447) and created by the
Florentine sculptor Antonio di Pietro Averlino (ca. 1400 – ca. 1469), better known as “il Filarete”. The Filarete
Door is the oldest one in the basilica. It was preserved and reused in the New Basilica in 1619. The two door
panels are made of bronze and decorated with scenes in bas-relief. The depiction of the ship carrying Dionysus
and the pirates may be found in one of the smaller bas-reliefs carved between the six main panels that are
­decorated with scenes from Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Aesop’s Fables and other subjects pertaining to the life of
 Eugene IV.
S . F R I T Z I L A S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                        · 327 ·




Fig. 6. Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian pirates. Jacob Matham, after David Vinckboons, 1616. Engraving. Amsterdam, Rijksmuseum, inv. no. RP-P-OB-102.850).



     Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian pirates form the subject of an engraving from the year 1616, now preserved
in Amsterdam (Rijksmuseum, inv. no. RP-P-OB-102.850; Matham 2007, 279, no. 284; Fig. 6). The Tyrrhenian
­pirates have been transformed into dolphins: when Bacchus turns himself into a lion and a vine stretches around
 the ship, the Tyrrhenians, panic-stricken, jump into the sea and are transformed into monstrous dolphins. The
 same subject also appears in a medieval edition of Ovid’s Metamorphoses, published by Veuve Langelier in 1619,
 which is preserved in the National Library of France in Paris.
    The transformation of Dionysus before the Tyrrhenian pirates was a subject that also inspired modern
painters and artists, as evident in the work of London-born painter and sculptor Glyn Warren Philpot, who
later became a representative of the Art Deco style. In the oil painting in question (1924), Philpot portrays the
god Dionysus, an upside-down pirate and some dolphins in the sea in the background (Fig. 7). The foregoing
brief story of the Tyrrhenians and Dionysus has provided artists throughout the ages, from the time of Homer
to the twentieth century, with the opportunity to present their own artistic version.




CONCLUDING REMARKS

The sources refer to the Tyrrhenians as violent, brutal kidnappers with a rapacious attitude. The marauders
served as the model of an impious and uncivilized nature, given the fact that their cruelty was proverbial.
Aristotle may be the earliest surviving source that refers to the infamous “Tyrrhenian torture”, the practice of
chaining rotting corpses together with live captives, face to face, limb to limb, one by one as precisely as possible
(Beatrice 2001). To those who referred indirectly to Aristotle’s passage in the Roman period, the “Tyrrhenian
torture” was a genuine Etruscan custom (Paleothodoros 2012, 470). Tyrrhenians pirates were infamous for tying
live captives to dead ones (Nonnus, Dion. 45.110). It is possible that their proverbially harsh and rigid character
became the ideal target for bringing to fruition another one of Dionysus’ divine plans, so that he may eventually
have his revenge, as he usually did with the opponents of his cult.
· 328 ·                                           T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




Fig. 7. The transformation of Dionysus before the Tyrrhenian pirates by Glyn Warren Philpot (1924). Oil on canvas. Private collection (Delaney 1999, pl. 15).



    Dionysus’ victims were transformed into dolphins, because these mammals were considered to have a lot in
common with humans. In the first half of the 5th century BCE, a fragment of Pindar refers to the human n       ­ ature
of dolphins, that loveable companion of ships, piratical or otherwise, in Mediterranean waters and beyond
(Pind. fr. 234; see also fr. 140b.13–17, 236). In Lucian’s Dialogues of the Sea Gods, intelligent dolphins are shown
conversing with Poseidon, god of the seas, and express remorse for their transgressions as they accompany
sailors or pirates in their voyages and assist them when they are shipwrecked, stating:

              Don’t be surprised, Poseidon, that we’re kind to men. We were men ourselves, before we became fishes
              (Luc. Dial. mar. 8, trans. M.D. MacLeod, Cambridge, Mass., 1961).

Between Myth, Lore and Historical Reality
Piracy in the Phournoi Archipelago, Eastern Aegean



George Koutsouf lakis
University of Thessaly
gkoutsouf lakis@uth.gr




ABSTRACT

The documentation pertaining to a considerable array of ancient, medieval and modern shipwrecks unearthed during
the recent investigations (2015–2020) conducted by the Ephorate of Maritime Antiquities in the Phournoi a­ rchipelago
has rekindled a long-standing public perception, portraying Phournoi as a historical hub for piracy. This paper delves into
the distinctive geomorphological features and coastal formations of Phournoi, elucidating the n   ­ avigational ­advantages
it a­ fforded and its association with piracy. It scrutinizes local toponyms, historical accounts and the ­archaeological
­remnants of approximately fifty shipwrecks to explore this narrative. Despite the multitude of archaeological traces left
 by the continuous maritime traffic passing Phournoi over an extended temporal span, the convergence of these investiga-
 tive methodologies reveals persisting gaps. Historical sources, toponymic evidence and archaeological discoveries exhibit
 limited chronological overlap. Furthermore, the archaeological record of shipwrecks on Phournoi predominantly suggests
 adverse weather conditions as the principal catalyst for maritime ­mishaps, rather than deliberate acts of piracy.




INTRODUCTION

In 2015, the Hellenic Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities initiated an extensive survey aimed at the
­documentation and cataloging of ancient, medieval and modern shipwrecks within the archipelago of Phournoi.
 Comprising a cluster of 20 islands, islets and rocky shoals positioned to the south of the channel separating
 Ikaria and Samos (Figs. 1–2), the Phournoi archipelago served as the focal point for this investigative endeavor.
 By the culmination of the project in 2020, the Phournoi initiative had successfully identified and documented
 over 50 shipwrecks spanning from the Archaic period through the first decades of the 20th century (Campbell
 and Koutsouflakis 2017, 2021; Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 142–225).
     Nevertheless, any scholarly assessment of these shipwrecks encounters an initial challenge rooted in a
­pervasive and somewhat stereotypical narrative prevalent among the indigenous inhabitants of Phournoi. This
 narrative posits the historical characterization of their island as a haven for pirates. Such a perception permeates
 various media channels, including websites, daily press publications, tourist guides and even scholarly articles
 and historical textbooks (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 159; Belavilas 1997, 33). Consequently, this
 ­perception has become widely accepted, ostensibly corroborated by the abundant presence of shipwrecks.
    In the ensuing discourse, I endeavor to elucidate the available historical evidence, discern Phournoi’s
­position within broader navigational networks, scrutinize the island’s coastal morphology and expound upon
 underwater archaeological discoveries.
· 332 ·                                T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                              Fig. 1. Phournoi island complex, Eastern Aegean (map by Peter Campbell).




GEOGRAPHY

In ancient sources, Phournoi, as a geographical entity, never occupied a central position in significant ­historical
events. References to them are extremely infrequent. Their landmass could not have accommodated a substantial
population, and their capacity for self-sufficiency in raw materials was constrained, contributing to an economy
characterized by its primary nature. From a political standpoint, the Phournoi archipelago ­consistently fell
within the dominion of major powers in the region, serving as a bastion for Samos and conceivably for Miletus
in earlier epochs (Haussoullier 1902; Rehm 1929; Shipley 1987, 10–12; Papalas 2002, 40–3; Viglaki Sofianou et
al. 2019, 40). Nevertheless, the strategic advantages conferred by their geographic placement were too signifi-
cant to be overlooked.
    Situated prominently along the sea route linking the northern, central and southern regions of Asia Minor,
Phournoi commanded a pivotal position (Fig. 1). The significance of this maritime thoroughfare along the ver-
tical axis of the eastern Aegean transcended the confines of local or intra-Aegean trade networks. To the south,
these navigational pathways extended along the Lycian and Cilician coastlines, stretching as far as Cyprus,
Phoenicia and Egypt. Meanwhile, their northern extension reached through the Hellespont and the Propontis
into the Black Sea (Belavilas 1997, 61–4; Tournefort 2014, 306).
     For seafarers traversing the axis along the central coast of Asia Minor, their choices were notably ­constrained.
Samos and Ikaria, islands aligned on an east-west axis, configured a sprawling land barrier, akin to a formi-
dable obstacle along this route, presenting three principal sailing alternatives (Fig. 3). The first, western route
­necessitated circumventing Cape Papas on Ikaria, exposing vessels entirely to the vagaries of the open sea
 ­between Ikaria and Mykonos. This trajectory lacked any viable harbors of refuge (Strabo 14.1.19; Georgirenes
  1677, 55–6; Tournefort 2014, 302) and lay vulnerable to the fierce winds and tumultuous waves of the Ikarian
G . KO U T S O U F L A K I S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                · 333 ·




              Fig. 2. Distribution of documented shipwrecks along the coast of Phournoi complex (Campbell and Koutsouflakis 2021, fig. 2).



Sea, renowned since antiquity for its inclement weather conditions (Tsagas 2005, 12–4). The virtual absence of
traces from ancient shipwrecks along the southern and western shores of Ikaria corroborates this reality.
   The second option, an eastern route, entailed navigating through the narrow channel flanked by Samos and
Asia Minor, necessitating a significant deviation from the ship’s trajectory. Undoubtedly, this path would have
been preferred by vessels bound for Samos, aiming to dock at Pythagorio or one of the ports in the Gulf of
Ephesus. However, under different circumstances, this route proved arduous and fraught with peril.
· 334 ·                                        T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




          Fig. 3. Sailing alternatives for navigating through the land barrier of Samos and Ikaria (Campbell and Koutsouflakis 2021, fig. 5).



     The third and final choice entailed passage through the Samos-Ikaria Strait, alternatively known as Grande
 Boughazi, Phournoi Pass, or the Great Samos Strait. This secure passage spanned approximately ten nautical
 miles, mainly dominated to the south by the fanning out twenty islands, islets and rocky outcrops of Phournoi.
 Consequently, navigating past the Phournoi islands emerged as virtually obligatory for ships traversing the
 vertical axis of the eastern Aegean (Belavilas 1997, 70; Campbell and Koutsouflakis 2021, 285–88). The heavy
 maritime traffic along this route over time finds corroboration in certain Ottoman cartographic works, such as
 the Piri Reis’ book of navigation (Kitȃb-I Bahriye) and its late 17th century versions (Özükan 2013, 53; W
                                                                                                          ­ alters
Art Museum, manuscript W658.82B; Fig. 6). However, the significance of increased maritime activity would be
­inconsequential if not for the distinctive morphological features characterizing these islands.
     The cross-shaped configuration of the three principal islands (Phournoi, Thymena, Ayios Minas) inherently
ensured the presence of expansive leeward shores along the coastline (Fig. 2). Vessels could readily identify these
leeward aspects of Phournoi and approach the shoreline for anchorage and overnight stays with ease. More-
over, to enhance safety and security further, the Phournoi shoreline featured a succession of deep and shallow
bays oriented diversely, offering optimal conditions for ship anchorage: relatively shallow waters, sandy seabeds
and accessible shores conducive to risk-free coastal approach. Consequently, upon approaching the Phournoi
island complex from the open sea, ships enjoyed multiple avenues for secure berthing and anchorage from any
­direction, notwithstanding prevailing winds. This endowed Phournoi not only with the status of a routine over-
 night stop, but also positioned it as an exceptional sanctuary in the event of sudden adverse weather conditions.
 In case of shifting wind patterns during their stay on the island, alternative leeward coastlines ­remained readily
 accessible within short distances (Fig. 4). The strategic advantages conferred by the complex’s morphology did
 not elude the notice of ancient mariners and the political powers operating in the vicinity.
    In subsequent epochs of Aegean history, as the administrative and functional unity of the Greek island
realm waned, fragmenting into smaller institutional and geographical entities, Phournoi likely found them-
selves situated beyond the spheres of influence, enjoying a status of autonomy akin to unclaimed territory –a
“no man’s land”– occupying an ambiguous interstice forming between the borders of neighboring powers. The
absence of overarching hegemony in the region precipitated the infiltration of smaller, transient powers active
in the Aegean into this political and geographical lacuna. In such instances, occasional denizens of the island
or itinerant groups from other Aegean islands capitalized on the morphological advantages of the complex in a
G . KO U T S O U F L A K I S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                              · 335 ·




Fig. 4. Coast formation of main island Phournoi (foreground), island of Kisiria (middle) and Thymena (background). Far in the background is Ikaria
                                                           (Viglaki et al. 2019, fig. 229).



distinctly alternative manner: by temporarily or semi-permanently establishing operational bases on Phournoi
and engaging in the ancient practice of piracy.
    The activities of pirates, operating independently for personal gain and devoid of the protection or sanction
of specific political authorities, have been documented across the broader maritime expanse of Phournoi since
the late Hellenistic era. The geomorphological attributes of the landscape, once conducive to navigation and
trade traffic, assumed a divergent purpose. Elevated vantage points transitioned into signaling stations, con-
cealed hinterlands behind promontories became sites for ambush and assault, the deep coves along the coastline
evolved into havens of refuge and concealment, and the open sea surrounding the archipelago transformed
into a theater of pursuit and plunder. These geographic conditions are universally recognized as pivotal factors
conducive to piracy (Semple 1916, 141). Concurrently, the narrow channels within the heart of the complex
served as escape routes in the event of an unforeseen turn of events. A recurring geographical feature was the
proliferation of small harbors and concealed alcoves serving as lairs for pirate fleets, with numerous promonto-
ries doubling as lookout posts and bastions. Utilizing swift, nimble rowing vessels, the temporary occupants of
the islands could menace any merchant ship within reach following brief pursuit.
      The distinctive topography of Phournoi consistently favored those acquainted with it and adept at ­exploiting
its unique attributes to their advantage (Belavilas 1997, 63). Pursued vessels could seek refuge in the expan-
sive dead-end bay of Chrysomilia or navigate the narrow channels flanking Kisiria island, thereby risking
­entrapment and capture. In instances when large sailing vessels were deployed to safeguard trade routes or
 ­undertake clearance operations, the shallow-drafted pirate craft could elude pursuit through these narrow
  straits. The constrained and shallow passages between the main island of Phournoi, Kisiria and Thymena served
  as escape conduits, dissuading larger vessels from navigating through them due to the perils of rocky shoals or
  grounding. This afforded pirate factions the essential time needed to evade capture and vanish into the plethora
  of blind spots the landscape afforded.
· 336 ·                              T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



TOPONYMS

The ancient name of modern Phournoi Korseon is evidenced by ancient Greek sources, which have ­documented
variations such as Korseai, Korsiai, Korsia, Korsoi, Kroussai and Korassiai nẽsoi (Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 27–
31). The etymology of the name remains elusive, although Korassiai bears a striking resemblance to ­korasion,
meaning “maiden” or “daughter”, purportedly due to the islands being endowed as dowry to the daughters
of Samos, son of Agaios, the inaugural king of Samos. Roman writers transcribed the name as Cursie, while
early cartographers depicted it as Crusiae (Buondelmonti, Lupazzolo), Hursit (Piri Reis), Crusia (Benedetto
Bordone, Anonymous of Lucca, Mercator, Piacenza, Blaeu), Cursie (Ortelius) and Cursia (Agnese). These
variations, undoubtedly linked to the ancient name of Phournoi, often coexist with variants of the name
“Phournoi”. ­Conversely, from the 18th century onwards, variants of the name “Phournoi” appear to prevail
among ­cartographers.
    The Latin transliteration of the ancient Greek name and its variants closely resemble the byzantine term for the
act of plunder (koursos/kourson), attested as early as the 8th century (Sophocles 1888, s.v. κοῦρσον 687; ­Kriaras
1982, s.v. κούρσο(ν), κούρσος) and correlate with derivatives of the Italian term corsario, loosely ­translated as
“one who has a license to raid” (letter de course), derived from Medieval Latin term cursarius (­“pirate”, from
Latin cursus; Heinz 2007, s.v. cursarius, cursus). The pronounced similarity between the ­numerous versions of
the ancient name of Phournoi and the various terms for loot and corsair in Latin languages and medieval Greek
has fostered a conjectural association in popular consciousness, often leading to the belief that the islands derive
their name from pirate activity. This somewhat arbitrary popular perception, however, does not preclude the
historical possibility that the archipelago of Phournoi was indeed a hub of intense pirate activity in the past.
     A series of coastal toponyms documented on maps or utilized in the modern vernacular of Phournoi
are probably the living remnants of pirate activity in the past: Kourniachto (a place for hiding or lurking),
­Kleftolimano (harbor of thieves), Fygou (escape), Fylakio (guard-post), Vardia (shift or guard), Tourkolimnionas
 (harbor of the Turks), Pano and Kato Maneta (upper and lower Maneta). Many of these names are common-
 place along the Aegean coastline and are also encountered on other islands historically associated with piracy.
 However, the two bays designated as Pano and Kato Maneta, situated roughly in the middle of the eastern coast
 of the main island of Phournoi, warrant further comment.
    It is highly probable that these two bays derived their names from the Zakynthian corsair Eustathios ­(Stathis)
Romanos or Manetas, who, between 1678 and 1684, operated as a pirate in the Aegean Sea while based in Melos,
commanding the only Greek privately owned corsair vessel at the time, most probably handed to him after the
death of its former owner, the Maltese corsair Hugues Creviliers (Krantonelli 1994, 289–91). Early records of
his exploits date back to 1683, when the rector of Tenos reported that Stathis Romanos Manetas had seized the
Venetian consul in Paros, extorting a monopoly over the supply of galette to Venetian fleet vessels. In May 1684,
Admiral Gerolamo Cornaro courted him on behalf of the Venetians, granting him a free pass permit (salvo-
condotto). Manetas subsequently conducted operations across the Aegean, Ionian and southern Adriatic, either
independently or in collaboration with the Venetians and the Knights of Malta (Krantonelli 1991, 300). At
the onset of the 6th Venetian-Turkish war (1684–1699), Morosini appointed him commander of the V         ­ enetian
cruiser flotilla, where he actively participated in the sieges of Lefkada and Preveza (Sathas 1869, 312–19; Donos
2007, 74–85, 101). Subsequently, he assisted the Venetian admiral in levying taxes on Aegean islands and aiding
in the siege of Chalkis (1688). Manetas resurfaced again in September 1694 in Chios, aiding Venetians and
Knights of Malta in temporarily occupying the island (Papadopoulos 1964, 187). During a naval skirmish near
Chios in 1695, Manetas seized a saika carrying the military treasury of the Turkish fleet, earning him the title of
colonel (Krantonelli 1991, 88, 133, 300–3, 372–73).
    No published documentation or official records indicate that Manetas ever conducted operations within
the island complex of Phournoi, although there is some evidence that he left Astypalaia in July 1682 en route to
Ikaria, to meet Capitan Bianco and set an ambush on ships from Barbary Coast (Krantonelli 1994, 291). Apart
from that, his sole documented involvement in naval activities in the broader area is recorded in the vicinity
G . KO U T S O U F L A K I S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                           · 337 ·




of Chios. However, Aegean folk legends may have preserved aspects of his activities that historical accounts
have overlooked. Manetas is etched into the popular consciousness due to his tumultuous personal life. Legend
has it that he married the beautiful Marioga in Melos, leaving her under the care of the island’s bishop when
he embarked on a pirate expedition. Marioga, steadfastly refusing the bishop’s advances, was falsely accused of
infidelity to Manetas. Subsequently, Manetas captured her and executed her at his place of business. This tragic
episode forms the central theme of “Manetas’ rhyme”, a popular Aegean folk song known in various renditions
today (Legrand 1874, 296–300; Spyridakis and Petropoulos 1962, 375–78; Poulianos 1964, 121–24). While each
version features adaptations of hero names and locales, the Ikarian rendition places Manetas’s attempt “in the
straits of Samos” (stes Samos ta boghazia), with his wife’s murder purportedly occurring there. Accordingly,
local traditions suggest that the murder took place either in Ikaria or Phournoi, specifically in the bays of Pano
and Kato Maneta. Nonetheless, whether Stathis Romanos Manetas utilized Phournoi as a base and secure an-
chorage during his operations in the Chios area in 1694 and 1695 remains a conjecture. Offspring of Manetas
continued the family tradition, engaging in acts of piracy for the most part of the first half of the 18th century
(Krantonelli 1998, 35–8, 168–69).




HISTORICAL EVIDENCE

Ancient and medieval sources provide scant information regarding piracy in the Phournoi archipelago. In
modern historiography, these islands are often depicted as geographical extensions of ancient Miletus initially,
later transitioning to Samos, possibly as part of an effort to establish an island defense enclosure, acquire naval
bases for overseas trade and extend naval dominance (Papalas 2002, 40–5). The “thalassocracy” of Samos’s
tyrant, Polycrates, exhibited characteristics of aggressive expansionism, as described by Diodorus Siculus
(10.16.1), who noted that Polycrates “by sending triremes to the most opportune places, plundered all those who
sailed”. Phournoi likely served as an overseas base for such naval operations, supported by clear evidence of
Samian guards stationed there until the Hellenistic period (Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 51–7), a fact corrobo-
rated for the island of Ikaria as well.
    One of the most renowned episodes of piracy in the ancient world occurred a few miles south-east of
Phournoi, in ancient Pharmakoussa (modern Pharmakonissi), involving the capture of Julius Caesar by Lycian
pirates during his voyage to Rhodes in 74 BCE (Ward 1975; Günther 1999; Osgood 2010). This incident is
recounted by various ancient writers, including Suetonius (Iul. 4), Plutarch (Caes. 1.4–2.4), Polyaenus (Strat.
8.23), Velleius Paterculus (2.41.3) and Valerius Maximus (6.9.15), with Velleius Paterculus providing the most
reliable testimony, written around 30 CE. Julius Caesar’s captivity occurred within a complex political context, a
year preceding the outbreak of the third Mithridatic War (73–63 BCE) and Mark Antony’s (Creticus) campaign
in Crete (72 BCE), during which pirates from Cilicia and Pamphylia expanded their activities across the Eastern
and Central Mediterranean. According to Plutarch:

              “This [the pirates’] power extended its operations over the whole of our Sea, making it unnavigable and
              closed to all commerce. This was what most of all inclined the Romans, who were hard put to it to get
              provisions and expected a great scarcity, to send out Pompey with a commission to take the sea away
              from the pirates” (Pomp. 25.1, trans. B. Perrin, Cambridge, Mass., 1917).

     The accounts provided by Suetonius, Plutarch and Velleius suggest that the pirate band responsible for
c­ apturing Julius Caesar were essentially opportunistic brigands with ships, owing no particular allegiance and
 driven solely by the prospect of immediate material gain. Such groups of stateless outlaws, acting independently
 and lurking in insignificant islands with the hope of a lucrative catch, were likely common during the turbulent
 late 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE, or during any period of maritime anarchy. The Phournoi complex, with its
 advantageous physical terrain, would likely have been no exception to this phenomenon.
· 338 ·                              T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



   Rome responded to the piracy threat by enacting the Gabinian Law in 67 BCE, granting extraordinary
powers to the outgoing consul Gnaeus Pompey to eradicate piracy throughout the Mediterranean. Pompey’s
campaign, meticulously planned and brief, relied heavily on diplomacy rather than outright armed conflict and
proved highly effective.
     Unlike Pharmakoussa, which gained notoriety due to a prominent incident, Phournoi never attracted
­significant attention from ancient historians. To uncover tangible evidence of pirate activity in Phournoi, one
 must turn to the late Byzantine and post-Byzantine periods.
   The earliest account mentioning Phournoi as an ambush site for Turkish pirates targeting merchant vessels
comes from the Florentine monk Cristoforo Buondelmonti in the early 15th century, who was shipwrecked
on the island and endured five days without food before being rescued by a passing ship (Buondelmonti 1897,
109–10 no. 55). Buondelmonti also noted the favorable anchorages provided by Phournoi, where ships could
seek shelter at night to avoid strong winds. However, he observed the island as deserted and abandoned by its
inhabitants. Apparently, its use by Turkish pirates was seasonal, a pattern recurring over the centuries.
    Historical records indicate that during the latter half of the 15th century, the Genoese administration
­ rchestrated a mass relocation of the population of Samos to Chios, primarily due to piracy thriving in neigh-
o
boring islands and Phournoi (Hasluck 1910–1911, 169; Melas 1957, 158–59). Ottoman admiral Piri Reis also
depicted a similar scene of desolation at the beginning of the 16th century (Bülent 2002, 157). The abandon-
ment described by Buondelmonti and Piri Reis seemingly rendered Phournoi an ideal refuge for various bands
of pirates to regroup and distribute their plunder.
     In the summer of 1602, the Spanish pirate Alonso de Contreras sought refuge on the deserted islands
of Phournoi with his Maltese frigate and companions, following a series of successful operations in Serifos,
­Astypalaia, Amorgos and Patmos, intending to regroup and divide their spoils. However, they were compelled
 to abandon the islands when two galleys under Suleiman of Catania, then Bey of Chios, appeared, forcing de
 Contreras to flee via Ikaria and Mykonos (Durant 1975, 146–56; Krantonelli 1991, 107–9, 333; de Contreras
 1994, 97–102).
    The involvement of corsairs from the Order of the Knights of St. John of Malta and other Christian forces in
the Archipelago of Phournoi is corroborated by the description of Ikaria by Joseph Georgirenes, the archbishop
of Samos and Ikaria, published in London in 1677, reflecting his experiences in the early 1670s (Georgirenes
1677, 3–4, 55; Papalas 2002, 258–67). Georgirenes notes the uninhabited islets of Phournoi, located three miles
south of the coast of Ikaria, boasting natural harbors capable of accommodating various vessels. He further
mentions that at other times, corsairs from Malta and other Christian factions would lie in wait on these islands,
ambushing ships trading between Chios and Rhodes.
    The daily routine of these corsair groups is vividly described by the English captive Mr. Roberts, who was
shipwrecked in Ios in 1692 and subsequently captured by pirates, forced to serve as a gunner on their ship.
­According to Roberts, the corsairs would spend the winter in Paros, Antiparos, Melos and Ios until early March.
 They would then relocate to Phournoi, where they would lie in wait from early spring to mid-summer, with
 lookouts stationed in the mountains overlooking the Samos-Ikaria strait, keeping watch for passing ships. They
 would also venture into the southern part of Ikaria, Gaidouronisi and Leipsoi, before moving further south to
 posts in Asia Minor, spanning from Cilicia to Cyprus. In autumn, they would return to the Aegean to sell their
 plunder and deliver profits to their backers in Livorno, Malta or Marseille (Hacke 1699; Ormerod 1924, 17–8;
 Krantonelli 1991, 89–93; Simopoulos 1994, 106).
    This cyclic movement of ambush, aligned with the routes of convoys between Alexandria and C   ­ onstantinople
or guided by intelligence from captured vessels, was undoubtedly a prevalent method of piracy during this era.
Similar tactics were employed by Jacopo Inghirami, the admiral of the Duchy of Tuscany, who amassed ­significant
riches in the early 17th century under the banner of the Order of the Knights of St. ­Stephen. ­Inghirami’s activi-
ties in the maritime regions of Ikaria, Phournoi and Samos between 1602 and 1617 are ­extensively ­documented,
causing considerable disruption to Turkish trade (Krantonelli 1991, 149–51, 158–63, 177–85). In 1621, French
G . KO U T S O U F L A K I S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                  · 339 ·




diplomat Louis Deshayes, Baron de Courmemin, reported from neighboring Samos that its few inhabitants,
lacking the protection of a castle, were left vulnerable to pirate invasions originating from Phournoi (Deshayes
1624, 315–21).
     From the 15th century onward, Phournoi remained virtually uninhabited according to almost all post-­
Byzantine sources. This assertion is supported by the absence of settlement remains on the island from this
period, with the oldest standing houses in Phournoi dating back to the mid-19th century. The initial attempt
to repopulate Phournoi is believed to have commenced around 1770, when the monk Nimphon (Nikolaos
­Nikolaras) departed from Patmos and, along with other monks, constructed the chapel of Evangelistria at
 ­Koumara. However, due to the persistent threat of pirate raids, he relocated to Ikaria, where in 1775 he oversaw
  the construction of the monastery of Evaggelistria in Mounde (Stamatiadis 1893, 82; Viglaki-Sofianou et al.
  2019, 74–5). Phournoi remained sparsely inhabited, with the population reaching only 120 families towards the
  end of the 19th century (Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 77).
    Reports of piracy based in Phournoi persisted well into the 19th century. E.D. Clarke, a traveler who visited
the islands in the early 19th century, affirmed that even during his time, a significant number of pirates lurked
in Phournoi and the neighboring island of Ikaria (Clarke 1814, 185; Tsagas 2003, 91–2). Disorder in the waters
around Phournoi persisted long after the widespread suppression of piracy by the newly formed Greek state.
In 1856, any act of raid (course) was declared illegal by law, and the Turkish administration of Rhodes granted
­English and French ships full freedom of action to eliminate the remaining pockets of piracy in the Eastern
 Aegean and the Ikarian Sea (Dimitrakopoulos 1977, 184; Pamphilis 1980, 141–42; Bakirtzis 2007, 230).
    Nineteenth-century historians and local press accounts from Samos extensively documented the activities
of Emmanuel (Manos) Mytikas, a native of Patmos, who lived and operated in Phournoi, and is often regarded
as the last pirate of the Aegean (Kritikidis 1869, 117–18; Stamatiadis 1893, 39; Viglaki-Sofianou et al. 2019, 76).
Mytikas was characterized as a robber (ληστής) or criminal (κακούργος), but the methods he employed, such
as traversing from island to island in a makeshift boat and engaging in robbery and murder, align closely with
the operations of a small-scale pirate. Upon his capture and subsequent trial in Samos in 1861, he was found
guilty of 48 murders and sentenced to death. The execution took place in Marathokampos on February 19, 1863,
following approval from the Sultan in Istanbul (Bakirtzis 2007, 319).




ARCHAEOLOGICAL FINDS

Regarding archaeological finds, during the ongoing archaeological research of Phournoi (2015 onwards),
no tangible archaeological evidence directly linked to piracy has been uncovered. While the presence of a
­significant number of shipwrecks along the coast could suggest heightened maritime activity, it is also attributed
 to extensive exploration of the seabed. Among the 50 identified shipwrecks, 48 were discovered to be laden with
 cargo, reducing the likelihood of piracy-related incidents. The causes of sinking, to the extent that they can be
 determined, predominantly stem from adverse weather conditions.
    Furthermore, the chronological distribution of shipwrecks in Phournoi reveals a notable scarcity of finds
from the period historically associated with piracy activity, beginning from the 15th century onwards (Fig. 5).
This discrepancy, however, should not be surprising. Shipwrecks identified during underwater surveys are pri-
marily recognized by the visual imprint they leave on the seabed. Consequently, amphorae cargoes comprise the
majority of the wrecks discovered in Phournoi, as is common in Mediterranean underwater surveys. Galleys,
smaller rowboats or sailing ships that did not transport ceramic cargo present far greater challenges in terms of
detection, as their visual traces on the seabed are considerably less distinct. Smaller-scale piracy activities, akin
to those documented in the 1553 voyage of French doctor and botanist Pierre Belon in the Aegean, are highly
unlikely to leave identifiable archaeological remnants (Simopoulos, 1994, 391–92; Braudel 2002, 605).
· 340 ·                                     T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                                                   Period                                                  Shipwrecks
             Archaic                                         (700–480 BCE)                                           3
             Classical                                       (480–323 BCE)                                           3
             Hellenistic                                      (323–31 BCE)                                       10
             Roman                                     (31 BCE–4th century CE)                                   11
             Late Roman                             (4th century–7th century CE)                                 21
             Byzantine                             (7th century–15th century CE)                                     3
             Post-Byzantine                        (15th century–20th century CE)                                    4
             Unknown                                                                                                 3

                           Fig. 5. Diagram of chronological distribution of documented shipwrecks around Phournoi.




     However, both the chronological and geographical distribution of shipwrecks in Phournoi can provide
­insights into the utilization of the seascape from antiquity to the steam age. The distribution of shipwrecks
 around Phournoi exhibits non-uniformity (Fig. 2). The highest concentration of shipwrecks is observed on the
 northeastern coast of the central island of the complex (the homonymous to the complex island of Phournoi)
 and on the northern coast of the island of Ayios Minas. Conversely, the northern and more exposed coasts of
 Phournoi show a lack of wrecks. Similarly, another cluster of wrecks is located on the westernmost island of the
 complex, along the northern coast of Thymena. This pattern suggests that vessels passing through the archi-
 pelago of Phournoi tend to navigate around rather than through the central area of the complex. Additionally,
 variations in cargo size are discernible. The cargoes identified around the island of Kisiria, situated between
 Phournoi and Thymena, indicate the transit of exclusively small vessels, whereas all larger cargoes are situated
 on the perimeter of the complex. It is evident that large ships avoided passage through unsafe narrow straits.
    The circumnavigation along the eastern coastline of Phournoi appears to have been the primary option for
ships traversing the Ikaria-Samos channel, a choice that seems to be corroborated by the Ottoman portolan of
the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore (Fig. 6). The existence of a small settlement dating back to Late Roman
times beneath the modern village of Kamari, which provided access to water supply, along with the safe an-
choring conditions offered by the continuous bays to the south, may be linked to this preference. Evidence
suggests that this settlement persisted through Byzantine times, with a large collection of abandoned anchors
discovered in the sea area in front of it, dating mainly to the late Byzantine and the Ottoman era.
    Isolated finds, primarily ceramics, on the seafloor of Phournoi indicate the ongoing utilization of certain lee-
ward bays, where no shipwrecks were found. Substantial quantities of discarded material were documented in
the bays of Vlychada at the southernmost cape of Phournoi, as well as in the bays of Kariotika and ­Vathylakas on
the northern side of Thymena. Notably, small size stone cannonballs are frequently found on the western shores
of the island of Ayios Minas, particularly in Kambi Bay, some of which have been recovered and are currently
housed in the Town Hall of Phournoi. Recently, a bronze arquebus dating to the 16th century was snagged by
a trawler in deep waters between Ikaria and Phournoi (Fig. 7). The fisherman who retrieved it turned it over to
the Port Police of Ayios Kyrikos in Ikaria, speculating that it might originate from a shipwreck.
     An isolated shipwreck (no. 23), sunk in front of the modern settlement of Bali in Phournoi, may be linked
to piratical activity, although the evidence it provides is somewhat limited. It comprises the hull of an ­elongated
ship discovered near the coast at a depth of 36 meters (Fig. 8). The wreck was found devoid of all cargo and
­nautical equipment, with an unusually large quantity of large-sized rough stones found inside the hull. This
 quantity exceeds the typical ballast expected for a ship of its size. The wreck was dated to the early 19th
 ­century, primarily based on the discovery of a glass inkpot, the sole identifiable object found within the hull.
G . KO U T S O U F L A K I S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                                                          · 341 ·




Fig. 6. Sea traffic along the Phournoi channel, according to a late 17th century version of Piri Reis’ book of navigation (Kitȃb-I Bahriye; Walters Art Museum,
                                                                     manuscript W658.82B)




The evidence suggests a deliberate sinking of the ship, possibly following its capture and looting, to erase any
trace of the incident, a common practice in the Aegean noted by travelers like Choiseul-Gouffier (Simopoulos
1999, 378). This timeframe aligns with accounts of pirate activity in the Phournoi archipelago as documented by
traveler E.D. Clarke (1814, 185). However, these hypotheses require validation through further archaeological
investigation of the shipwreck.
· 342 ·                                         T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                 Fig. 7. 16th century arquebus raised from the deep by a trawler between Ikaria and Phournoi (photo by the author).




           Fig. 8. Photomosaic of shipwreck no. 23 sunk in front of the modern settlement of Bali in Phournoi (Viglaki et al. 2019, fig. 285).




CONCLUSION

The comprehensive evaluation of all available testimony regarding piracy in the Phournoi archipelago suggests
that archaeological findings align with historical accounts only to a certain extent. Underwater investigations of
Phournoi indicate that the island complex served as a vital waypoint and intermediate step-stone for maritime
traffic in the eastern Aegean. Throughout various historical periods, sailors recognized and utilized the strategic
advantages offered by Phournoi’s location and geomorphology.
    Piracy, however, presents challenges in archaeological identification on the seabed. The traces left by pirate
activity often resemble those of regular merchant shipping, complicating the interpretation of archaeological
data. Consequently, distinguishing between the two can be ambiguous and the archaeological record alone may
not definitively confirm instances of piracy.
   Furthermore, terrestrial archaeological research on the island is still in its early stages, particularly ­concerning
remains from the second millennium CE. As investigations expand to encompass terrestrial ­settlement remains,
there may be opportunities to establish clearer connections between archaeological evidence and historical
accounts.

Searching for Traces of Corsair Activity in the Aegean during
Early Modern Times
From Historical Accounts to Archaeological Remains



George Koutzakiotis
National Hellenic Research Foundation – Institute of Historical Research
geokoutz@eie.gr




ABSTRACT

The pirate phenomenon in the Aegean –and generally in the Mediterranean– is inscribed in the longue durée and formed
an economic activity that was not always illegal. Nevertheless, the difficulty to detect its traces is a commonplace among
historians and archaeologists. This paper attempts to respond to this challenge by focusing on the period of the extended
Venetian-Ottoman wars of the 17th century (1645–1669, 1684–1699). During this period, the pirate phenomenon, in its
corsair version, was manifested with particular intensity in the Aegean and was normalized. The normalcy with which
corsairing was vested is fragmentarily attested in various types of contemporary sources, and still echoes to this day in the
collective memory of islanders and the microtoponymy of the Archipelago. These testimonies, though few in number, show
that various monuments and architectural remains in the island complexes of the Aegean are or could be linked with the
needs of the corsairs to defend themselves, guard their captives, heal their bodies and strive for the salvation of their souls.




INTRODUCTION

In the Mediterranean, the pirate phenomenon –which is “as old as history”, as F. Braudel writes (1973, 866)– is
an economic activity of island and coastal populations, tantamount to the banditry practiced by the inhabitants
of mountainous areas. In any case, the proximity of the islands to the mountains of the mainland allowed for
a switching of roles. The example of the bandits of Olympus, who also acted as pirates in the wider area of the
Northern Sporades, is fairly well known (Vasdravellis 1970). After all, pirate activity was not confined to the sea
and attacks on ships, but also developed in coastal areas, where settlements were assaulted by marauders and
people were captured on the coast.
    Despite its brutality, this activity was not always illegal. In early modern times, corsairing was lawful, at
least insofar as the corsairs respected the terms of their license (patente). In any case, however, the success of
pirate or corsair operations, which depended on their ability to surprise their victims, required the same level
of planning and organization as any other economic activity, all the more so since the attacks were carried out
using ships as the main modus operandi, which in turn required regular maintenance and purveyance. The
cost of ­maintaining a ship and buying supplies could be covered by the sale of the spoils (ships, goods and also
people), thus creating a cycle of activities that replicated the pirate phenomenon. Therefore, it was the needs
of the ship that, first and foremost, determined the schedule of pirate or corsair operations and dictated their
· 346 ·                               T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4



interruption from time to time. During that cessation of activity, pirates and corsairs would come ashore and
certain ­anchorages would then become their safe havens and bases of operation.
    Based on the above, is it possible for one to detect traces of the pirate phenomenon on land? We will attempt
to answer this question by focusing on the period of the extended Venetian-Ottoman wars of the 17th century
(1645–1669, 1684–1699). In doing so, we will not concentrate on traces of material destruction related to the
pirate phenomenon, which is a commonplace concern among both historians and archaeologists. Instead, we
will focus on traces of material construction on land that could be associated with corsair activity.




THE MEDITERRANEAN CORSO

In the early modern period, and especially in the 17th century, a particular form of corsairing had developed
in the Mediterranean with endemic characteristics, which was not only manifested in times of war but also
in times of peace. This was the corso, a term coined by M. Fontenay (2010, 212–14, 341–42), waged by both
­Catholic Christians and Muslims of North Africa in the context of an alleged “war against the Infidels”. These
 obtained licenses to practice the corso from their respective rulers in exchange for a portion of their loot. In
 essence, this was an organized economic operation under a religious pretext, securely backed by investors with
 access to the authorities, from whence they secured their licenses. For this reason, those who obtained such per-
 mits had at their disposal means (ships, equipment, capital) that contemporary pirates could not even fathom.
 In addition to the “private” corso, there was also the “public” or “state” corso, which was practiced by the fleets
 of Malta, Tuscany and the Regencies of North Africa (Fontenay 1997, 211–12; Calafat and Kaiser 2016). This
 paper will concentrate on the former manifestation of the pirate phenomenon and, more specifically, we will
 examine the activity of “private” Catholic corsairs, who mainly operated and sojourned for extended periods of
 time in the Aegean (Fontenay 2010, 228–31, 357–406). As observed by S. Bono (1993, 54–71), several facets of
 the ­activity of “private” Catholic corsairs remain unknown.




THE ANNUAL CYCLE OF CATHOLIC CORSO

Various sources of the last three decades of the 17th century inform us that the activity of Catholic corsairs in the
Eastern Mediterranean followed an annual cycle, which was imposed by weather conditions and, ­consequently,
by the schedule of the Ottoman fleet. The fleet of Kapudan Pasha sailed in the Aegean to collect taxes from the
islands only when the weather was favorable, between the feast of Saint George and the feast of Saint Demetrius
(Hidrellez and Kasim respectively in Islam). More specifically, the corsairs acted as follows:
    During the winter months, from mid-December until March or, according to another source (Deloffre and
Rougeot 1976, 233), until the end of April, they retreated to islands of the southern Aegean, where no Otto-
mans resided, mainly Melos, Kimolos, Paros, Antiparos, Ios and Astypalaia (Fig. 1). In the spring, the cor-
sairs boarded their ships and headed eastwards to Phournoi and their environs, between Ikaria, Agathonisi
and Leipsoi, where, until the first summer months, they would ambush ships following the Asia Minor route,
namely those that sailed through the passage between the Dodecanese and the Asia Minor coast that connected
the ports of Syria-Palestine and Alexandria with Smyrna and Constantinople. Around the middle of July, they
sailed along the coast of Cyprus and, as soon as they received the slightest news about the presence of Algerian
or Ottoman vessels in Rhodes, they would head for the coasts of Alexandria and Damietta, where the shallow
waters would prevent these vessels from approaching. Around the end of the summer, the corsairs would ap-
proach the Syrian coast, where they could disembark their ships and go ashore in feluccas, capturing people in
and releasing them for ransom. In the autumn, they would return to the Aegean, where they would continue
their operations until the advent of winter (ANF, A.E. BI 862, f. 75v; Magni 1679, 292–95; Hacke 1699, 8–9).
G . KO U T Z A K I O T I S • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4                                                        · 347 ·




                                       Fig. 1. South Aegean, with all the mentioned islands (map by the author).




MAINTENANCE OF THE PIRATE AND CORSAIR SHIPS

As already pointed out, pirate and corsair operations were interrupted from time to time to cater for the
­maintenance and supply needs of the ships. The success of the operations, after all, heavily depended on the
 speed of sailing, which could only be ensured by regular maintenance of the keel, scraping it clean from marine
 organisms and coating it with a mixture of grease and tar. These particular jobs, namely careening and graving,
 were carried out at least twice a year. Another job that took place at regular but less frequent intervals was
 caulking, namely the sealing of the hull with a tar-soaked oakum.
    In order to complete all these maintenance operations, the ship had to be disarmed in a suitable cove (Jal
1848, 388–89, 423, 655–56; Jurien de La Gravière 1885, 219–20; Fennis 1995, 454, 491–92, 849–50). In the case
of pirates and corsairs, the cove in question had to fulfill a number of conditions in order to be considered
suitable. First, it had to allow the ship to approach the shore as far as possible; then, it had to be secluded, and,
finally, it had to provide opportunities for defense during the works, which we shall discuss below. The German
scholar Johann Michael Wansleben, who traveled in the Ottoman territories in the 1670s, notes in one of his
manuscripts that the corsairs graved their ships during the winter months in Astypalaia and Ios, while in June
and July in Porto Chevalier (Fethiye or Şövalye Adası) and one other anchorage on the coast of Lycia (BNF, MS
NAF 4193, f. 195v).1 Other sources, however, attest that the corsairs maintained their ships on Ios, Melos (­ Gazette
1668, 650, 660; Argenti 1954, 152) and evidently on other islands even during the summer months. I­ n­deed, a
text containing comments on maps of the Archipelago informs us that sometimes the corsairs careened their
ships at Arkioi (ANF, Marine, 3JJ 221, no. 4), in the wider area of which, as we have already ­mentioned, they lay
in wait to ambush passing ships from spring until early summer.


1 I am grateful to my colleague Alastair Hamilton for pointing out this unpublished note by J.M. Wansleben.
· 348 ·                                    T H E A R C HA E O L O G Y O F P I R AC Y I N A N T I Q U I T Y • AU R A S U P P L E M E N T 1 4




                               Fig. 2. Astypalaia island, with all the mentioned toponyms (map by the author).



    In Astypalaia, French portolans of the same period specify that the corsairs maintained their ships in the bay
of Agrelidi and on the islets of Ligno and Chondro, otherwise known as Diaporia, on the bay of Maltezana (Fig.
2). Ligno was also called Espalmador or Despalmador by Western Europeans, a name derived from the verb “es-
palmar”/“despalmar”, which in the nautical lingua franca meant “to grave”. Other data has led me to hypothesize
that the bay of Vathy played a similar role (Koutzakiotis 2023).
    On Ios, the corsairs are attested to grave their ships in the bay of Chora, called Gialos (Gazette 1668; Argenti
1954, 143, 152), while in the gulf of Melos, as is explicitly mentioned in various sources, they performed this
task exclusively in the bay of Patrikia, which was used for the same reason by non-corsair ships later on (Fig.
3; ANF, Marine, 2JJ 44, no. 2; ANF, Marine, 3JJ 219, no. 8, 49; ANF, Marine, 3JJ 221, no. 2; BNF, MS FR 14682,
7–8; Hacke 1699, 25–6).
    As regards Paros, the Englishman Anthony Roberts, who was captured in 1692 by members of a corsair
crew, on whose ship he would serve for several months until his escape, informs us that the corsairs wintered in
the bay of Ayios Ioannis Detis but, more than that, they would stop by the bay two or three times a year (Hacke
1699, 47; Fig. 4). Also, according to Roberts, when the corsairs were careening their ships in the spacious gulf
of Naoussa, they would anchor “under a small Isle at the Head of the Bay” (Hacke 1699, 46–7), a location which
should be identified with the bay of Ayioi Anargyroi opposite the islet of Galiatsos, which is still mentioned
today as the former site of the shipyard of Naoussa.2

Paros, for this piece of information.
